research.question: Why is California the #1 out-of-state buyer state on every island, and why the Bay Area and Los Angeles specifically?
research.answer: California leads on every island mainly because it is by far the biggest state in the western US, and the West as a whole buys Hawaiʻi homes at about five times the rate of the rest of the country. Californians are not unusually eager buyers. Title Guaranty counted 1,271 California buyers in 2025. That is 38.4% of the 3,314 out-of-state US buyers and 4.6 times runner-up Washington. In Jan–Jun 2026 the count was 552 (37.0%). DBEDT's 2008–2015 analysis put California at 38.6% of mainland purchases, so the share has hardly moved in 17 years. Per million residents, California (32 buyers) buys at the same rate as Washington (35), Nevada (41), Oregon (31) and Utah (30), and about five times the rate of Texas (5.5) or Florida (6.8). Three things make the West different. It is close: SFO and LAX are 2,400–2,550 miles from Honolulu, against 3,800 from Dallas and 5,000 from New York. It is only 2–3 hours behind. And it has dense nonstop service: California airports scheduled 57.5% of domestic nonstop seats to Hawaiʻi in July 2026 and 53.5% in October, rising to 64–67% into Kona and Līhuʻe. Those links feed a large, loyal visitor base. California sent 2.80 million arrivals in 2025, 37.7% of all US visitors on domestic flights. Only 18% were first-timers, and the average visitor had made 7.2 trips. California's share of buyers is almost exactly its share of visitors, and it turns about 0.45 of every 1,000 visitors into buyers, the same rate as other western states. Wealth explains how much Californians spend more than how many buy. California files 16.8% of US tax returns over $1M against 11.6% of all returns. Its buyers paid an average $1.50M in 2025, against $0.82M for Hawaiʻi buyers. On the neighbor islands the gap is wider: 2.0 times on Maui, 2.8 times on Kauaʻi and 3.6 times on the Big Island. With 7.5% of sales, California buyers brought 12.3% of all purchase dollars. The Bay Area and Los Angeles–Orange County lead because they are the two largest visitor sources (842K and 829K in 2025) and the two largest air gateways. Together they account for 77% of the Oʻahu homes owned by California individuals. Per resident, the Bay Area counts about twice as much as LA: 127 vs 65 visitors per 1,000 residents, and about 466 vs 239 Oʻahu homes per million. That matches its income advantage. In 2022 the average adjusted gross income per tax return (AGI) was $199K–$233K in San Francisco, San Mateo and Santa Clara, against $98K in LA, and net capital gains were $30–35K per return against $8K. Seattle shows the same pattern at half the scale. Family ties add a steady base, especially on Oʻahu, where California buyers pay close to local prices. California is the #1 origin and the #1 destination for households moving to and from Hawaiʻi, and 95,165 Native Hawaiians lived there in 2020. Remote work sped things up in 2020–22: the average income of Bay Area households moving in reached $189K, and net Bay Area arrivals tripled. It is not the cause, because California's share was the same before and after. Taxes do not explain it either. Hawaiʻi's top rate (11%, rising to 13% above $500K single or $1M joint from 2027) is close to California's 13.3%. Most California buyers keep California residency, and only 1.6% of the households that left California in 2022–23 chose Hawaiʻi. I am highly confident in the counts and rates. The split between closeness, air service and visitor familiarity is less certain (medium), because all three move together.

drivers.driver: Size plus western location: California is the largest state in the high-buying West (the core reason it ranks #1)
drivers.quantified_effect: Per million residents, 2025 buyers: CA 32.3, WA 34.7, NV 40.8, OR 31.1, UT 29.7, CO 22.6, AZ 11.1, FL 6.8, TX 5.5. At the average WA/NV/OR/UT rate (~34 per million), California would have had ~1,340 buyers (actual 1,271). At the Texas/Florida rate (~6 per million) it would have had ~240. Being in the West is worth about a 5x multiplier, and California's 39.4M population does the rest. There is no extra California-only premium in buyer counts.

drivers.driver: Visitor familiarity: Californians make up the biggest group of visitors, and repeat visitors become buyers
drivers.quantified_effect: California's share of out-of-state buyers (38.4%) almost equals its share of US visitors (37.7%). Its conversion rate (0.45 buyers per 1,000 visitor arrivals) matches WA 0.39, OR 0.41, CO 0.44, UT 0.46 and AZ 0.46. The volume of visitors, not a higher conversion rate, produces the lead. This is a correlation: distance and income drive both visiting and buying.

drivers.driver: Nonstop air access: California airports supply most domestic seats, especially to the neighbor islands
drivers.quantified_effect: California's seat share (54–58% of domestic seats) is well above its visitor and buyer shares (~38%), because California hubs also carry travelers connecting from other states. Seat share does not line up with buyer share island by island: Oahu has the lowest California seat share (54%) but the highest California share of out-of-state buyers (43%). Air access makes owning a Hawaii second home easy, but it does not scale buyer counts proportionally.

drivers.driver: Wealth and home equity: explains how much Californians spend, and part of the Bay Area's lead
drivers.quantified_effect: California buyers paid 1.8 times the Hawaii-buyer average statewide in 2025, and 2.0–3.6 times on the neighbor islands. With 7.5% of sales they brought 12.3% of dollars, and 23–26% of all purchase dollars on Kauai and the Big Island. Wealth raises spending more than buyer counts: per capita, California's count matches poorer western states. The home-equity edge has narrowed since 2019 (FHFA: SF-San Mateo +14% vs Honolulu +47%).

drivers.quantified_effect: A 9 a.m. Pacific meeting is 6-7 a.m. in Hawaii, while 9 a.m. Eastern is 3-4 a.m. This helps Pacific-time remote workers and part-year residents. Its effect cannot be measured separately from distance and air service, which favor the same states.

drivers.driver: Taxes: not a meaningful driver (California 13.3% vs Hawaii 11%, rising to 13% from 2027)
drivers.quantified_effect: For the typical California second-home buyer the state income-tax effect is about zero, because they remain California taxpayers. Only 6% of mainland-owned Oahu parcels carry a homeowner exemption. For relocating high earners, the 2027 top-rate gap shrinks to 0.3 points (13.3% vs 13%). Hawaii's 7.25% capital-gains cap vs California's up to 13.3% is the one material difference, and California can still tax income earned there (our read). Californians who move for tax reasons go to Texas, Arizona and Nevada, not Hawaii.

counter_evidence: California is not exceptional per resident or per visitor. Nevada (40.8 buyers per million) and Washington (34.7) beat California (32.3) statewide. Alaska buys 74.6 per million on the Big Island. Florida (0.96) and Nevada (0.84) convert more visitors into buyers than California (0.45). Any explanation that relies on something unique to California (taxes, tech) over-explains the count.

Air seats over-predict. California airports carry 54-58% of domestic seats but California buyers are about 38% of out-of-state buyers, because California hubs also carry connecting travelers. Island by island the two do not line up: Oahu has the lowest California seat share (54%) but the highest California share of out-of-state buyers (43%).

Measurement: Title Guaranty classifies buyers by the home address on the deed. Trusts, LLCs, management companies and Hawaii residents using mainland mailing addresses can land in the 'California' count. Title Guaranty publishes only the top 10 states and no metro detail, so the Bay Area vs LA comparison relies on owner rolls (homes owned, not recent purchases) and visitor data, not on buyer records. Example: in Maui's roll, LA ZIP 90067 has 317 parcels at 16 addresses (289 at addresses with 10+ parcels), almost certainly institutional.

Data anomaly: Title Guaranty's 2024 Hilo district lists 232 California buyers for $35.0M (average $151K), against 29 in 2025, with no cause given. Excluding it, California's 2024 share of out-of-state buyers drops from 45.6% to about 42.0%. Year-over-year declines from 2024 are overstated.

California's lead is narrowing. California buyers fell from 639 (H1 2025) to 552 (H1 2026, -14%) while Washington rose from 150 to 175. On Maui, Washington (38) nearly matched California (55) in H1 2026. California visitor arrivals are down 12% since 2022 while Colorado, Oregon and Washington grew.

The 'cheap Hawaii' price story is weaker than often assumed. California's statewide median listing price ($725K) about equals Hawaii's ($732K). Kauai's Kapaa median ($1.51M) is higher than San Jose's ($1.39M). Since 2019Q4, SF-San Mateo prices rose only 14% vs 47% in Honolulu and 62% in Kahului, so Bay Area home equity now buys less Hawaii housing than in 2019.

Military relocation: San Diego County is the #1 county source of households moving to Oahu (819 in 2021-22, IRS), consistent with Navy transfers. Some California-address buyers on Oahu may be service members, which fits their near-local average price. Not quantifiable from public data. Military domicile choices likely also inflate Texas and Florida (Texas had 12.1% of mainland house purchases in 2008-15).
Remote work and the 2027 tax change are recent. California's share was the same (38.6%) in 2008-15, before either existed, so neither can explain a ranking that has been stable for 17 years.
Visitor volume and buying share common causes (distance, income, air service). The visitor-to-buyer link here is a correlation, not proof that visiting causes buying.
research.for_brokers: Treat California as two markets. Neighbor-island second homes: California buyers paid $1.6-2.8M on average in 2025-26, against $0.5-1.1M for local buyers, and brought about a quarter of all purchase dollars on Kauai (23%) and the Big Island (26%). Market resort and luxury listings in the Bay Area (Peninsula and Silicon Valley ZIPs such as 94010, 95014, 94404, 94539) and coastal LA-OC (Palos Verdes, South Bay, Newport), where the owner rolls show the clusters. Oahu: California buyers pay close to local prices ($1.03M vs $0.87M). That demand comes from relocation, family, military and condo investors, so build referral ties with South Bay/Torrance, Daly City and San Diego relocation and VA lenders. Use the visitor funnel: 82% of US West visitors are repeat visitors, and Californians average 7.2 trips. Partner with resort, timeshare and vacation-rental managers, and stress the 5-hour nonstop flight and the 2-3 hour time gap to remote workers. Watch for softening. California arrivals are down 12% since 2022, California buyers fell 14% in H1 2026, and Washington nearly matched California on Maui. Bay Area home equity has lost ground against Hawaii prices since 2019 (+14% vs +47%). Add Seattle, Portland, Denver and Salt Lake City to every campaign. The 2027 13% bracket will not move second-home buyers, who stay California taxpayers. For relocating clients, lead with lifestyle, not tax, and send them to a CPA on Hawaii's 7.25% capital-gains cap. For listings: about 8,700 Oahu residential parcels owned by California individuals and about 9,400 Maui County parcels are mailed to California. Bay Area and LA-OC owners are the largest pool of likely off-island sellers as HOA, insurance and Residential A costs rise.
research.for_locals: California demand is steady and structural. It has been about 38% of mainland buyers since at least 2008, so it will not disappear with a tax change or a rate cycle. On the neighbor islands it lands mostly at the top: California buyers pay 2-3.6 times what local buyers pay. They compete less for entry-level homes than for coastal and resort homes and land, but they still take scarce housing out of local use. Few mainland-owned homes are primary residences (6% of mainland-owned Oahu parcels carry the homeowner exemption), and about one in six Maui and Kauai homes is held for seasonal use. On Oahu, California buyers are only 5-6% of purchases and pay near-local prices, and some are returning family: California is home to 95,165 Native Hawaiians and is the #1 place Hawaii households move to and from. Policies aimed at second homes (Honolulu's Residential A tiers, Maui's Bill 9 phase-out of apartment-zoned vacation rentals) mostly reach California owners. The 2027 13% income bracket mainly affects Hawaii's own top earners, not California second-home buyers. California's pull is easing slightly (fewer California visitors, flat Bay Area prices since 2019), which modestly reduces outside competition. For local families, mortgage rates above 7% still matter far more for affordability than who the out-of-state buyers are.

challenge.question: Why is California the #1 out-of-state buyer state on every island, and why the Bay Area and Los Angeles specifically?

verdicts.driver: Size plus western location: California is the largest state in the high-buying West (the core reason it ranks #1)
verdicts.reason: Re-checked against the local Title Guaranty extract (new/tg.json) and FRED Vintage-2025 populations (https://fred.stlouisfed.org/series/CAPOP, accessed 2026-10-08). California is #1 out-of-state on all four island panels in 2024, 2025, Q1 2026 and H1 2026. 2025 counts: CA 1,271 of 3,314 other-US buyers (38.4%), WA 278. Per million residents in 2025: CA 32.3, WA 34.7, NV 40.8, OR 31.1, UT 29.7, CO 22.6, AZ 11.1, FL 6.8, TX 5.5. The result holds in 2024: CA 44.0 (38.1 without the Hilo anomaly), WA 42.3, NV 44.0, OR 26.3, TX 5.5, FL 4.8. The DBEDT 2008-2015 report confirms CA bought 37.7% of mainland-bought houses and 39.2% of condos (https://files.hawaii.gov/dbedt/economic/data_reports/homesale/Home%20Sales%20in%20Hawaii%20to%20Mainland%20Buyers%20by%20Property%20Type.pdf, 2016). Recomputed great-circle distances match (SFO 2,396 mi, LAX 2,553, SEA 2,677, DFW 3,778, JFK 4,975). The 41 states outside the top 10 had at most 838 buyers among roughly 213M people, about 4 per million or less, so a '5x' gap is if anything conservative. This is a decomposition, not a mechanism: 'western location' stands in for distance, flight time and ties.
fact_errors: The distance evidence cites 49 CFR 71.12 (the time-zone rule) as its source. The distances are correct but come from airport coordinates, not that regulation.

'The West' is too broad. Arizona (11.1 per million) and Colorado (22.6) are western but buy at one-third to two-thirds of California's rate. The high-rate group is the Pacific Coast states plus Nevada and Utah (and Alaska, at 74.6 per million on the Big Island alone).

'Share has hardly moved in 17 years' rests on two endpoints: 2008-15 pooled (38.6%) and 2024-26. Title Guaranty state counts for 2016-2023 are not in hand. Recent years range from 37.0% (H1 2026) to 45.6% (2024; about 42% without the Hilo anomaly).
Washington overtook California per resident in H1 2026: about 44 vs 28 per million, annualized and subject to seasonality.
verdicts.corrected_wording: California ranks #1 mainly because it is by far the most populous state within about 2,400-2,700 miles of Hawaii. Per resident it buys at about the same rate as Washington, Nevada, Oregon and Utah (30-41 per million in 2025, 26-44 in 2024) and 5-6 times the rate of Texas or Florida. Farther western states such as Arizona and Colorado buy at one-third to two-thirds of the California rate. There is no California-only premium in buyer counts.

verdicts.driver: Visitor familiarity: Californians make up the biggest group of visitors, and repeat visitors become buyers
verdicts.reason: Every number re-checked against the DBEDT 2025 Annual Visitor Research workbook (https://files.hawaii.gov/dbedt/economic/tourism/annual-reports/2025-annual-visitor.xlsx, published 2026). Table 19: CA 2,795,276 arrivals, 37.7% of 7,415,500. Table 20: CA 18.3% first-timers, 7.2 trips. Table 15: US West 82.4% repeaters, 11.9% stayed with friends or relatives, 10.7% came to visit friends or relatives. California's visitor share has been 37.8-41.1% every year from 2013 to 2025 except 2020, close to its buyer share. The data cannot show that visiting causes buying. (1) Conversion is not stable. Florida visitors are 46% first-timers yet convert at 0.96 buyers per 1,000 arrivals, twice CA's 0.45. Within California, Oahu-owner counts per 1,000 metro visitors are about 3.9 for the Bay Area and 3.7 for LA-OC but about 1.0 for the Inland Empire. Income, not familiarity, sets conversion. (2) Reverse causation, our interpretation: out-of-state owners' trips to their own Hawaii homes count as visitor arrivals, so ownership also produces repeat visits. (3) Common causes such as distance, income and air service drive both.
fact_errors: 'The California visitor base is shrinking' depends on 2022 as the base year, a pandemic-era peak (3,177,044). Against 2019 (2,637,893), California arrivals were up 6.0% in 2025. That is slower than WA (+13.0%), OR (+14.0%), NV (+24.0%) and CO (+49.2%), so California's share fell from 39.5% (2019) to 37.7% (2025).
The 2024 conversion rate was higher for CA (0.60 per 1,000; about 0.52 without Hilo) than for WA (0.49) or OR (0.40). 'Same rate as other western states' holds for 2025 only.
verdicts.corrected_wording: California sends about 38% of US visitors, and its buyer share matches that, so the visitor pipeline carries California demand. But visiting does not explain buying on its own. Conversion to ownership varies about fourfold within California by income, Florida converts at twice California's rate, and owners' own trips inflate the repeat-visitor counts. Treat visitor volume as a channel and a correlate, not an independent cause.

verdicts.driver: Nonstop air access: California airports supply most domestic seats, especially to the neighbor islands
verdicts.reason: Recomputed from the HVCB Air Service Grid PDFs, both as of 2026-06-16 (July: https://assets.simpleviewinc.com/simpleview/image/upload/v1/clients/hawaii/07_Air_Service_Grid_July_2026_as_of_06_16_26_9dba7bde-158f-4ce3-bbeb-fd30b8758fe7.pdf; October: https://assets.simpleviewinc.com/simpleview/image/upload/v1/clients/hawaii/10_Air_Service_Grid_October_2026_as_of_06_16_26_64ced702-ad79-478e-be3d-bd799c881838.pdf). All figures match. July: 9 CA airports 604,426 of 1,050,314 domestic seats (57.5%); HNL 53.8%, OGG 58.5%, KOA 63.8%, LIH 67.2%; LA basin 292,835, Bay Area 218,142, SAN 56,838, SMF 36,611. October: 467,876 of 874,457 (53.5%). Two limits. First, seats are largely endogenous: airlines schedule capacity where demand is, so seat share partly restates California demand. Second, island seat shares do not predict island buyer shares. Maui has the lowest California buyer share in all three periods (40.0%, 33.9%, 30.7%) despite a mid-range 58.5% seat share. Within California, the Inland Empire has nonstop ONT-HNL service (10,943 seats in July) yet owns Oahu homes at about 44 per million residents, against 239 for LA-OC.
fact_errors: 'Oahu has the lowest California seat share but the highest California share of out-of-state buyers (43%)' is true only for 2025. In 2024, Kauai (49.6%) and Hawaii Island (46.9%) were above Oahu (45.1%). In H1 2026, Kauai (45.9%) was above Oahu (39.8%).
The grids are preliminary schedules as of June 16, 2026, not flown seats.
verdicts.corrected_wording: Dense nonstop service from California makes a Hawaii second home easy to use. But it mostly follows California demand rather than creating it, and island-level seat shares do not track island-level buyer shares. Treat air access as an enabler (moderate); distance is the part that is truly fixed.

verdicts.driver: Wealth and home equity: explains how much Californians spend, and part of the Bay Area's lead
verdicts.reason: The spending numbers hold (Title Guaranty Q4 2025: CA average $1.495M vs HI $0.819M; Oahu $1.03M vs $0.87M; Hawaii Island $1.74M vs $0.49M; Maui County $2.21M vs $1.09M; Kauai $2.75M vs $0.99M; CA $1.9B of $15.5B = 12.3% of dollars on 7.5% of sales). IRS SOI 2023 confirms CA filed 132,720 returns with AGI of $1M or more (https://www.irs.gov/pub/irs-soi/23in55cmcsv.csv, 2025). IRS 2022 county AGI per return confirmed: San Mateo $232.8K, Santa Clara $213.1K, San Francisco $199.3K, King $161.4K, Los Angeles $97.5K, Honolulu $87.5K; net capital gains $35.2K, $30.1K, $31.4K, $18.2K, $7.8K and $4.8K (https://www.irs.gov/pub/irs-soi/22incyallagi.csv). FHFA and Realtor.com figures re-pulled from FRED and confirmed. The claim that wealth drives spending more than counts fails inside California. Oahu individual owners per million residents (Honolulu roll, 2026-10-05, approximate ZIP3 metro mapping): Bay Area 466, San Diego 243, LA-OC 239, Sacramento 149, Inland Empire 44. Inland Empire AGI per return is $67-73K (Riverside $73.0K, San Bernardino $67.1K) and its residents have the same distance and nonstop service. Across states, wealth alone does not produce buyers. $1M+ returns per 1,000 returns: FL 6.5, WA 6.2, NV 5.4, TX 5.1, OR 3.1. Florida and Texas buy at about one-fifth the Washington and Nevada rate, while Oregon, with the fewest high earners, buys at California's rate. Distance limits which wealthy households are in range, and within that range wealth decides how many buy as well as how much they spend.
fact_errors: CA's share of $1M+ returns is 16.6% of the IRS US total (132,720 of 799,320). The 16.8% figure uses the sum of states as the denominator.

'The home-equity edge has narrowed since 2019' uses the weakest Bay Area division (SF-San Mateo +14%). FHFA 2019Q4-2026Q2: San Jose +35%, Oakland-Berkeley +22%, LA +50%, Anaheim-Santa Ana-Irvine +63%, vs Honolulu +47% and Kahului +62% (FRED ATNHPIUS series, accessed 2026-10-08). The edge narrowed for SF, San Jose and Oakland owners but not for LA-OC.
verdicts.corrected_wording: Wealth works together with distance. Across states, nearness decides who is in range: wealthy Florida and Texas buy little. Within reach, income strongly drives both how many buy and how much they spend. Inside California, Oahu ownership per resident is about ten times higher in the Bay Area than in the Inland Empire, and California buyers pay 2-3.6 times local prices on the neighbor islands. Since 2019, Bay Area home equity has lost ground to Hawaii prices; LA-OC equity has not.

verdicts.driver: Why the Bay Area and Los Angeles specifically: the two biggest visitor and air pipelines, with Bay Area wealth doubling its per-capita weight
verdicts.reason: DBEDT 2025 Table 21 confirmed: LA-Long Beach-Anaheim 829,276 arrivals (64.6 per 1,000); SF-Oakland-Fremont 626,588 (135.3); San Jose 215,671 (108.7); Seattle 460,243 (110.6). Honolulu roll individual owners confirmed: Bay Area 3,641, LA-OC 3,064, Seattle 1,355, all CA 8,681 of 19,302 (45.0%); Bay plus LA = 77.2% of CA owners against about 52% of CA's population. Maui roll confirmed: CA 9,421 (42.4%), Bay Area 3,610, LA-OC 3,413. IRS corridors confirmed: Bay Area average AGI $108K per in-moving household, net +3,473; LA-OC $71K, net +3,248. The direction holds, with caveats. (1) The two Bay Areas are defined differently: the visitor figure (842K) covers only the SF and San Jose MSAs, while the owner figure uses ZIP3 940-951 plus 954, roughly 5-6 MSAs and 7.8M people. (2) Counting all parcels, LA-OC (5,086) leads the Bay Area (4,610) on Oahu. LA's lead in absolute ownership disappears only after dropping addresses holding 10 or more parcels; 15.2% of LA-OC's out-of-state parcels sit at such addresses, against 5.7% for the Bay Area. (3) DBEDT metro estimates swing sharply year to year (San Jose -16%, Sacramento -25% from 2024 to 2025). (4) Owner rolls measure existing homes, not recent buyers, and Title Guaranty publishes no metro data.
fact_errors: The visitor and owner figures use different Bay Area boundaries (2 MSAs vs about 5-6).
Calling the Bay Area the larger owner base holds only for individual owners. Counting all parcels on Oahu, LA-OC is larger.
verdicts.corrected_wording: The Bay Area and LA-Orange County lead because they are the two largest pools of nearby high-income households and the two largest air gateways. In absolute terms they are about tied: depending on whether institutional addresses are counted, either can lead on Oahu, and they are near-equal on Maui. Per resident, the Bay Area visits and owns about twice as much as LA-OC, in line with roughly 1.5-2.4 times the income per tax return. Seattle shows the same pattern at a smaller scale.

verdicts.driver: Family and diaspora ties: California is Hawaii's main two-way migration partner
verdicts.reason: Confirmed: IRS state flows 2011-12 to 2022-23, CA to HI 69,260 households and HI to CA 62,990. California is the #1 origin and #1 destination state. DBEDT Data Book Table 1.37 shows 95,165 Native Hawaiians (alone or in combination) in California in 2020, and 362,893 of 680,442 (53.3%) living outside Hawaii (https://files.hawaii.gov/dbedt/economic/databook/2022update/013723.pdf, 2023). This explains volume but not California's rank beyond its size. Per 1,000 residents (2020 populations, FRED), Native Hawaiians number 2.4 in CA, against 8.5 in NV, 4.0 in WA, 3.6 in OR and 3.6 in UT. Across the nine top buyer states, that ranking matches 2025 buyers per million closely (Spearman 0.92). Ties may help explain why Nevada and Washington out-buy California per resident, but diaspora is itself shaped by distance. The 'Asian-American suburb ZIPs' point is untested. The near-local Oahu price (1.18x) fits family, relocation or military buyers but does not single out family.
fact_errors: '9 of the top 30 owner ZIPs are Asian-American suburbs' is an untested interpretation, not data, and should not be cited as evidence of family ties.
verdicts.corrected_wording: California is Hawaii's largest two-way migration partner and home to about 95,000 Native Hawaiians, which adds a steady base of family, returning-resident and relocation buyers, mostly on Oahu. Per resident, though, California's diaspora is thinner than Nevada's, Washington's, Oregon's or Utah's. Ties help explain volume and those states' slightly higher rates, not California's #1 rank. The effect cannot be separated from distance.

verdicts.driver: Remote work: a 2020-22 accelerant concentrated in the Bay Area, not the reason for the ranking
verdicts.reason: The conclusion that remote work does not explain the rank stands, because California led in 2008-15. Census CB22-155 (2022-09-15, https://www.census.gov/newsroom/press-releases/2022/people-working-from-home.html) confirms SF-Oakland-Berkeley and San Jose had about 35% home-based workers in 2021 vs 17.9% nationally. Mainland purchases rose from 3,225 (2020) to 5,806 (2021) (Data Book 2025). The quantified Bay Area evidence is overstated. (1) The IRS 2019-20 pair compares addresses on returns filed in 2019 and 2020, so most of those moves predate the pandemic. Bay Area in-mover AGI was already rising before ($99K, $120K and $113K in 2016-19). (2) The 'tripled' net gain is about half driven by fewer Hawaii-to-Bay Area moves: inflows rose 31-51% (958 to 1,252, 1,442 and 1,272) while outflows fell (763 to 582, 572 and 707). (3) California's share of buyers in 2020-23 is not observed, so 'same share before and after' does not test the pandemic years.
fact_errors: 'Net Bay Area arrivals tripled' is driven about equally by fewer Hawaii households moving to the Bay Area; gross Bay Area inflows rose only about 30-50%.
Counting the 2019-20 IRS pair as remote-work years mislabels mostly pre-pandemic moves.
verdicts.corrected_wording: Remote work lifted mainland buying in 2021-22 (+80% statewide in 2021) and pulled richer Bay Area households to Hawaii (average AGI about $188-189K in 2020-22). Gross Bay Area inflows rose about a third to a half while moves the other way fell, and both had normalized by 2022-23. California led well before remote work existed, so remote work is not why it ranks first.

verdicts.driver: Time zone: 2-3 hours from California vs 5-6 from the East Coast
verdicts.reason: Hawaii is on UTC-10 all year with no daylight saving time, 2-3 hours behind Pacific and 5-6 behind Eastern. As the researcher says, its effect cannot be separated from distance and air service, which favor the same states. The weak rating is appropriate.
verdicts.corrected_wording: A minor convenience for Pacific-time remote workers and part-year residents. It cannot be measured separately from distance.

verdicts.driver: Taxes: not a meaningful driver (California 13.3% vs Hawaii 11%, rising to 13% from 2027)
verdicts.reason: Verified from primary texts. Act 24 SLH 2026 (SB3125 CD2, signed 2026-05-21, https://data.capitol.hawaii.gov/sessions/session2026/bills/GM1124_.PDF) sets 13% over $500K single, $750K head of household and $1M joint for tax years after 2026, with 11% on $325K-$500K single and $650K-$1M joint. The California FTB 2025 schedule (https://www.ftb.ca.gov/forms/2025/2025-540-tax-rate-schedules.pdf) has single rates of 10.3% up to $445,771, 11.3% up to $742,953 and 12.3% above, plus the 1% surcharge over $1M. So from 2027, a single filer earning roughly $325K-$1M faces a higher marginal rate in Hawaii than in California. That is the opposite of a tax pull. IRS 2022-23 outflows confirm Hawaii received 5,598 of 353,260 departing CA households (1.58%, rank 17) (https://www.irs.gov/pub/irs-soi/stateoutflow2223.csv). Per destination resident, that flow is similar to Oregon's or Arizona's, so the rank reflects Hawaii's small size, not tax avoidance. Hawaii's 7.25% capital-gains cap is confirmed in 2026 bill text. HB1850 and SB2587, which proposed 9%, show no record of enactment as of 2026-10-08.
fact_errors: The 6% 'homeowner exemption' share of mainland-owned Oahu parcels is the share with any land or building exemption (6.3%). The roll does not separate exemption types.
'Californians who move for tax reasons go to Texas, Arizona and Nevada' is an interpretation. The IRS data show destinations, not motives.
verdicts.corrected_wording: Taxes do not explain California's lead. Most California buyers keep California residency. From 2027, Hawaii will tax high earners at about the same or higher marginal rates than California across most of the $325K-$1M range. The one real difference, Hawaii's 7.25% cap on capital gains, matters only to a few relocating sellers of large gains.

missing_drivers: Military transfers between California bases and Oahu. San Diego County is the #1 county source of households moving to Oahu (781-819 households a year in 2019-20 to 2022-23, about 2 people per return; IRS SOI county migration, https://www.irs.gov/statistics/soi-tax-stats-migration-data). VA loans were 27.1% of Honolulu home-purchase mortgages in 2025 (HMDA, FFIEC Data Browser, 2025 data, local file new/hmda.json). Some California-address Oahu buyers are likely service members, which fits their near-local prices. Not quantifiable from public data.

Former Hawaii residents living in California (boomerang buyers). California received 62,990 Hawaii households in 2011-12 to 2022-23, more than any other state (IRS SOI). Their share among buyers is unmeasured. No published count of Hawaii-born people living in California was found.

Measurement: address-based classification and institutional mail drops. Title Guaranty does not publish its method or full state lists. On Oahu, LA ZIP 90017 has 588 parcels at 6 mailing addresses; on Maui, ZIP 90067 has 317 at 16 (owner rolls 2026-10-05 and 2026-10-04). CA-based trusts, LLCs, managers and developers can inflate the 'California' count. A Hilo bulk anomaly in 2024 (232 CA buyers averaging about $151K) shows how one transaction can move shares.

Within-reach income gradient: wealth sets how many buy, not only how much. Oahu individual owners per million residents: Bay Area 466, LA-OC 239, San Diego 243, Sacramento 149, Inland Empire 44, despite equal distance and nonstop ONT service (Honolulu roll 2026-10-05; DBEDT 2025 Table 21 populations).

1031 exchanges of appreciated California investment property into Hawaii rentals (hypothesis, untested). California requires form FTB 3840 for any exchange of California property for out-of-state property (https://www.ftb.ca.gov/forms/2025/2025-3840-instructions.html, accessed 2026-10-08), so this channel exists, but its volume into Hawaii is unknown.

Airline network shifts, notably Alaska Airlines' growing Seattle network after the Hawaiian merger. This is a possible reason Washington is closing the gap (WA buyers 150 to 175 from H1 2025 to H1 2026 while CA fell 639 to 552). Hypothesis: seat-history data were not compared.

Timeshare and vacation-ownership exposure as a try-before-you-buy channel. 491,939 US West visitors planned timeshare stays in 2025 (DBEDT 2025 Table 15). Its link to fee-simple purchases is untested.
challenge.final_answer: California is the top out-of-state buyer state on every island in 2024, 2025 and January-June 2026 (Title Guaranty). The main reason is that it is by far the biggest pool of people living within about 2,400-2,700 miles of Hawaii, not that Californians are unusually eager buyers. In 2025 Title Guaranty counted 1,271 California buyers: 38% of the 3,314 out-of-state US buyers and 4.6 times runner-up Washington. Per million residents, California (32) bought at about the same rate as Washington (35), Nevada (41), Oregon (31) and Utah (30), and 5-6 times the rate of Texas (5.5) or Florida (6.8). The same pattern held in 2024. California's roughly 38% share matches its share of US visitors (38-41% in every normal year since 2013) and its 38.6% share of mainland purchases in 2008-15. Distance decides who is in range; income decides who buys within it. Florida and Texas have about as many $1M-plus tax filers per tax return as Washington or Nevada, yet buy at a fifth of the rate. Inside California, Oahu homes owned per resident run from about 466 per million in the Bay Area and 240 in Los Angeles-Orange County down to 44 in the Inland Empire, which has the same flight time and its own nonstop service. That is why the Bay Area and LA dominate: they are the two largest concentrations of nearby high-income households and the two largest air gateways. They are roughly tied in absolute ownership, but per resident the Bay Area owns about twice as much, in line with its higher income per tax return. Nonstop seats (57.5% of July 2026 domestic seats from California) and repeat visiting (82% of West Coast visitors are repeat visitors) are the channels this demand flows through rather than independent causes, since airlines put seats where demand already is. Family and military links add a steady base, especially on Oahu, where California buyers pay close to local prices. California is Hawaii's largest two-way migration partner, and San Diego County is the top county source of households moving to Oahu. These links cannot be measured separately. Taxes do not explain the pattern: from 2027 Hawaii taxes most high earners at the same or higher marginal rates as California, and most California buyers keep California residency. Remote work raised volumes in 2021-22, but California led long before. The lead is narrowing: California buyers fell 14% in January-June 2026 while Washington buyers rose 17%. California visitor arrivals are 12% below their 2022 peak, though still 6% above 2019. Confidence is high on the pattern and medium on how much each mechanism contributes. Title Guaranty classifies buyers by address, publishes only its top 10 states and has no metro detail, so the metro comparisons rely on owner rolls of existing homes.

research.question: Why do Washington, Oregon, Alaska, Colorado and Utah show up as the next buyer states after California, with island-specific patterns (Alaska and Oregon on Hawaii Island; Colorado and Utah on Kauai; Washington everywhere)?
research.answer: These five states make the list because, for their residents, Hawaii is close, easy to fly to and a habit. They are not simply big states. Per resident, Alaskans, Washingtonians, Oregonians and Utahns visit Hawaii 6 to 20 times as often as Texans or Floridians. They have taken more trips before (6 to 8 on average, against 4 to 4.5), they stay longer, and more of them stay in condos. Across 10 states, the number of visitors per resident predicts the number of buyers per resident very closely (log-log r about 0.96; when visitors per resident double, buyers per resident rise about 1.8 times). Which island a state's buyers choose mostly follows which island its visitors choose (r about 0.73 across 23 state-and-island pairs), and that largely follows the flight map. Seattle is the main hub for Alaska and Hawaiian Airlines and had 1.47 million seats to all four islands in 2025. Washington residents have more Hawaii seats per person than Californians, and Washington buyers turn up on every island at about California's per-person rate. Anchorage flies to Honolulu, Kona and a little to Maui, with no seats to Lihue. Alaskans make 63% of their trips between November and March, and Anchorage gets about 5.5 hours of daylight at the winter solstice. Alaskans buy almost only on Hawaii Island, mostly in Kona and Kohala, at about $708k on average, the lowest of any state. Oregonians split between Kona/Kohala and very cheap Puna lots. Colorado and Utah on Kauai is real in the visitor data: the whole interior West sends about 1.4 times its share of visitors to Kauai. But flights do not explain it, because Salt Lake City has no seats to Lihue. The buyer counts are also small (Colorado 11, 24, 4 and Utah 13, 16, 3 for 2024, 2025 and early 2026). Colorado's #2 rank on Kauai in 2025 came partly from one group of 12 low-priced purchases in the Hanalei district, and the Kauai lean disappeared in January–June 2026. Utah's strongest Hawaii link is Laie on Oahu, not Kauai. Utah mailing addresses hold 47% of the mainland-owned parcels in Laie (39% leaving out addresses that receive mail for 10 or more parcels), against 2% island-wide. That comes from the Church of Jesus Christ's university, cultural center and land company there. Having no state income tax adds little: Texas and Florida have none and their residents rarely buy. Family and migration ties add some pull (Washington and Oregon are top destinations for households leaving Hawaii), and so do large home-equity gains in Utah, Washington and Colorado.

drivers.driver: Visitor funnel. Some states send far more visitors per resident, who come back often, stay long and stay in condos, and visitor rates predict buyer rates. The data is the visitor and buyer counts. Interpretation: repeat condo stays lead to buying a second home.
drivers.quantified_effect: Across CA, WA, OR, AK, CO, UT, NV, AZ, TX and FL: log(buyers per million residents) vs log(visitors per 100 residents) gives r = 0.96, slope 0.86, Spearman 0.77 (n=10; AK uses its Hawaii Island count as a lower bound). Island choice: buyer island index vs visitor island index gives log r = 0.73, slope about 1.0, across 23 state-island cells with uncensored counts (r = 0.70 without Alaska). Compared with each state's share of the US population outside Hawaii (2025 other-US buyers), the over-representation is: AK on Hawaii Island about 22x (4.7% of buyers vs 0.22% of people), UT on Kauai 5.4x, OR on Hawaii Island 5.2x, CO on Kauai 4.8x, WA statewide 3.6x, CA 3.3x, TX 0.57x, FL 0.70x.

evidence.fact: Statewide top out-of-state buyer states in 2025 by number of purchases (Hawaii is #1 overall). Other-US buyers totaled 3,314. Alaska is not in the statewide top 10 (so at most 84) but had 55 purchases on Hawaii Island alone.
evidence.source: Title Guaranty Hawaii, Buyer Statistics Q4 2025 edition (statewide panel)

evidence.fact: Buyers per million residents, computed from Title Guaranty counts and Census Vintage 2025 populations. Alaska figures use the Hawaii Island count only, so they are lower bounds.
evidence.source: Derived from Title Guaranty Q4 2024 and Q4 2025 editions plus Census NST-EST2025-ALLDATA

evidence.fact: Visitors arriving on domestic flights in 2025, and visitors per 100 state residents (Census V2025 population)
evidence.source: DBEDT 2025 Annual Visitor Research Report, Table 53

evidence.fact: Market penetration in 2025: visitors per 1,000 metro residents. Anchorage is the highest of all listed US metros.
evidence.value: Anchorage 176.7; San Francisco 135.3; Seattle 110.6; Bend 97.2; Portland 94.1; Provo 73.9; Ogden 69.5; Salt Lake City 61.2; Denver 57.3; Boise 55.9; vs Dallas 9.9; New York 11.1; Miami 5.7
evidence.source: DBEDT 2025 Annual Visitor Research Report, Table 21

evidence.fact: Repeat-visit and stay profile by state of residence, 2025: average number of Hawaii trips, % first-time visitors, % staying only in condos, and length of stay in days
evidence.source: DBEDT 2025 Annual Visitor Research Report, Table 20

evidence.fact: Island lean of visitors in 2025: the share of a state's visitors going to each island, divided by the all-US share. The all-US shares are Oahu 52%, Maui County 30%, Kauai 17% and Hawaii Island 19%; they add to more than 100% because visitors see more than one island.
evidence.value: AK: Hawaii Island 1.41 (Kona 1.45), Kauai 0.50; OR: Hawaii Island 1.24, Maui 1.22, Oahu 0.65; CO: Kauai 1.64, Maui 1.15; UT: Kauai 1.42, Hawaii Island 0.69; WA: Oahu 0.97, Maui 0.98, Hawaii Island 0.98, Kauai 0.71
evidence.source: Derived from DBEDT 2025 Annual Visitor Research Report, Table 53

evidence.fact: Island lean of buyers, pooled 2024, 2025 and Jan-Jun 2026: a state's share of an island's other-US buyers divided by its share of statewide other-US buyers
evidence.value: AK: Hawaii Island 2.56 (137 of about 142 identified AK purchases); OR: Hawaii Island 1.49; CO: Kauai 1.77, Maui 1.47, Oahu 0.44; UT: Kauai 1.79, Oahu 1.02; WA: Maui 1.52, Hawaii Island 1.07, Oahu 0.86, Kauai 0.74
evidence.source: Derived from Title Guaranty Q4 2024, Q4 2025 and Q2 2026 island editions

evidence.fact: Purchases in 2025 per 10,000 visitors to the same island. Alaskan visitors to Hawaii Island become buyers at about twice the rate of Californians.
evidence.value: Hawaii Island: AK 19.2, OR 10.2, CO 9.2, TX 9.2, WA 8.6, CA 8.5. Kauai: UT 2.9, CO 2.8, CA 2.7, WA 2.1
evidence.source: Derived from Title Guaranty 2025 and DBEDT Table 53

drivers.driver: Flight network. Seattle and Portland (Alaska/Hawaiian hubs), Anchorage (Alaska), Denver (United) and Salt Lake City (Delta) have different nonstop menus by island. This explains 'Washington everywhere' and 'Alaska on Hawaii Island' well, Oregon partly, and Utah-on-Kauai not at all.
drivers.quantified_effect: Share of each origin's 2025 seats going to an island, compared with the US West average (HNL 53.4%, OGG 22.7%, KOA 12.8%, LIH 11.1%). Seattle: KOA 1.26x, LIH 1.28x, OGG 1.12x. Anchorage: KOA 1.34x, LIH 0. Portland: OGG 1.48x, KOA 1.15x, LIH 0.44x. Denver: KOA 1.67x, LIH 1.15x. Salt Lake City: HNL 1.50x, KOA 0.10x, LIH 0. Hawaii seats per state resident: WA 0.186, NV 0.224, CA 0.135, AK 0.129, OR 0.091, CO 0.087, AZ 0.075, UT 0.062, TX 0.013. Interpretation: seats and demand reinforce each other. Routes such as Anchorage–Kona were added in response to existing Alaskan demand, so seats are partly a result of demand, not only a cause.

evidence.fact: Domestic air seats operated to Hawaii in 2025, by mainland departure city and Hawaii airport
evidence.source: DBEDT 2025 Annual Visitor Research Report, Table 101 (Diio MI schedules)

evidence.fact: Alaska Air Group closed its acquisition of Hawaiian Holdings. Seattle remains the largest base and Honolulu becomes the second; Portland and Anchorage stay hubs.
evidence.source: Alaska Air Group Form 8-K (SEC); hub roles as reported by aviation press

evidence.fact: Alaska Airlines began seasonal Anchorage–Kona nonstops in November 2012, running in winter. Current schedule listings show the 2026–27 season running Nov 21, 2026 to Apr 10, 2027.
evidence.value: Seasonal ANC–KOA since 2012; DBEDT counts 16,233 ANC–KOA seats in 2025 (+9% vs 2024)
evidence.source: Alaska Airlines newsroom (2012 announcement); 2026–27 dates from third-party schedule listings

evidence.fact: Delta added a seasonal Salt Lake City–Kona route (Dec 19, 2025 to Mar 28, 2026, Boeing 767-300ER), its third Hawaii destination from Salt Lake City after Honolulu and Maui. No Salt Lake City–Lihue nonstop was found.
evidence.source: Aviation A2Z (reported); DBEDT Table 101 for seats

evidence.fact: Alaskan buyers on Hawaii Island cluster in West Hawaii, near the Kona airport where the Anchorage flights land
evidence.value: Jan–Jun 2025: Kohala Coast 10 ($11.9M), Kona 12 ($10.7M), Hilo 3, North Kohala 1. 2024: Kohala Coast (which then included most of Kona) 26 ($39.6M), Ka'u 7 ($1.6M), Kona 3, Hamakua 1
evidence.source: Title Guaranty Hawaii Island district panels, Q2 2025 and Q4 2024 editions

evidence.fact: Southwest's Hawaii expansion for 2026–27 is five California routes plus Las Vegas–Hilo (from Aug 6, 2026). None of its Hawaii gateways is in WA, OR, AK, CO or UT.
evidence.source: Bolt Flight / Airline Geeks citing Cirium (reported)

evidence.fact: Washington's statewide share of other-US buyers rose in Jan–Jun 2026. On Maui, Washington reached 21% of other-US buyers.
evidence.source: Derived from Title Guaranty editions

drivers.driver: Winter escape. Dark, cloudy or snowy home winters push trips and second-home use into November–March. This is strongest for Alaska, moderate for Oregon, Washington, Utah and Idaho, and weak for Colorado.
drivers.quantified_effect: Share of 2025 arrivals in November–March: AK 62.6%, ID 52.7%, OR 50.6%, UT 46.6%, WA 45.7%, AZ 42.6%, CO 40.5%, NV 37.8%, CA 35.6% (US West 40.4%). Natural experiment: Arizona has a warm winter, is a similar distance from Hawaii (Phoenix–Honolulu 2,913 miles) and has more seats per resident than Utah (0.075 vs 0.062). Yet it sends 2.4 visitors per 100 residents and 11–16 buyers per million, against Utah's (Salt Lake City 2,991 miles) 6.5 and 28–30. Colorado's peak month is October (14.4% of its arrivals, a school fall break), which suggests family vacation timing rather than escaping winter.

evidence.fact: 2025 arrivals by month and state. Alaska's January–March months are each about 15k, against about 2.4k in September.
evidence.value: AK Nov–Mar 62.6%; OR December 45,720 (14.3% of its year); CO October 44,070 (14.4%)
evidence.source: DBEDT 2025 Annual Visitor Research Report, Table 16

evidence.fact: Length of stay of Alaskan visitors on Hawaii Island in 2025
evidence.value: 10.75 days on Hawaii Island (Alaska overall 10.29; California 7.9)
evidence.source: DBEDT 2025 Annual Visitor Research Report, Table 55

evidence.fact: Anchorage daylight at the winter solstice (National Weather Service figure as reported)
evidence.source: Anchorage Daily News citing NWS Anchorage (reported)

evidence.fact: Seattle's average number of cloudy days per year (1961–90 NOAA Comparative Climatic Data, as compiled)
evidence.source: Current Results compilation of NOAA NCDC data (reported)

evidence.fact: Alaska's 2025 Permanent Fund Dividend, paid from early October just before the Anchorage–Kona season. This is a minor cash-timing factor that is not tested here.
evidence.source: Alaska Department of Revenue

drivers.driver: Price and wealth. Hawaii Island is the cheapest island, and home equity in Utah, Washington, Colorado and Oregon grew faster than Hawaii's. Alaskan and Oregonian buyers are mid-market or budget buyers, not luxury buyers.
drivers.quantified_effect: Average price paid on Hawaii Island, 2024–25 pooled: AK $708k (lowest of any listed state), OR $993k, CO $1.07M, WA $1.28M, CA $1.33M; Hawaii-resident buyers $477k. Oregon buyers split between budget and upscale: 29 of 77 Hawaii Island purchases in 2025 (38%) were in Puna at about $272k average, while Kohala Coast purchases averaged about $2.7M. FHFA home price index, 2015Q4 to 2026Q2: UT +129%, WA +116%, CO +95%, OR +91% vs HI +80%, CA +82%, AK +60%. Interpretation: owners in UT, WA, CO and OR gained buying power against Hawaii prices; Alaskans gained less and buy cheaper.

evidence.fact: Single-family median price by island, August 2026
evidence.source: DBEDT monthly island housing series (report dataset)

evidence.fact: 2025 single-family median price by county
evidence.value: Hawaii County $465k; Honolulu $1.11M; Maui $1.175M; Kauai $1.10M. Puna ZIPs: 96778 $250k, 96749 $450k, 96760 $376k; Ocean View 96737 $365k
evidence.source: UHERO, The Hawaii Housing Factbook 2026 (Title Guaranty data)

evidence.fact: Hawaii Island district panels for 2025 show bimodal Pacific Northwest buying: cheap Puna lots plus upscale Kona and Kohala
evidence.value: Puna: OR 29 ($7.9M), WA 34 ($7.3M), Hawaii residents 1,133 ($213.5M, about $188k each). Kona: OR 24 ($24.6M), WA 29 ($27.0M). Kohala Coast: OR 15 ($40.2M), WA 34 ($64.9M)
evidence.source: Title Guaranty Hawaii Island Q4 2025 district panels

evidence.fact: FHFA all-transactions house price index, percent change
evidence.source: FHFA HPI (state, all transactions)

drivers.driver: Religious and education ties: Laie, Oahu (BYU–Hawaii, the Polynesian Cultural Center, and Hawaii Reserves Inc., the Church's land company). This is a strong but narrow link. It explains Utah buyers on Oahu's north and windward side, not Utah buyers on Kauai.
drivers.quantified_effect: Oahu owner roll (Oct 2026). Utah addresses hold 46.6% of the mainland-owned parcels in TMK section 5-5 (Laie) and 19.8% in zone 5 (Koolauloa), against 2.0% island-wide (about 23x and 10x). Leaving out addresses that receive mail for 10 or more parcels, the shares are 38.8% in Laie, 15.2% in Koolauloa and 1.9% island-wide. Koolauloa holds 2% of Oahu parcels but 36% of the individually addressed Utah-owned Oahu parcels.

evidence.fact: Mailing state of the primary owner, by tax map key (TMK) zone and section: aggregate counts computed from the county owner roll
evidence.value: Zone 5: UT 234 of 1,182 non-HI owners. Section 5-5: UT 55 of 118. Oahu: UT 529 of 26,069. 59 Oahu parcels mail to ZIP 84150 (Salt Lake City, the Church's headquarters ZIP), 19 of them in Laie; Provo and Orem ZIPs also appear
evidence.source: City & County of Honolulu, HoLIS OWNINFO owner tables (aggregate counts only)

evidence.fact: Utah ranks #2 among other-US buyer states in Title Guaranty's North Shore and Windward districts in 2025
evidence.value: North Shore UT 7 (CA 20); Windward UT 13 (CA 60); Central UT 7
evidence.source: Title Guaranty Oahu Q4 2025 district panels

evidence.fact: BYU–Hawaii's Fall 2025 headcount and where students come from. Most students are international, so the Utah link runs more through Church, faculty, alumni and family networks than through students.
evidence.value: 2,822 students; 76% from Oceania and the Asian Rim; 818 student employees at the Polynesian Cultural Center
evidence.source: BYU–Hawaii Quick Facts 2025–2026

evidence.fact: Hawaii Reserves Inc., a for-profit subsidiary of the Church's Deseret Management Corp., owns or manages about 7,000 acres in and around Laie, including the land under the BYU–Hawaii campus and the Polynesian Cultural Center
evidence.source: Honolulu Civil Beat (reported)

drivers.driver: Family, diaspora and two-way migration ties: Native Hawaiian and Hawaii-born communities, departing Hawaii households, and military moves between bases. Interpretation: some 'out-of-state' buyers are former residents or relatives of residents.
drivers.quantified_effect: Native Hawaiians per 1,000 residents (2020 count divided by 2025 population): NV 8.1, AK 5.6, WA 3.9, OR 3.6, UT 3.3, CA 2.4, TX 0.7. This ranks states much like buyers per resident do, but it does not separate cause from effect. IRS household moves to Hawaii over 2011–23 per 1,000 current residents: AK 6.3, NV 2.8, WA 2.7, OR 2.2, CO 1.8, CA 1.8, UT 1.3, TX 0.7, FL 0.7. Alaska is the only one of the five that sent Hawaii more households than it received.

evidence.fact: 2020 Census count of Native Hawaiians (alone or in combination) by state outside Hawaii
evidence.source: Office of Hawaiian Affairs, Ka Wai Ola 2020 Census map (Census DHC-A)

evidence.fact: Hawaii, Alaska and Utah were the only states where at least 1% of residents identified as Native Hawaiian and Other Pacific Islander alone
evidence.source: US Census Bureau, America Counts story

evidence.fact: IRS state-to-state migration with Hawaii, sum of tax years 2011-12 through 2022-23 (households filing returns)
evidence.source: IRS SOI migration data (report dataset)

evidence.fact: Active-duty personnel stationed in each state, supporting the idea of military moves between Hawaii and Joint Base Lewis-McChord (WA), Joint Base Elmendorf-Richardson (AK) and Fort Carson (CO)
evidence.value: HI 44,279; CO 40,158; AK 19,773 (MOAA 2026 packet); WA 52,019 (Military OneSource, DMDC data as of Dec 31, 2025)
evidence.source: MOAA state demographics 2026 (reported)

evidence.fact: Owner mailing addresses per million residents of the mailing state (includes addresses that receive mail for many parcels)
evidence.value: Maui County: AK 544, WA 325, CA 239, OR 187, CO 151, UT 143, TX 22. Oahu: NV 343, CA 299, AK 293, WA 250, UT 149, OR 133, CO 91, TX 37
evidence.source: Maui County GIS parcel fabric mailing fields; Honolulu OWNINFO (aggregate counts)

drivers.driver: Interior West lean toward Kauai. The direction is real in visitor data; the size of the buyer effect is fragile. Interpretation: outdoor-recreation buyers who stay in condos or vacation rentals prefer Kauai, whether or not their home airport has a nonstop.
drivers.quantified_effect: Kauai visitor lean in 2025: Mountain region 1.36 (CO 1.64, WY 1.49, UT 1.42, ID 1.32, AZ 1.31, MT 1.28; NV 0.89), against 0.77 for AK+OR+WA. This holds with or without a nonstop: SLC and BOI have no Lihue seats, while DEN and PHX do. Buyer lean on Kauai: CO 1.68 (2024), 2.06 (2025), 0.90 (Jan–Jun 2026); UT 2.21, 1.78, 0.93. Without the Hanalei cluster, Colorado's 2025 Kauai count would be about 12–13, roughly its 2024 level of 11.

evidence.fact: Colorado and Utah buyers on Kauai, with district detail
evidence.source: Title Guaranty Kauai Q4 2024, Q2 2025, Q4 2025 and Q2 2026 district panels

evidence.fact: Price context for the Colorado cluster: Princeville (96722) medians
evidence.source: UHERO Hawaii Housing Factbook 2026, ZIP profiles

evidence.fact: Idaho also ranks among Kauai's top buyer states, consistent with a lean across the whole Mountain West
evidence.value: ID on Kauai: 8 (2024), 13 (2025); statewide ID not in the top 10
evidence.source: Title Guaranty Kauai Q4 2024 and Q4 2025

drivers.driver: No state income tax (WA, AK, NV, TX, FL). This is weak and mixed up with other factors.
drivers.quantified_effect: Buyers per million, 2024–25 average: no-tax states AK about 78, NV 43, WA 39, TX 6, FL 6; income-tax states CA 38, UT 29, OR 29, CO 21, AZ 14. Within the Northwest, no-tax WA buys about 35% more per resident than OR (top rate 9.9%), but the no-tax Sun Belt states are 5–7 times below. Interpretation: Hawaii's 11% top rate gives everyone a reason to keep their legal residence on the mainland and own Hawaii as a second home rather than move. It does not explain which states buy.

evidence.fact: 2026 top state income tax rates
evidence.value: HI 11% (2nd highest); OR 9.9%; CO 4.4% flat; UT cut to 4.45% (retroactive to Jan 1, 2026); WA taxes capital gains but not wages; AK none
evidence.source: Tax Foundation 2026 state rates, as summarized by NJBIA (reported)

counter_evidence: Size alone does not explain the list. Texas (31.7M people) and Florida (23.5M) rank #4–5 statewide on raw counts but produce only 5–7 buyers per million residents. Washington (8.0M) produces 35–42 per million, about California's rate, and Alaska produces at least 75–80.

The flight-network explanation fails for Utah on Kauai: Salt Lake City had zero Lihue seats in 2025, yet Utah visitors lean toward Kauai at 1.42. Denver's seats lean most toward Kona (1.67x), not Lihue (1.15x), yet Colorado buyers lean more toward Kauai and Maui than toward Hawaii Island. Seats are part of the story, not all of it.

The causation can run both ways. Airlines add routes where demand already exists (Anchorage–Kona began in 2012 as a winter route for Alaskans), so seat shares partly reflect earlier demand. Visitor and buyer leans could also both be driven by a third factor such as climate, wealth or family ties. Visitor data is a strong correlate, not proof of cause.

Small numbers. The Kauai cells for Colorado and Utah are 3–24 purchases a year. Colorado's #2 rank on Kauai in 2025 relied on 12 Hanalei purchases in Jan–Jun 2025 averaging about $458k, in a district where the single-family median is $2.3M. That could be a bulk, fractional or related-party transaction, not 12 separate households. In Jan–Jun 2026, both Colorado and Utah fell to a Kauai index of about 0.9.

Title Guaranty's classification is not fully transparent. UHERO defines out-of-state as the home address on the deed transfer documents, so LLC, trust or management-company addresses can move a purchase into another state. Example: Wyoming appears on Kauai in 2026 with 4 purchases ($10M), probably trusts or LLCs. The owner rolls also show addresses in Portland 97232 and Salt Lake City 84117/84150 that receive mail for many parcels each.

Only each panel's top 10 states are published. Alaska's statewide total is unknown (55 to about 84 in 2025), and missing island counts are capped by each panel's 10th-place value, which biases some indices.

A 2024 Hilo anomaly (232 California purchases at about $151k each, unexplained by the source) inflates Hawaii Island's 2024 other-US total. This makes the 2024 Alaska and Oregon Hawaii Island leans understated, if anything.

Utah's tie is not mainly students: 76% of BYU–Hawaii students come from Oceania and Asia. The Laie concentration reflects Church land, faculty, alumni and family networks, plus institutional mailing addresses (19 Laie parcels mail to the Church headquarters ZIP). Even leaving out addresses that receive mail for 10 or more parcels, Utah is still 38.8% of individual mainland owners in Laie.

Retirees, people moving back and second-home buyers cannot be told apart. IRS data shows Washington, Oregon, Colorado and Utah each received more Hawaii households than they sent (net loss to Hawaii), so some of their 'buyers' may be former residents or relatives of residents.

Military moves (JBLM, JBER, Fort Carson to and from Oahu bases) likely add to Oahu buying. Alaskan owners are 1.4–2.6% of mainland owners in Oahu's Wahiawa and Waianae zones, against 0.8% island-wide. But this does not explain the neighbor-island patterns.

The 2026 shift: Washington's share of other-US buyers jumped to 11.7% statewide and 21% on Maui in Jan–Jun 2026. This is consistent with growing Alaska/Hawaiian capacity out of Seattle, but half a year is too short to rule out noise.
research.for_brokers:
Rank target markets by visitors per resident, not by population. Anchorage (177 per 1,000), Seattle (111), Portland (94), Provo/Ogden/Salt Lake City (61–74) and Denver (57) far exceed Dallas (10) or New York (11). Match each market to its island.

(1) Washington: market all islands, especially Maui, where Washington reached 21% of other-US buyers in Jan–Jun 2026. Seattle has nonstops to all four airports (1.47M seats in 2025). On Hawaii Island, Washington buyers split between Puna lots (about $215k) and Kohala/Kona ($0.9–1.9M).

(2) Alaska: Hawaii Island only, in West Hawaii (Kona and Kohala Coast), at mid-market prices ($600k–$1.2M; $708k average). Time campaigns for October–November, before the Anchorage–Kona season (Nov 21–Apr 10) and the early-October Permanent Fund Dividend; 63% of Alaskan trips fall in November–March. Alaskans have the most repeat trips (8.4) and longest stays, so long-term condo renters are a warm pipeline.

(3) Oregon: Hawaii Island in two tiers, Puna entry-level (about $272k average) and Kona/Kohala. Oregon visitors are the most condo-heavy (38.5% condo-only), so condo managers make good referral partners. Peak months are March and December.

(4) Colorado and Utah: Kauai's Poipu/Koloa (Utah, about $2M) and Princeville/Hanalei (Colorado), plus Maui. Treat this as a smaller, volatile segment (3–24 purchases a year), and do not budget on 2025's spike. Colorado travel peaks in October (fall break) and March; Utah in March and September.

(5) Utah on Oahu: the Laie, Hauula and Kahuku corridor is where Utah owners concentrate. Referral relationships with BYU–Hawaii and Church-affiliated networks matter more there than mass advertising.

Housekeeping: check each Title Guaranty quarter before quoting ranks, because these cells are small. Mailing addresses that belong to LLCs or trusts can mislabel origin. Washington and Oregon are also where Hawaii families relocate, so agents there can refer business both ways.
research.for_locals:
Competition from these five states falls unevenly.

On Hawaii Island, buyers from Alaska, Oregon and Washington are not mainly luxury buyers. Alaskans average about $708k. Oregonians and Washingtonians bought 63 Puna properties in 2025 at about $215–272k each, close to the roughly $188k Puna average for Hawaii-resident buyers. They compete directly for the cheap lots and starter homes that local families use to get into ownership, and many use the homes mainly in winter (63% of Alaskan trips fall in November–March). That means more homes sit empty part of the year, even though Hawaii Island is still the most affordable county (single-family median about $465–580k).

On Oahu's Koolauloa coast, Utah-based owners hold nearly half of the mainland-owned parcels in Laie (39% even after setting aside addresses that receive mail for 10 or more parcels). Church and alumni networks shape demand there, and Hawaii Reserves' earlier plans for workforce housing were scaled back.

On Kauai, Colorado and Utah buyers are mostly in Poipu and Princeville at about $1.8–2M, so they overlap less with local family budgets. Their effect comes more through rentals and land use.

What this does not show: whether these buyers move here or keep second homes. IRS data shows Washington and Oregon are also where many Hawaii households go when they leave, so some 'mainland' buyers may be returning family. For policy, the useful levers are the ones that apply to non-owner-occupied homes (property tax classes, vacation-rental rules), because a buyer's home state is not something the state or counties can screen for.

challenge.question: Why do Washington, Oregon, Alaska, Colorado and Utah show up as the next buyer states after California, with island-specific patterns (Alaska and Oregon on Hawaii Island; Colorado and Utah on Kauai; Washington everywhere)?

verdicts.driver: Visitor funnel (high visitor rates, repeat trips and condo stays lead to buying)
verdicts.reason: I re-checked DBEDT 2025 Tables 20, 21 and 53 in the local workbook (raw/visitors/2025-annual-visitor.xlsx, files.hawaii.gov, last modified 2026-09-28), and they match the researcher. Reproducing the 10-state log-log fit with Census V2025 populations gives r = 0.95 and slope 0.82 for 2025, and r = 0.95 and slope 0.91 for 2024 (the researcher had 0.96 and 0.86). Almost all of that fit comes from Texas, Florida and Arizona at the low end and Alaska at the high end. Across the six western states (CA, WA, OR, UT, CO, NV), r is 0.16 in 2025 and 0.32 in 2024, and the Spearman rank correlation is about 0. So visitor rates separate the West from everyone else but do not rank the western states. Nevada has the second-highest buyer rate (41 per million) but only 4.9 visitors per 100 residents. For island choice, I reproduced 21 uncensored state-island cells pooled over 2024, 2025 and Jan–Jun 2026: r = 0.80 and slope 1.04, so the direction holds. There are clear misses, though: Washington's buyer index on Maui is 1.52 against a visitor index of 0.98, and Nevada's on Kauai is 1.28 against 0.89. Causation can also run backwards. DBEDT counts non-resident owners staying in their own units as visitors (Table 15 has no 'own home' category), so the repeat-trip and condo-only figures partly measure existing ownership. 'They stay longer' is wrong for Washington (8.81 days) and Utah (8.58), both shorter than Florida (9.61). Only Alaska (10.29), Colorado (9.31) and Oregon (9.26) stay notably long. The Alaska island index is overstated because Alaska's statewide count is hidden in every full-year panel (only the top 10 states are published). Jan–Jun 2025 is the only period with a published statewide Alaska count (50), and it gives 36 of 50 (72%) on Hawaii Island and an index of 1.94, not 2.56.
fact_errors: 'Alaskans buy almost only on Hawaii Island (137 of about 142)': the 142 leaves out Oahu and Kauai counts that are hidden below each panel's 10th place. In Jan–Jun 2025, statewide Alaska = 50 and Hawaii Island = 36 (72%).
Alaska's Hawaii Island buyer index of 2.56 uses an understated statewide denominator. Jan–Jun 2025 gives 1.94.
'They stay longer': Washington (8.81 days) and Utah (8.58) stay shorter than Floridians (9.61) and about as long as Texans (8.65), per DBEDT Table 20.
Log-log r = 0.96 and slope 0.86 reproduce as 0.95 and 0.82 (2025), and as 0.95 and 0.91 (2024).
verdicts.corrected_wording: Western states send far more visitors per resident than Texas or Florida (WA 8.9, OR 7.5, UT 6.5, CO 5.1 per 100 residents vs TX 1.1, FL 0.7), and their visitors repeat more often (6.2–8.4 average trips vs 4.2–4.5). Across 10 states, visitor rates track buyer rates closely (log r ≈ 0.95), but that mostly reflects the gap between the West and everyone else. Within the West, visitor rates do not predict which state buys more. A state's visitor island lean roughly predicts its buyer island lean (r ≈ 0.8 over 21 cells), with exceptions (Washington on Maui). Some of the repeat-visit signal probably comes from people who already own homes here. About 72% of Alaskan purchases are on Hawaii Island (Jan–Jun 2025), not almost all. Strength: moderate.

verdicts.driver: Flight network (Seattle/Portland/Anchorage/Denver/SLC nonstop menus by island)
verdicts.reason: DBEDT Table 101 seat counts (2025, Diio schedules) match exactly: Seattle 1,470,327; Anchorage 94,893 with 0 to Lihue; Salt Lake City 218,865 with 0 to Lihue and 2,776 to Kona. Alaska Air Group's 10-Q (sec.gov, period ending 2024-09-30) confirms the Hawaiian acquisition closed on 2024-09-18. Alaska Airlines' Anchorage–Kona service began in November 2012 (search snippets of the Alaska Air newsroom and West Hawaii Today, 2012). The Nov 21, 2026–Apr 10, 2027 dates come only from a third-party schedule listing (roame.travel). Delta's SLC–Kona seasonal service (Dec 19, 2025–Mar 28, 2026, 767-300ER) is confirmed as reported (aeroroutes.com, 2025-03-26; travelpulse). The HVCB October 2026 air service grid (as of 2026-06-16, assets.simpleviewinc.com) still shows no SLC–Lihue flights. It also shows Alaska now flying SLC–Honolulu (31 flights), Portland–Lihue at 31 flights a month (2025 PDX–LIH was only 19,080 seats for the whole year), Denver–Lihue on United (31 flights), and Southwest from Phoenix and from Las Vegas to all islands including Hilo. Seats per resident do not rank states on their own. Nevada (0.224) is above Washington (0.186). Arizona (0.075) is above Utah (0.062), yet Arizona buys at 11 per million against Utah's 30. Seats also carry Hawaii residents outbound (Las Vegas). The pattern extends past the US: British Columbia supplies 44.6% of Canadian visitors (DBEDT Table 25, 2025), which fits a Pacific Northwest geography effect. Hilo had no mainland nonstop from January 2023 until Southwest's LAS–ITO service started on 2026-08-06 (Hawaii Tribune-Herald, as reported). So the cheap Puna buying by Oregonians and Washingtonians does not come from the flight map.
fact_errors: 'Seattle is the main hub for Alaska and Hawaiian Airlines': Seattle is Alaska Air Group's largest hub, while Hawaiian's hub is Honolulu, now the group's second-largest (Alaska Air Group 10-Q, Q3 2024; ch-aviation, Sept 2024).

Southwest's Hawaii network is not only California plus Las Vegas–Hilo. The October 2026 HVCB grid shows Southwest from Phoenix (Honolulu, Kahului) and from Las Vegas to Honolulu, Kahului, Kona, Lihue and Hilo. The researcher's narrower point, that none of its gateways is in WA, OR, AK, CO or UT, still holds.
The 2026–27 Anchorage–Kona dates come from a third-party aggregator, not from Alaska Airlines.
verdicts.corrected_wording: The flight map explains 'Washington everywhere' (Seattle, Alaska Air Group's largest hub, flew 1.47M seats in 2025 to all four main airports) and the Kona lean of Alaskans (Anchorage–Kona winter nonstops since 2012; no Anchorage–Lihue seats). It does not explain Utah on Kauai (no SLC–Lihue nonstop in 2025 or the October 2026 schedule) or Puna lot buying (no Hilo mainland nonstop between January 2023 and August 2026). Seats and demand reinforce each other, and seats per resident alone do not rank states (Arizona has more than Utah but buys a third as much). Strength: strong for WA and AK island patterns, weak for the rest.

verdicts.driver: Winter escape (dark/snowy winters push trips and second-home use into Nov–Mar)
verdicts.reason: Table 16 (DBEDT 2025) confirms Alaska at 62.6% of arrivals in Nov–Mar, and Table 55 confirms 10.75-day Alaskan stays on Hawaii Island. Outside Alaska, the seasonal share is not a clean climate signal. Arizona, with a warm winter, has 42.6% of its arrivals in Nov–Mar, more than Colorado (40.5%) and close to Washington (45.7%), so much of the winter share reflects Hawaii's high season and school calendars. The Arizona-versus-Utah 'natural experiment' has other differences too, including income, age mix and retirees who already own Sun Belt homes. Arizona's single biggest month is September (24.7k), not winter. Nevada has a warm winter yet the highest per-capita buyer rate after Alaska (41 per million), and Texas and Florida's low rates can be explained by distance alone. The ADN/NWS daylight figure and the $1,000 2025 PFD (Alaska DOR, 2025-09-19) are confirmed, but the PFD remains untested as a driver.
verdicts.corrected_wording: Winter escape is strong for Alaska (63% of trips in Nov–Mar, 10.75-day stays on Hawaii Island, and buying concentrated near Kona). For Oregon, Washington, Utah and Colorado the evidence is weak: Arizona, with a warm winter, has a higher winter share of trips than Colorado, so seasonal timing mostly reflects Hawaii's high season and school breaks. Strength: strong for Alaska, weak otherwise.

verdicts.driver: Price and wealth (cheap Hawaii Island; faster home-equity growth in UT/WA/CO/OR)
verdicts.reason: I confirmed the FHFA all-transactions numbers (local hpi_at_state.csv, through 2026Q2). Equity growth does not pick out these states, though. From 2015Q4 to 2026Q2, Florida rose 130%, Arizona 123%, Nevada 122%, Idaho 161% and Texas 95%, all at or above Colorado and Oregon and near Utah, yet Florida, Arizona and Texas buy at 6–11 per million. California (82%) grew at about Hawaii's pace (80%) and is still the top buyer state. The price-tier facts hold up in the Title Guaranty panels: Alaska's 2024–25 Hawaii Island average is $80.7M / 114 = $708k, the lowest of any listed state, and $587k in Jan–Jun 2026. The 2025 Puna panel shows Oregon 29 ($7.9M), Washington 34 ($7.3M) and Hawaii residents 1,133 ($213.5M, about $188k each). But California also bought 112 Puna properties ($25.8M, about $230k), more than Oregon and Washington combined, so cheap-lot buying is a general mainland behavior, not a Northwest trait. The Aug 2026 DBEDT medians are confirmed (Hawaii Island single-family $580k). The UHERO Princeville 'out-of-state share 75%' is the local file's own weighted mix. UHERO publishes 66.7% for single-family and 79.8% for condos.
fact_errors: UHERO's Princeville 75% out-of-state share is a derived blend, not a published figure (published: single-family 66.7%, condo 79.8%).

The 'for_locals' text says Colorado and Utah buyers on Kauai pay about $1.8–2M. Colorado's 2025 Kauai average was $26.8M / 24 = about $1.12M, and its Hanalei purchases averaged about $736k (14 for $10.3M). Only Utah's Koloa/Poipu purchases (9 for $18.6M) are about $2M.
verdicts.corrected_wording: Price shapes how much these buyers spend, not which states they come from. Hawaii Island is the cheapest island, and Alaskans buy there in the mid-market (about $708k on average in 2024–25). Oregonians and Washingtonians, like Californians, also buy cheap Puna lots (about $215–272k). Home-equity gains do not explain the list: Florida, Arizona and Nevada gained as much or more than Utah, Washington and Colorado but rarely buy. Strength: moderate for price tier, weak for state selection.

verdicts.driver: Religious/education ties (Laie, BYU–Hawaii, PCC, Hawaii Reserves)
verdicts.reason: Recounting from the Honolulu OWNDAT roll (raw/owners_oahu/owndat, data edited 2026-10-05) gives the same aggregates. In TMK section 5-5 (Laie), Utah addresses hold 55 of 118 mainland-addressed parcels (46.6%). In zone 5, the figure is 234 of 1,182 (19.8%), and island-wide 531 of 26,075 (2.0%). Of the 55 Laie parcels, 19 mail to ZIP 84150, the Church headquarters. The tie is narrow, though. The 55 Utah parcels are 5.8% of Laie's 944 parcels, and only about 36 are individually addressed (3.8%). Utah's overall Oahu buyer index is about 1.0 (Oahu 42, 48 and 23 for 2024, 2025 and Jan–Jun 2026), so Laie explains where some Utah buyers on Oahu go, not why Utah ranks as a buyer state. Utah buyers are 13 in Windward, 7 on the North Shore and 7 in Central (TG Oahu Q4 2025). As a suggestive sign of a BYU/Church channel, Provo has the highest Hawaii visitor rate in Utah (73.9 per 1,000, vs Salt Lake City 61.2; DBEDT Table 21). The BYU–Hawaii student-origin figure was misread. The 2025–26 Quick Facts sheet (as extracted by search; the PDF could not be fetched here) gives 2,822 students. Its 76% 'target area' includes Hawaii (about 22%) and the Philippines (about 12%). Oceania plus Asian Rim are only about 41%, and about 21% (592) come from the other 49 states, so mainland students are a meaningful channel. Sources disagree on Hawaii Reserves' parent. Wikipedia names Property Reserve Inc., while a BYU–Hawaii news piece names Deseret Management Corp. About 7,000 acres is the reported figure.
fact_errors: '76% from Oceania and the Asian Rim' is wrong. The 76% is BYU–Hawaii's 'target area', which includes Hawaii (~22%) and the Philippines (~12%). Oceania plus Asian Rim are ~41%, and ~21% come from the US mainland (search extraction of the 2025–26 Quick Facts, last updated 2025-10-31).
Hawaii Reserves is described as a Deseret Management Corp. subsidiary. Sources disagree, and Wikipedia lists Property Reserve Inc.
verdicts.corrected_wording: Utah's most distinctive Hawaii tie is Laie on Oahu. Utah addresses hold about 47% of the mainland-addressed parcels there (55 of 118, 19 of them mailed to the Church headquarters ZIP), against 2% island-wide. In absolute terms that is about 6% of all Laie parcels. Utah buyers on Oahu overall are about average for an out-of-state group. This link explains where some Utah owners on Oahu are, not why Utah ranks among buyer states, and it says nothing about Kauai. Strength: strong locally, weak statewide.

verdicts.driver: Family, diaspora and two-way migration ties (incl. military moves)
verdicts.reason: I confirmed the IRS 2011–23 sums in page_data.state_corr: WA 21,937 in / 28,604 out; OR 9,489 / 12,206; AK 4,608 / 3,835; CO 10,735 / 12,690; UT 4,696 / 6,436. The same file shows Texas at 22,083 in / 28,218 out, about as large as Washington in absolute terms, and Nevada at 9,272 in / 19,172 out. So the migration channel is strongest for Nevada (the Las Vegas diaspora) and for military-heavy states. Utah's per-capita tie is weak (1.3 per 1,000) even though its buyer rate (30 per million) is high, so migration does not explain Utah. Being at least 1% NHPI in Alaska and Utah (I could not re-fetch the Census story) largely reflects Samoan and Tongan communities, which are Pacific Islander ties rather than Hawaii-born family ties. The Native Hawaiian per-capita ranking (OHA 2020 map) roughly tracks buyer rates but cannot separate cause from effect. The military piece should be its own driver (see missing drivers).
fact_errors: The Census claim that HI, AK and UT are the only states at or above 1% NHPI alone could not be re-verified (census.gov blocked). A secondary ranking lists HI 10.1%, AK 1.2%, UT 1.0%. In AK and UT this is mostly Samoan and Tongan, not Native Hawaiian.
verdicts.corrected_wording: Family and migration ties add pull for Nevada, Washington, Oregon and Alaska, where many former Hawaii households live (IRS 2011–23: Hawaii lost a net 6,667 households to Washington and 9,900 to Nevada). They do not explain Utah or Colorado well, and part of the two-way flow is military moves rather than family. Strength: moderate for NV/WA/AK, weak for UT/CO.

verdicts.driver: Interior West lean toward Kauai (Colorado and Utah)
verdicts.reason: The visitor side holds. Table 53 indices reproduce (CO Kauai 1.64, UT 1.42, Mountain region 1.36), and they hold after correcting for multi-island trips by dividing by island-visits instead of visitors (CO 1.65, UT 1.48, Mountain 1.40). Arizona shares the lean (1.32) and does have a Phoenix–Lihue nonstop, so the lean does not depend on flights. The buyer side is fragile. Colorado's Kauai counts were 11, 24 and 4, and Utah's 13, 16 and 3 (Jan–Jun 2026). The Kauai Q2 2025 district page confirms Colorado's Hanalei 12 purchases for $5.5M in Jan–Jun 2025 (about $458k each). The buyer indices fell to 0.90 (CO) and 0.93 (UT) in Jan–Jun 2026. No evidence supports the 'outdoor-recreation buyers' interpretation. There is also an important alternative for the district pattern: Kauai limits vacation rentals to Visitor Destination Areas (Ordinance 864 of 2008), and about 95% of Princeville is VDA-zoned, as is the Poipu area (reported by Hawaii Life brokerage and the Kauai County TVR renewal form). Out-of-state buyers from any state concentrate in Poipu and Princeville for that reason.
verdicts.corrected_wording: Colorado and Utah visitors really do favor Kauai (about 1.5–1.65 times the US average share, even after adjusting for multi-island trips), with or without a nonstop. Their buying on Kauai is small (3–24 sales a year) and unstable. Colorado's 2025 jump came largely from 12 sub-$500k Hanalei purchases in one half-year, and both states were back to an average share in Jan–Jun 2026. Kauai's resort-zone rental rules, more than buyer origin, explain why they buy in Poipu and Princeville. Strength: moderate for visitors, weak for buyers.

verdicts.driver: No state income tax
verdicts.reason: As a reason why particular states buy, the data reject it, which matches the researcher's own 'weak' rating. In 2024–25, Texas and Florida (no income tax) bought about 6 per million against 29–38 for income-tax states California, Utah and Oregon. The Texas and Florida counts are also inflated by military buyers, because service members can keep their legal residence in a no-tax state under the Servicemembers Civil Relief Act (50 U.S.C. §4001, per base legal guidance as reported). That makes their civilian rate even lower. The tax facts need updating. Washington enacted a 9.9% tax on household income above $1M, signed 2026-03-30 and effective 2028-01-01, now facing a constitutional lawsuit (KPTV 2026-03-30; OPB 2026-05-05; reported). Utah's cut to 4.45% retroactive to 2026-01-01 is confirmed (S.B. 60, signed 2026-03-23; EY 2026-04-21).
