The idea that Hawaii's 11% top rate pushes buyers to keep a mainland domicile and own a second home here is plausible but untested.
fact_errors: 'WA taxes capital gains but not wages' is out of date. Washington's 9.9% tax on income over $1M was signed on 2026-03-30 and takes effect in 2028 (under legal challenge, as reported).
verdicts.corrected_wording: Having no state income tax does not explain which states buy. Texas and Florida have none and buy at about 6 per million residents, a fifth of Utah's or Oregon's rate. Hawaii's 11% top rate may lead buyers to keep their legal residence on the mainland, but that applies to every state equally. Strength: none detectable.

missing_drivers: Distance and Western geography as the common cause. The main split is the West against everyone else, in both visiting and buying. Within the West, visitor rates do not rank buyer rates (r 0.16–0.32 across CA, WA, OR, UT, CO and NV). The same Pacific Northwest pattern appears in Canada: British Columbia supplies 44.6% of Canadian visitors (DBEDT 2025 Table 25, files.hawaii.gov, 2026-09-28).

Military moves and military domicile rules. VA loans were 27.1% of Honolulu purchase originations in 2025 (1,830 of 6,746; HMDA via local hmda.json), against 4.7–10.8% on the neighbor islands. The Servicemembers Civil Relief Act lets service members keep legal residence in no-tax states such as TX, FL, WA, AK and NV. This explains Texas, Florida, Virginia and New York in Oahu's top 10 (Texas 42 purchases in the Honolulu district in 2025; Virginia 17–19 in the Jan–Jun panels) and some Washington and Alaska buying on Oahu, and it distorts the income-tax comparison.

Nevada was left out of the question. In 2025 it had 41 buyers per million residents (above Washington's 35) and 134–143 purchases a year statewide, even though its visitor rate is low (4.9 per 100). IRS 2011–23 shows 19,172 Hawaii households moved to Nevada and 9,272 moved the other way, which points to the Las Vegas diaspora rather than tourism.

The premise itself only partly holds. By raw count, Texas ranks 3rd or 4th statewide in every period and Florida 4th or 5th in 2025. Alaska is never in the statewide top 10 for a full year. Colorado's per-capita rate (23 per million) is below California's (32). The five states stand out only per resident or on specific islands.

County vacation-rental zoning. Kauai allows vacation rentals mainly in Visitor Destination Areas (about 95% of Princeville, and Poipu), which steers out-of-state buyers of every origin into those districts. Maui's Bill 9 was signed on 2025-12-15 (HPR, 2025-12-16, reported). It phases out about 6,000 apartment-district short-term rentals by 2029 in West Maui and 2031 elsewhere and faces lawsuits. It could be shifting 2026 Maui buying, including Washington's jump to 21% of Maui's out-of-state buyers, but this is untested.

Reverse causation inside the visitor data. Non-resident owners staying in their own homes are counted as visitors, and DBEDT has no 'own home' accommodation category. So repeat-trip, length-of-stay and condo-only figures partly measure the existing stock of owners in a state, not a pipeline of future buyers.

Data artifacts. Only each panel's top 10 states are published, which hides Alaska's statewide total and its Oahu and Kauai counts. Deed and mailing addresses of entities and trusts can relabel a buyer's origin (Wyoming 4 purchases for $10.5M on Kauai in Jan–Jun 2026; Salt Lake City metro owner addresses 27% institutional on Oahu). The 2024 Hilo anomaly (232 California purchases at about $151k) distorts 2024 Hawaii Island indices.
Household income and wealth levels by state, as opposed to equity growth rates, were not tested and could separate Utah, Colorado and Washington from Arizona.
challenge.final_answer: The question's premise only partly holds. By raw purchase counts, Texas (175 in 2025) and Florida (159) outrank Colorado (136), Oregon (133) and Utah (105) statewide, Nevada (134) is level with them, and Alaska never appears in the statewide top 10 for a full year. What sets these five states apart is buying per resident and on particular islands. In 2025, Alaska bought at least 75 Hawaii homes per million residents, Nevada 41, Washington 35, California 32, Oregon 31, Utah 30 and Colorado 23, compared with about 6 for Texas and 7 for Florida. The clearest pattern is the West against everyone else. Western residents live closer, have more nonstop flights, visit Hawaii far more often (Washington 8.9, Oregon 7.5 and Utah 6.5 visitors per 100 residents, against 1.1 for Texas), and come back more (6 to 8 trips on average, against 4 to 4.5). Within the West, though, visit rates do not predict which state buys more, so 'visiting leads to buying' is a correlation, not proof, and some repeat visitors are probably people who already own here. Each island pattern has its own explanation, and they differ in strength. Washington appears everywhere because Seattle, Alaska Air Group's largest hub, flies nonstop to all four main airports (1.47 million seats in 2025). Alaskans favor Hawaii Island because of the winter Anchorage–Kona nonstops, because 63% of their trips fall in November–March, and because prices are lowest there (they averaged about $708k, the lowest of any listed state). That still means about 70% of their purchases, not nearly all. Oregon's Hawaii Island lean is real but modest. Oregonians buy both in Kona/Kohala and on cheap Puna lots, and Californians buy even more Puna lots. Puna buying is about price, not flights: Hilo had no mainland nonstop from January 2023 until August 2026. Colorado and Utah visitors really do favor Kauai, even without a nonstop from Salt Lake City. But the buyer numbers are tiny (3 to 24 a year), Colorado's 2025 jump came largely from 12 sub-$500k Hanalei purchases in one half-year, and both states were back to an average share in early 2026. Their concentration in Poipu and Princeville mostly reflects Kauai's rule that vacation rentals are allowed mainly in resort zones. Utah's distinctive tie is the Church community in Laie on Oahu, but it is small: 55 of 944 Laie parcels, 19 of them mailed to the Church headquarters ZIP. It explains where some Utah owners are, not Utah's statewide rank. Three ideas do not hold up as reasons these states buy. Home-equity gains fail because Florida, Arizona and Nevada gained as much as or more than Utah or Washington and rarely buy. No state income tax fails because Texas and Florida have none and also rarely buy. Winter escape fails outside Alaska, because warm-weather Arizona sends a larger share of its trips in November–March than Colorado does. Military moves explain much of the Texas, Florida and Virginia buying on Oahu, where 27% of 2025 home-purchase loans were VA loans. Confidence is medium for the West-against-the-rest pattern and for Washington and Alaska, and low for Colorado and Utah on Kauai.

research.question: Why does Japan dominate foreign buying, concentrated on Oahu (mostly Honolulu condos), and why did Japanese purchases rise in H1 2026 despite a historically weak yen? Why is Korean buying rising on Oahu (40 in 2024 to 87 in 2025)?
research.answer: Japan dominates because of long tourism ties, not new demand. Almost all Japanese visitors stay on Oahu (97.6% in 2025), 71% are repeat visitors, and Japanese buyers have spent decades building a base of Honolulu condo owners (2,024 Japan-mailing parcels, 62% of foreign-owned Oahu parcels, nearly all of them condo units in Waikiki and Ala Moana/Kakaako). Mitsui Fudosan Realty's Japanese sales channel for Ward Village has kept new towers on Japanese buyers' radar. The H1 2026 rise is mostly a timing effect of tower closings, not a sign that buyers shrugged off a ¥158 dollar. Japanese buying on Oahu went from 32 in Q1 2026 to 101 in Q2 2026, the same quarter Howard Hughes closed 527 units at The Park Ward Village ($706.3M, about $1.34M per unit, matching the $1.34M average foreign purchase in Q2). That tower began public sales in July 2021 and was 90.6% pre-sold by mid-2022, when the yen was about 110-135. Today's county owner roll shows 61 Japan-billed owners in the tower, enough to account for the whole +49 year-on-year H1 rise. Without it, Japanese purchases were roughly flat to down (about 72 vs 84). The Korean jump is the same pattern, concentrated in two towers. Korea went from 2 and 6 purchases in Q1-Q2 2025 to 39 and 40 in Q3-Q4 2025, when developer closings began at The Park on Keeaumoku (972 units on Honolulu's informal Koreatown corridor). That building now holds 80 of Oahu's 249 Korea-billed condo units, and The Park Ward Village holds 24 more. Together that is about 90% of the 116 Korean purchases from H2 2025 to H1 2026. Underneath the timing there are real but smaller forces. Japanese wealth rose sharply in equities (the Nikkei is up about 64% in dollar terms since end-2024), which offsets part of the currency hit. Korean money is moving abroad (Bank of Korea data show a five-year-high $590.5M in 2025 remittances for overseas property, with the US the top destination in 2026), driven by Seoul's lending and multi-home rules and a wish to hold assets outside the won. Seoul air seats have nearly recovered to 2019 levels while Japan's are at 64%. A weak yen is a headwind, not a driver: Japanese home-purchase value fell 13.3% a year from 2016 to 2025.

drivers.driver: Closing-timing of pre-sold new towers: contracts signed in 2021-22 recorded as purchases when the towers deliver (explains the H1 2026 Japanese rise and the 2025 Korean rise)
drivers.quantified_effect: Oahu Japanese purchases by quarter (TG, cumulative editions differenced): Q1-25 39, Q2-25 45, Q3-25 69, Q4-25 49, Q1-26 32, Q2-26 101. The Park Ward Village (527 closings in Q2 2026) carries 61 Japan-billed and 24 Korea-billed owners on the Oct 2026 tax roll. That is at least the entire Oahu H1 Japanese increase (+49), implying non-Park Japanese buying of about 72 in H1 2026 vs 84 in H1 2025 (about -14%). Korea by quarter: Q1-25 2, Q2-25 6, Q3-25 39, Q4-25 40, Q1-26 11, Q2-26 26. The Park on Keeaumoku (80 Korea-billed units) plus The Park Ward Village (24) equal 104, about 90% of the 116 Korean purchases from H2 2025 to H1 2026.

evidence.source: Title Guaranty of Hawaii, Buyer Statistics, Oahu editions Q1-2025, Q2-2025, Q3-2025, Q4-2025, Q1-2026, Q2-2026

evidence.fact: Korea buyers on Oahu: Jan-Mar 2025 2; Jan-Jun 2025 8 ($11.3M); Jan-Sep 2025 47 ($46.5M); Jan-Dec 2025 87 ($93.2M); Jan-Mar 2026 11; Jan-Jun 2026 37 ($48.7M). TG Honolulu district: 2023 22, 2024 40, 2025 86
evidence.source: Title Guaranty of Hawaii, Buyer Statistics, Oahu Q3-2025 and Q4-2025 editions (district panel)

evidence.fact: The Park Ward Village was completed in Q2 2026 and 527 of its 545 units closed in the quarter; condo sales revenue $706.3M (vs $0.2M in Q2 2025)
evidence.source: Howard Hughes Holdings Form 10-Q (Q2 2026) and supplemental 8-K

evidence.fact: The Park Ward Village public sales launched July 2021 and it was 90.6% pre-sold as of mid-2022
evidence.source: Howard Hughes press release, groundbreaking of The Park Ward Village

evidence.fact: Yen per dollar when those contracts were signed vs at closing (half-year averages of daily noon rates)
evidence.source: Federal Reserve H.10 historical rates, Japan

evidence.fact: Honolulu County Q2 2026: foreign buyers 146 at average $1,343,414; condo average $888,177 vs $627,815 in Q2 2025
evidence.value: Foreign average $1.34M = The Park Ward Village per-unit average
evidence.source: DBEDT Quarterly Statistical & Economic Report, Title Guaranty tables (local file an/page_data.json tg_q)

evidence.fact: Honolulu tax roll (tax-bill country) by building: The Park Ward Village (TMK 2-3-002:115) 550 units: HI 368, other US 83, Japan 61, Korea 24. The Park on Keeaumoku (TMK 2-3-018:052) 1,002 units: HI 784, other US 93, Korea 80, Japan 13. Victoria Place/1100 Ala Moana (closed late 2024) 350 units: Japan 43, Korea 17. Of 249 Korea-billed Oahu condo units, 32% are in The Park on Keeaumoku
evidence.source: City & County of Honolulu RPAD OWNDAT (structured tax-bill country) and LEGDAT (building names), aggregated by TMK

evidence.fact: The Park on Keeaumoku: 972 residences (826 market-rate) in two towers; first Liona Tower occupancy Fall 2025, sales launched 2021; developer sales recorded Sep 15, 2025 ($954,000, contracted Feb 2022) and Oct 16, 2025 ($1,184,000)
evidence.source: OahuNewHomes project page; Hawaii Living unit history

evidence.fact: Victoria Place delivery drove record 2024 condo revenue of $779M; Q4 2024 Honolulu foreign buyers spiked to 173 (average $1.93M); 2024 Japanese statewide purchases $415.6M (average $1.56M)
evidence.source: Howard Hughes Q4 2024 release; DBEDT QSER; Title Guaranty Q4 2024

drivers.driver: Oahu-centric tourism ties, repeat visitation and an installed base of Japanese condo owners (why Oahu and why Honolulu condos)
drivers.quantified_effect: 92.6% of Japanese home purchases (2016-2025) were on Oahu. In 2025 the TG Honolulu district held 187 of 202 Oahu Japanese purchases (93%) and 86 of 87 Korean. 94% of foreign-mailing Oahu parcels are condo/CPR units and 79% sit in ZIPs 96815 (Waikiki) and 96814 (Ala Moana/Kakaako). Japanese purchases per 1,000 Japanese visitors rose from 0.20 (2019) to 0.27 (2025), so the remaining visitors are more likely to buy.

evidence.fact: 2025 Japan air visitors 749,596, of whom 731,979 visited Oahu; 71.2% repeaters; average 5.5 trips; 108,593 planned condo stays and 68,123 timeshare stays
evidence.source: DBEDT 2025 Annual Visitor Research Report, Table 22

evidence.fact: 2025 Korea air visitors 171,766 (+14.2%), of whom 169,176 visited Oahu; 66% first-timers; average stay 8.1 days; rental-house stays +37.6%
evidence.source: DBEDT 2025 Annual Visitor Research Report, Table 33

evidence.fact: Between 2016 and 2025, 92.6% of all Japanese single-family and condo purchases were on Oahu; Japanese are consistently the largest international buyers
evidence.source: DBEDT, Hawaii-Japan Economic Relationship and Impact

evidence.fact: Oahu owner roll: 3,251 parcels with foreign mailing address; Japan 2,024 (62%), Canada 500, South Korea 275; 3,051 of the 3,251 are CPR (condo) units; 96815 has 1,463 and 96814 has 1,002
evidence.source: City & County of Honolulu HoLIS OWNINFO owner tables (local file an/new/owners_oahu.json)

evidence.fact: Japan-billed ownership is heaviest in Waikiki/Ala Moana resort condos: 383 Kalaimoku 108 (34.3% of units) plus Tower 2 63; Trump International Waikiki 148 (31.6%); Ala Moana Hotel Condominium 157; Ilikai 131
evidence.value: Up to about one-third of units in some Waikiki towers
evidence.source: City & County of Honolulu RPAD OWNDAT/LEGDAT, aggregated by TMK

evidence.fact: TG Honolulu district 2025: Japan 187 ($200.1M), Korea 86 ($91.5M); Jan-Jun 2026: Japan 125 ($163.0M), Korea 37 ($48.7M)
evidence.value: Japan + Korea = 7.4% of Honolulu-district sales in H1 2026 (162 of 2,186)
evidence.source: Title Guaranty Buyer Statistics, Oahu Q4 2025 and Q2 2026 district panels

drivers.driver: Developer marketing channels in Asia (Ward Village sold in Japan through Mitsui Fudosan Realty)
drivers.quantified_effect: In 2019 Howard Hughes put Japan at 19% of Ward Village buyers (vs 9% mainland, 67% Hawaii residents). On today's roll, Japan-billed owners are 11-14% of units in recent Ward Village towers (Park 11.1%, Victoria Place 12.3%) vs 1.3% for The Park on Keeaumoku, which had no confirmed Japan channel.

evidence.fact: Howard Hughes and Mitsui Fudosan Realty signed an agreement for Mitsui to support sales of Ward Village residences in Japan
evidence.source: Mitsui Fudosan Realty news release

evidence.fact: Limited one-on-one presentations at Mitsui Premier Lounge Nihonbashi Muromachi (Tokyo) for The Launiu Ward Village, Oct 25-31, 2025
evidence.source: Mitsui Fudosan Realty resort site

evidence.fact: Howard Hughes' Hawaii head said Ward Village buyers were 67% Hawaii residents, 19% Japan and 9% US mainland, with sales in Japan handled by Mitsui Fudosan Realty and others
evidence.source: Toyo Keizai Online

evidence.fact: Japanese-language Ward Village broker booklet (August 2025 edition)
evidence.source: Ward Village broker portal

evidence.fact: Pipeline still to close: Kalae about 93% pre-sold, The Launiu about 71%, Melia and 'Ilima about 60%; 287 units ($1.6B) contracted in 2025
evidence.source: Ward Village / Howard Hughes Q4 2025 release

drivers.driver: Wealth effects and diversification out of yen and won (why buying persists despite weak currencies)
drivers.quantified_effect: Nikkei in dollar terms is about +64% from end-2024 (39,894.54 at about ¥153.8) to June 3, 2026 (68,402.13 at about ¥160.8), more than offsetting the yen's slide for equity-rich buyers. Korean overseas-property remittances rose 41% in 2025 to $590.5M; Hawaii's $93.2M of Korean purchases equals about 16% of that, though the two are not directly comparable since some purchases may be financed in the US.

evidence.fact: Nikkei 225 closed 2025 at 50,339.48 (+26.18% from 39,894.54 at end-2024); closed at 68,402.13 on June 3, 2026
evidence.source: Nikkei Inc. index archive; Jiji/Adnkronos

evidence.fact: Japan's wealthy and ultra-wealthy households (net financial assets of ¥100M or more) reached a record 1.653 million holding ¥469 trillion in 2023, up about 11% in households and 29% in assets from 2021; NRI cites stock gains and the weak yen raising asset values
evidence.source: Nomura Research Institute news release (Feb 13, 2025), via LIMO

evidence.fact: A Hawaii broker described Japanese buying in a weak-yen period as a hedge: holding dollar assets protects buyers if the Japanese market falls
evidence.source: Hawaii Business Magazine

evidence.fact: Korean residents remitted $590.5M abroad for real estate in 2025 (five-year high; $419.5M in 2024) and $210.3M in Jan-Apr 2026, with the US the top destination ($112M); analysts cite domestic multi-home rules and asset diversification
evidence.source: Bank of Korea data via lawmaker Kim Eun-hye, The Herald Business

drivers.driver: Home-country housing and tax rules
drivers.quantified_effect: Korea: rules that tighten domestic lending and multi-home ownership push money abroad, but the June and October 2025 measures came after the 2021-22 contracts that closed in 2025, so they bear on future contracts, not the 2025 count. Japan: central-Tokyo new condos (about ¥195M, roughly $1.30M) now cost about the same as the average Japanese Oahu purchase (about $1.15-1.29M), which removes the old 'Honolulu is pricey' gap. The 2021 loss-offset rule removed a tax-shelter motive for buying older units.

evidence.fact: Korea's June 27, 2025 package capped mortgages in Seoul metro and regulated zones at 600 million won; Oct 15, 2025 measures made all 25 Seoul districts land-transaction-permit zones effective Oct 20 through Dec 31, 2026
evidence.value: 600M won cap; all of Seoul under permit rules
evidence.source: Korea Herald; Financial News (Korea)

evidence.fact: Overseas properties are not counted toward a Korean owner's number of homes, so they avoid domestic multi-home lending limits and heavier taxes
evidence.source: The Herald Business (citing industry observers)

evidence.fact: Japan's FY2020 tax reform (Act on Special Measures Concerning Taxation art. 41-4-3): from 2021 income, rental losses from depreciation on foreign used buildings (simplified useful-life method) are treated as not arising and cannot offset other income
evidence.source: Act on Special Measures Concerning Taxation, art. 41-4-3 (Zeiken law database)

evidence.fact: Tokyo 23-ward average new condo price ¥137.84M in FY2025 (+18.5%); central 6 wards ¥195.03M in 2025 (+20.2%)
evidence.value: About $871K and $1.30M at 2026H1 and 2025 average rates
evidence.source: Real Estate Economic Institute, via nippon.com and FP Trendy

drivers.driver: Air capacity (Haneda/Narita/Incheon)
drivers.quantified_effect: Long run: Japan seats in 2025 were 64% of 2019 and Japanese purchases 63% of 2019, which moved together. H1 2026: Japan seats -0.4% while purchases +52%, so capacity did not cause the H1 jump. Seoul seats in 2025 were 96% of 2019 (+12.2% y/y), and Korean buying per 1,000 Korean visitors rose from 0.13 (2019) to 0.51 (2025).

evidence.fact: Scheduled seats from Japan: 1,999,204 in 2019 (Narita 1,038,135; Haneda 292,730) vs 1,284,581 in 2025 (Narita 467,523, -21.2% y/y; Haneda 535,936)
evidence.source: DBEDT Annual Visitor Research Reports 2019 (Table 95) and 2025 (Table 102)

evidence.fact: H1 2026: 612,837 seats from Japan (-0.4%) and 339,588 Japanese visitors (+6.3%); full-year 2026 scheduled Japan seats 1,230,444 (-5.6%), with Fukuoka service ended and Narita Q4 -18.4%
evidence.value: Seats flat/down while arrivals and purchases rose
evidence.source: HTA Japan Fact Sheet (June 2026 data)

evidence.fact: Seoul seats 326,398 in 2019 vs 313,125 in 2025 (+12.2% y/y); Korea visitors 229,056 in 2019 vs 171,766 in 2025
evidence.source: DBEDT Annual Visitor Research Reports 2019 and 2025

evidence.fact: Korea H1 2026 visitors 73,763 (-1.7%); Seoul seats Q3 2026 -10.6% and Q4 2026 -27.6% as Asiana suspends Incheon-Honolulu Jul 1-Oct 24, 2026 (Korean Air adds 5 weekly)
evidence.source: HTA Korea Fact Sheet (June 2026 data)

evidence.fact: Air Premia scheduled a 5th and 6th weekly Incheon-Honolulu frequency for winter 2025/26
evidence.source: AeroRoutes

drivers.driver: Currency (a headwind that cuts volume over time, not a cause of the 2026 rise)
drivers.quantified_effect: The 2026H1 yen average (158.2) makes dollar assets 45% dearer than in 2019 (109.0). The average Japanese Oahu purchase cost ¥204.8M in H1 2026 vs ¥111.1M in 2019 (+84%, combining FX and higher prices). Over 2016-2025 Japanese purchase value fell 13.3% a year in real terms. The won averaged 1,483 in 2026H1 (1,529.5 in June) but strengthened to about 1,355-1,359 by Sep-Oct 2026, about 11% more buying power than in June.

evidence.source: Federal Reserve H.10 historical rates (Japan, Korea), averaged from daily data

evidence.fact: Japanese residential purchases fell at a compound -13.3% a year from $990.3M (2016) to $273.3M (2025) in constant 2025 dollars, coinciding with yen weakness and fewer arrivals; in 2025 the dollar was 37.7% stronger against the yen than in 2016; 2025 Japanese arrivals were 46.4% of 2019
evidence.source: DBEDT, Hawaii-Japan Economic Relationship and Impact

evidence.fact: Japanese buyers bought 581 Oahu homes worth $700M in 2018 (more than three-quarters of foreign sales); Oahu fell to 319 in 2019, 114 in 2020 and 211 in 2021
evidence.source: Hawaii Business Magazine (Title Guaranty data); TG Oahu Q4 2019

counter_evidence: Buyer origin is a proxy. Title Guaranty classifies by the buyer's address on deed documents, so Japanese or Korean buyers who use a Hawaii address, a US LLC or a local attorney count as local or mainland (DBEDT, May 2026, notes this limitation). Hawaii residents with Korean or Japanese billing addresses could be overcounted. The counts are best read as a floor on true national-origin buying.

The tower attribution is an inference from two different datasets. TG quarterly counts are by buyer address at recording; the county roll shows the current tax-bill country in October 2026. Owners may have resold, used property managers' addresses, or been counted in a different quarter. The fit is close (Park Ward Village: 61 JP and 24 KR vs Q2 2026 Oahu JP 101 and KR 26; Park on Keeaumoku: 80 KR vs H2 2025 KR 79 plus Q1 2026 KR 11) but not a transaction-level match.

Underlying Japanese demand may be weakening, not strengthening. Excluding The Park Ward Village, H1 2026 Oahu Japanese purchases were about 72 vs 84 a year earlier, Q1 2026 (32) was the lowest quarter in the series shown, and 2025 (213 statewide) was below 2024 (267) and 2023 (292).

Flight capacity cannot explain the H1 2026 jump: Japan seats were down 0.4% in H1 2026 and Narita is down 55% from 2019, while purchases rose 52%. Korean arrivals fell 1.7% in H1 2026 even as Korean purchases stayed elevated.

Korean home-country rules (June 27 and Oct 15, 2025) post-date the 2021-22 pre-sale contracts that closed in H2 2025, so they cannot explain those closings. They may show up in future contracts and resales instead.

I found no source confirming that The Park on Keeaumoku was marketed in Korea. The Korean concentration may reflect the project's location on Honolulu's informal Koreatown corridor (Keeaumoku, 'Korea-moku', Hawaii News Now 2023-12-29), Korean-American networks using Korean addresses, or a few multi-unit buyers, rather than a campaign.

Small numbers. Korea's 87 purchases are 0.8% of Oahu sales, and a single building moves the total. TG and DBEDT counts also differ slightly (Oahu foreign H1 2026: TG 195 vs DBEDT 199; 2024 statewide DBEDT 18,007 vs TG 16,709).

Wealth-effect and diversification motives come from aggregate data (Nikkei, NRI, Bank of Korea remittances) and broker quotes, not buyer surveys. No public data shows how these buyers funded purchases (yen, existing dollar holdings, or US mortgages).

The figure of 55.5% of foreign-held property, plant and equipment owned by Japanese entities (BEA 2023, via DBEDT) covers commercial and corporate assets, not home purchases. It should not be quoted as a share of residential buying.
research.for_brokers: Treat Japanese and Korean buyer counts as lumpy, closing-driven series. Forecast them from the tower delivery schedule, not from the exchange rate. The next spikes will come when Kalae (about 93% pre-sold), The Launiu (about 71%) and Melia/'Ilima (about 60%) close (Ward Village, Feb 2026). Expect a step-down in recorded Japanese and Korean purchases in quarters with no deliveries; Q1 2026 had only 32 Japanese and 11 Korean purchases on Oahu. Japan demand reaches Ward Village mainly through Mitsui Fudosan Realty's Tokyo channel. A sizable Japan-billed resale base sits in Waikiki and Ala Moana resort condos: Trump Waikiki 148 units, 383 Kalaimoku about 171, Ala Moana Hotel Condo 157, Ilikai 131. Ward Village towers that closed in 2016-2026 hold about 290 more. As these owners age or rebalance, expect listings that need Japanese-language service and early planning for HARPTA/FIRPTA withholding on nonresident and foreign sellers. On currency, the yen is still weak (about ¥157-158 in early October 2026), so price new-contract Japanese demand conservatively. The won strengthened about 11% from June to September 2026 (1,529.5 to 1,359.2), but Seoul seats are scheduled 27.6% lower in Q4 2026 during the Asiana suspension. Korean buyers clustered in the Keeaumoku/Ala Moana corridor and in Ward Village. Bank of Korea data show the US as the top destination for Korean overseas-property money in 2026. Any country-targeted outreach should be reviewed for fair-housing compliance.
research.for_locals: Japanese and Korean buyers are visible but small. Together they made about 2.6% of Oahu purchases in 2025 (289 of 11,097) and about 3.3% of dollar volume. Their buying is concentrated in new Kakaako/Ala Moana towers and Waikiki resort condos, at average prices around $1.0-1.3M, far above the Oahu condo median of $510,000 (HBR, August 2026). Most local condo shoppers are therefore not bidding against them for the same units. The 2026 'surge' reflects towers sold in 2021-22 finally closing, not a new wave of overseas demand. In the Honolulu district they reached about 7% of H1 2026 sales (162 of 2,186). Where they matter more is specific buildings: up to about one-third of units in some Waikiki towers and 8% of The Park on Keeaumoku are owned from abroad, which means more part-time occupancy. Overseas pre-sales also help finance towers that carry reserved housing; Ulana Ward Village delivered 690 reserved units to local households in Q4 2025. Foreign-mailing owners hold about 1% of Oahu parcels overall, 6.2% in Waikiki (96815) and 5.1% in 96814.

challenge.question: Why does Japan dominate foreign buying, concentrated on Oahu (mostly Honolulu condos), and why did Japanese purchases rise in H1 2026 despite a historically weak yen? Why is Korean buying rising on Oahu (40 in 2024 to 87 in 2025)?

verdicts.driver: Closing-timing of pre-sold new towers: contracts signed in 2021-22 are recorded as purchases when the towers deliver
verdicts.reason: I re-checked this and it holds. It is even stronger than the researcher stated. The quarterly counts check out against the Title Guaranty PDFs and tg.json. Japan on Oahu: 39, 45, 69, 49 in 2025, then 32 and 101 in H1 2026. Korea: 2, 6, 39, 40, then 11 and 26. Howard Hughes' Q2 2026 supplemental (8-K, Aug 2026, https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/0001981792/000162828026053303/hhhsupplemental2q26.htm) confirms 527 units closed at The Park Ward Village for $706.3M, 97% of the building. Ward Village releases (https://communities.howardhughes.com/press-releases/ward-village-breaks-ground-on-the-park-ward-village/, 2022) show the tower was 84.2% pre-sold by end-2021 and 90.6% by mid-2022. Fed H.10 rates over the selling window were ¥111.8 (2021H2) and ¥123.1 (2022H1). I re-ran the tax-roll aggregation on the local OWNDAT pull (tax-bill country, data dated 2026-10-05). The bundled script's seq filter drops most units, so I removed it. The result: The Park Ward Village has 550 parcels with 61 Japan-billed and 24 Korea-billed owners. The Park on Keeaumoku has 1,002 parcels with 80 Korea and 13 Japan. Victoria Place has 350 parcels with 43 Japan and 17 Korea. There are 249 Korea-billed condo units in all. New evidence the researcher missed: the 2024 Korean base was itself a closing spike. The TG Oahu Jan-Sep 2024 edition shows Korea at 9 and Japan at 133, so Q4 2024 alone had 31 of the year's 40 Korean purchases and 127 of 260 Japanese. Victoria Place closings began in November 2024 (HHH Q3 2024 8-K, https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1981792/000162828024044983/hhhearningsreleaseq32024.htm). History shows the same pattern. Honolulu foreign purchases (DBEDT Data Book, local page_data tg) peaked at 703 in 2016 and 739 in 2018, the Waiea and Ae'o delivery years. Japanese Oahu purchases fell from 581 in 2018 (Hawaii Business, 2022-07-19) to 319 in 2019 (TG Oahu Q4 2019). In those same years the yen was flat (110.4 to 109.0) and Japanese arrivals rose 5.8% (DBEDT 2019 annual, Table 20). Two caveats. First, matching roll owners to quarterly purchases is approximate: Victoria Place's 43 Japan-billed owners explain only about half of Q4 2024's roughly 83 above-baseline Japanese purchases. Second, the match between the $1.34M foreign average and The Park's per-unit price is a coincidence and proves nothing.
fact_errors: The '40 in 2024 to 87 in 2025' Korean rise compares two closing-inflated years. 31 of 2024's 40 came in Q4 2024 when Victoria Place closed (TG Oahu Jan-Sep 2024 Korea = 9). In quarters with no deliveries, Korean purchases ran 2-6 per quarter.
Treating the Q2 2026 Honolulu foreign average ($1,343,414) as evidence because it matches The Park Ward Village per-unit price ($706.3M / 527 = $1.34M) is coincidence, not attribution. Drop it.

'61 Japan-billed owners ... enough to account for the whole +49' should be stated as approximate. In the Victoria Place case the roll explains only about half of the quarter's excess Japanese purchases (43 vs ~83).

Minor: Japan-billed share is 11.2% of The Park Ward Village parcels (61/550) and about 12.5% of Victoria Place known-address units. TG Honolulu-district Korea 2023 (22) exceeds the island-level figure in the Q4 2023 Oahu edition (21), most likely a revision.
verdicts.corrected_wording: Recorded Japanese and Korean purchases on Oahu track when big pre-sold towers deliver, not when buyers decide. Oahu Japanese purchases jumped from 32 in Q1 2026 to 101 in Q2 2026, the quarter Howard Hughes closed 527 units at The Park Ward Village. Those contracts were signed mainly in July 2021-mid 2022, when the yen was about ¥112-123. The county roll now shows 61 Japan-billed owners there. Outside that tower, Japanese buying was roughly 72 in H1 2026 vs 84 in H1 2025. Korea shows the same pattern twice: 31 of 2024's 40 Korean purchases came in Q4 2024 as Victoria Place closed, and 79 of 2025's 87 came in H2 2025 as The Park on Keeaumoku (80 Korea-billed units today) began closing. In quarters with no deliveries, Koreans bought 2-6 Oahu homes per quarter. Matching buildings to quarterly purchases is approximate, not a transaction-level match.

verdicts.driver: Oahu-centric tourism ties, repeat visitation and an installed base of Japanese condo owners (why Oahu, why Honolulu condos)
verdicts.reason: This explains where Japanese buyers buy. It does not explain changes in volume. Visitor figures re-checked in the DBEDT 2025 Annual Visitor Research Report, Table 22 (https://files.hawaii.gov/dbedt/economic/tourism/annual-reports/2025-annual-visitor.xlsx): 749,596 Japan MMA air visitors, 731,979 of them visiting Oahu (97.6%), 71.2% repeaters, 108,593 planned condo stays. Table 33 (Korea): 171,766 visitors, 169,176 on Oahu. The DBEDT Hawaii-Japan report (May 2026, https://files.hawaii.gov/dbedt/economic/reports/Hawaii-Japan-Economic-Relationship-and-Impacts_May2026.pdf) confirms 92.6% of 2016-2025 Japanese home purchases were on Oahu. It adds a structural fact the researcher left out: 'As of 2026, all the air seat capacity between Japan and Hawai'i was through O'ahu.' The owner-roll figures re-check (owners_oahu.json): 2,024 Japan-mailing parcels (62% of 3,251 foreign), 3,051 of the 3,251 are CPR units, and 78.9% sit in 96815/96814. Building concentrations re-check: Trump Waikiki 148, 383 Kalaimoku 108 + 63, Ala Moana Hotel Condo 157, Ilikai 131. The visitor-propensity argument does not survive. Japanese purchases per 1,000 Japanese visitors were 0.39 in 2018 (581 / 1.49M), against 0.20 in 2019 and 0.27 in 2025, so the trend depends on the base year. The 2025 numerator also includes closings of contracts signed in 2021, when Japanese arrivals were only 18,936 (HTA Japan Fact Sheet, July 2026). For Korea, tourism ties are thin. 66.4% of 2025 Korean visitors were first-timers (HTA Korea Fact Sheet, https://hta.hawaii.gov/wp-content/uploads/2026/07/Korea-Fact-Sheet-with-June-2026-data-final-1.pdf, 2026-07-31). The Keeaumoku pre-sales opened in August 2021, when Korean arrivals were running at 10,652 a year.
fact_errors: 'Japanese purchases per 1,000 Japanese visitors rose from 0.20 (2019) to 0.27 (2025), so the remaining visitors are more likely to buy' depends on the base year (2018 was about 0.39). The 2025 count is inflated by closings of contracts signed when few Japanese could visit.
Tourism ties do not explain the Korean pre-sale contracts. They were signed in 2021-22, when Korean arrivals were 10,652 (2021) and 111,863 (2022).
verdicts.corrected_wording: Oahu and Honolulu condos dominate because Japan's links to Hawaii run only through Oahu. All scheduled Japan-Hawaii seats land at Honolulu (DBEDT, May 2026), 97.6% of 2025 Japanese visitors spent time on Oahu, 71% were repeat visitors, and Japanese owners already hold about 2,000 Oahu parcels, almost all condo units in Waikiki and Ala Moana/Kakaako. This explains where Japanese buyers buy, not why the count moves from year to year. It explains little about Korean buyers, two-thirds of whom are first-time visitors.

verdicts.driver: Developer marketing channels in Asia (Ward Village sold in Japan through Mitsui Fudosan Realty)
verdicts.reason: Supported as an explanation of which buildings Japanese buyers choose, with moderate strength. Toyo Keizai (2019, https://toyokeizai.net/articles/-/568755, saved locally) quotes Howard Hughes' Hawaii head: buyers were 67% Hawaii residents, 19% Japan and 9% mainland, and Mitsui Fudosan Realty and others handle sales in Japan. The Ward Village 2025 release (https://ward-village.prezly.com/ward-villager-reports-record-2025-residential-sales-and-major-community-milestones, 2026-02-19) is consistent. The cited Feb 2018 Mitsui press-release PDF returned HTTP 403, and the Mitsui resort site is blocked here, so the 2018 start date and the Oct 2025 Tokyo event could not be re-verified. On the roll, Ward Village towers are 4-12% Japan-billed, against 1.3% for The Park on Keeaumoku. That fits a channel effect, but it is confounded with product type and price. The 19% (contracts, 2019) vs roughly 11% (current tax-bill country) gap shows that roll counts undercount Japanese buyers who use Hawaii billing addresses. Recount of Japan-billed owners in the seven market-rate Ward Village towers: Waiea 10, Anaha 20, Ae'o 30, 'A'ali'i 31, Ko'ula 44, Victoria Place 43, The Park 61, total 239. The researcher said about 290. Pipeline figures are now from HHH's Aug 2026 supplemental: Kalae 94% contracted, delivery 2028; The Launiu 75%, 2028; Melia 70%, 2030; 'Ilima 63%, 2030. The '287 units ($1.6B) contracted in 2025' figure could not be reconciled from the release text I could read.
fact_errors: 'Ward Village towers that closed in 2016-2026 hold about 290 more' Japan-billed units: the rerun gives 239 across the seven market-rate towers.
Pipeline percentages are out of date. HHH Q2 2026 supplemental (Aug 2026): Kalae 94%, The Launiu 75%, Melia 70%, 'Ilima 63%. Delivery: Kalae and Launiu 2028, Melia and 'Ilima 2030.
The Feb 2018 Mitsui-Howard Hughes agreement date could not be independently re-verified (source PDF returned 403). Mitsui's sales role is confirmed only by the 2019 Toyo Keizai article.
verdicts.corrected_wording: Ward Village has been sold in Japan through Mitsui Fudosan Realty and others. In 2019 Howard Hughes put Japanese buyers at 19% of Ward Village contracts. Today the recent Ward Village towers are about 11-12% Japan-billed on the tax roll, against 1.3% at The Park on Keeaumoku. Marketing channels plausibly steer which buildings Japanese buyers choose, but they do not explain the national totals, and the channel effect cannot be separated from price and product.

verdicts.driver: Wealth effects and diversification out of yen and won
verdicts.reason: The numbers are right but they do not explain the pattern. The Nikkei closed 2025 at 50,339.48, up 26.18% (Jiji via nippon.com, https://www.nippon.com/en/news/yjj2025123000562, 2025-12-30), and closed at 68,402.13 on June 3, 2026 (Nikkei archive, https://indexes.nikkei.co.jp/en/nkave/archives/record?select=0). The H1 2026 rise, however, came from contracts committed in 2021-22, so a 2025-26 wealth effect is not needed to explain it. In quarters with no tower deliveries, Japanese buying actually slipped, from about 44 per quarter (Q1-Q3 2024) to about 36 in H1 2026 excluding The Park, while the dollar value of the Nikkei rose about 64%. That is evidence against a wealth effect raising volume. One reading the data does support: about 97% of The Park's units closed (HHH Aug 2026) even though the yen sat near ¥158, so wealth, earlier dollar holdings or sunk deposits likely kept buyers from walking away. That is untested. On Korea, the Herald Business article (https://biz.heraldcorp.com/article/10776633, 2026-06-05) confirms $590.5M in 2025 remittances for overseas real estate. The same article shows 2021 at $589M and 2022 at $540.9M, so the '2025 five-year high' is only $1.5M above 2021. It is a return to the 2021 level, not a break-out. The BOK figures are national and not Hawaii-specific, and the motive evidence comes from analysts and broker quotes, not buyer surveys.
fact_errors: 'Five-year-high $590.5M in 2025' overstates the trend: 2021 was $589M (same Herald/BOK article).
The wealth effect cannot explain the H1 2026 rise, which was closings of 2021-22 contracts. Underlying Japanese buying fell while the Nikkei rose.
Minor: the won's move from 1,529.5 (June) to 1,359.2 (Sep) means dollar assets cost about 11% fewer won. The won itself appreciated about 12.5%.
verdicts.corrected_wording: Japanese equity gains (Nikkei about +64% in dollar terms, end-2024 to June 3, 2026) and Korean asset diversification may help explain why nearly all pre-sale buyers closed despite weak currencies. They did not raise underlying Japanese buying, which slipped. Korean overseas-property remittances in 2025 ($590.5M) only matched 2021's $589M, and no data ties them to Hawaii purchases.

verdicts.driver: Home-country housing and tax rules
verdicts.reason: Partly mistimed and partly speculative. The researcher concedes that Korea's June 27 and Oct 15, 2025 measures (600M-won mortgage cap, all of Seoul under permit rules; Financial News, https://en.fnnews.com/news/202510200846485506) came after the contracts that closed in 2025. The timing-consistent Korean rule is the July 10, 2020 package. It raised acquisition tax on multi-home buyers to 8-12% and the comprehensive holding tax ceiling to 6%, effective 2021 (Asia Economy, https://www.asiae.co.kr/en/article/2020071011451095231, 2020-07-10). It came just before the 2021-22 pre-sale wave, and BOK overseas-property remittances were $589M in 2021 and $540.9M in 2022. Overseas homes do not count toward a Korean owner's number of homes (Herald, 2026-06-05). This is circumstantial and reported, not shown at buyer level. Japan's FY2020 reform (Special Taxation Measures Act art. 41-4-3; loss offset denied for foreign used buildings from 2021) is real (https://www.zeiken.co.jp/hourei/HHSOZ000000/41-4-3.html). No source measures its effect on Hawaii, and Japanese buying had already fallen from 581 (2018) to 319 (2019) before it applied. The Tokyo-vs-Honolulu price comparison is accurate on the numbers: REEI FY2025 23-ward average ¥137.84M, +18.5% (Jiji/nippon.com, https://www.nippon.com/en/news/yjj2026042000838/, 2026-04-20). There is no evidence it changes buying.
fact_errors: The Korean rules cited (June 27 and Oct 15, 2025) post-date the contracts behind the 2025 closings. The timing-consistent rules are the July 10, 2020 multi-home tax measures (effective 2021).
The claim that similar Tokyo and Honolulu condo prices 'removed the old Honolulu is pricey gap' and so drove buying has no supporting evidence.
verdicts.corrected_wording: Korea's 2020 multi-home tax increases (acquisition tax up to 12%, holding tax up to 6%, effective 2021) came just before the 2021-22 wave of Korean pre-sale contracts in Honolulu. Overseas homes do not count toward Korean multi-home limits. The link is plausible but circumstantial. Japan's 2021 rule ending loss offsets on foreign used buildings may have reduced resale-condo buying, but its effect on Hawaii has not been measured. The 2025 Korean lending curbs can only affect future contracts.

verdicts.driver: Air capacity (Haneda/Narita/Incheon)
verdicts.reason: The seat counts re-check: DBEDT 2019 Table 95 (Japan 1,999,204; Narita 1,038,135; Haneda 292,730; Seoul 326,398) and 2025 Table 102 (Japan 1,284,581; Narita 467,523; Haneda 535,936; Seoul 313,125). The long-run co-movement (seats 64% of 2019, purchases 63%) is not robust. From 2018 to 2019, Japanese Oahu purchases fell 45% (581 to 319) while Japanese arrivals rose 5.8% (DBEDT 2019 Table 20) and seats were roughly flat (-2.1%). The 2021-22 contracts closing now were signed when air service was a fraction of normal. The Q4 2026 Seoul attribution is wrong. The HTA Korea Fact Sheet (2026-07-31) says Asiana's Incheon-Honolulu suspension runs Jul 1-Oct 24, 2026, and that Korean Air adds 5 weekly flights 'to maintain route capacity'. The -27.6% Q4 seat figure comes from a Diio schedule snapshot dated Feb 23, 2026, 'subject to change', so it cannot be pinned on Asiana. What survives is the structural point: all Japan capacity lands at Honolulu (DBEDT, May 2026).
fact_errors: 'Seoul seats Q4 2026 -27.6% as Asiana suspends': HTA says Korean Air adds 5 weekly to maintain capacity, the suspension ends Oct 24, and the Q4 figure is a Feb 23, 2026 schedule snapshot subject to change.
The '64% seats vs 63% purchases' co-movement is coincidental: 2018-2019 purchases fell 45% while arrivals rose 5.8%.
Minor source mismatch: the HTA Japan fact sheet gives 1,303,505 Japan seats for 2025, the DBEDT annual report Table 102 gives 1,284,581.
verdicts.corrected_wording: Air links explain where Japanese buyers buy (all Japan seats land in Honolulu), not when or how many. Japanese purchases fell 45% from 2018 to 2019 while arrivals rose, and the contracts closing in 2025-26 were signed when travel was near zero. Seoul capacity was 96% of 2019 in 2025. Q4 2026 Seoul schedules look lower in a February snapshot, but HTA says Korean Air is offsetting Asiana's summer suspension.

verdicts.driver: Currency (a headwind that cuts volume over time, not a cause of the 2026 rise)
verdicts.reason: The narrow claim holds: the weak yen did not cause the 2026 rise, because the contracts were signed in US dollars in 2021-22 and closed on the developer's schedule. FX re-checks from FRED/H.10 daily data (local DEXJPUS/DEXKOUS): yen 109.0 (2019), 151.5 (2024), 149.6 (2025), 158.2 (2026H1), 157.81 (Oct 2); won 1,165.8 (2019), 1,421.4 (2025), 1,483.3 (2026H1), 1,529.5 (Jun 2026), 1,359.2 (Sep 2026). The yen cost per average purchase re-checks (¥204.8M in H1 2026 vs ¥111.1M in 2019). The DBEDT -13.3% per year real decline (May 2026) re-checks, but DBEDT only says it 'coincides with marked Yen weakness and lower Japanese visitor arrivals'. It is a correlation over a period confounded by Covid, the tower-delivery calendar and Japan's 2021 tax change. The 2018-2019 drop of 45% with a flat yen shows the currency is not the main driver of year-to-year swings. A plausible but unquantified effect is on new contracts.
fact_errors: The -13.3% per year decline should not be attributed to the yen alone. DBEDT presents it as coinciding with yen weakness and lower arrivals, not as caused by them.
verdicts.corrected_wording: The weak yen (¥158 in H1 2026 vs ¥109 in 2019) raises the yen cost of a Honolulu condo and is a plausible drag on new Japanese contracts. It cannot explain the 2026 jump, which was closings of dollar-priced contracts signed at ¥112-123. Japanese purchase value fell about 13% a year in real terms from 2016 to 2025 (DBEDT), but that decline also reflects Covid, fewer visitors, tower timing and a 2021 Japanese tax change.

missing_drivers: Delivery calendar going forward. Per HHH's Q2 2026 supplemental (Aug 2026), the next Ward Village deliveries are Kalae (329 units, 94% contracted) and The Launiu (485, 75%) in 2028, and Melia (220, 70%) and 'Ilima (148, 63%) in 2030. Inference: until then, recorded Japanese and Korean purchases should revert toward their non-delivery pace, about 30-45 Japanese and a handful of Korean purchases per quarter on Oahu. Other developers' 2026-27 deliveries were not checked.

History of the same mechanism. Honolulu foreign purchases spiked to 703 in 2016 and 739 in 2018, the Waiea and Ae'o delivery years (DBEDT Data Book). Japanese Oahu purchases fell from 581 in 2018 to 319 in 2019 with the yen flat (110.4 to 109.0) and Japanese arrivals up 5.8%.
Air access geography: all scheduled Japan-Hawaii seat capacity lands on Oahu (DBEDT Hawaii-Japan report, May 2026). There is no Japan-Kona nonstop.

Developer identity and network for the Korean concentration. The Park on Keeaumoku was developed by Nan Inc. founder Nan Chul Shin, reported (third-party profile) to be Korean-born. A Korean investor group bought the site block in 2007 (Honolulu Advertiser, 2010). The tower sits on the Keeaumoku corridor. No Korea-based marketing campaign was found.

Timing-consistent Korean push factor: the July 10, 2020 multi-home tax package (acquisition tax up to 12%, holding tax up to 6%, effective 2021) and BOK overseas-property remittances of $589M (2021) and $540.9M (2022), coinciding with the 2021-22 pre-sale contracting.

Dollar price lock-in: pre-sale prices were fixed in dollars at contract, and about 97% of The Park Ward Village closed in Q2 2026 even with the yen near ¥158. The currency changed buyers' cost, not when the purchases were recorded.

Measurement. Title Guaranty counts deeds by buyer address at recording, while the MLS misses most developer closings: HBR Oahu condo sales in Apr-Jun 2026 were 1,114 (local page_data) against 2,079 Honolulu condo recordings in DBEDT/TG Q2 2026. The 'surge' is largely invisible in MLS data.

Untested alternatives (not checked because the web-search budget ran out). First, zoning that allows transient vacation rentals in resort-zoned Waikiki condo-hotels may explain the Japan-billed concentration in Trump Waikiki, 383 Kalaimoku, Ilikai and the Ala Moana Hotel Condo. Second, a Korean long-stay or education motive (Korean rental-house stays +37.6% in 2025) has no direct evidence.
challenge.final_answer: Japan leads foreign buying on Oahu because its ties to Hawaii run almost entirely through Honolulu. All scheduled seats from Japan land there (DBEDT, May 2026). 97.6% of the 749,596 Japanese visitors in 2025 spent time on Oahu, and 71% were repeat visitors. Japan-billed owners already hold about 2,000 Oahu parcels, nearly all condo units in Waikiki and Ala Moana/Kakaako. Ward Village has also been sold in Tokyo through Mitsui Fudosan Realty. The H1 2026 'rise' is not new demand defying a weak yen. It is the recording of contracts signed in 2021-22, when the yen was about ¥112-123, at The Park Ward Village. Howard Hughes closed 527 units there in Q2 2026, the same quarter Oahu Japanese purchases jumped from 32 to 101, and the county roll now shows 61 Japan-billed owners in the tower. Outside that building, Japanese buying ran about 72 in H1 2026 against 84 a year earlier: flat to slightly down. Korean buying followed the same pattern twice. 31 of 2024's 40 Korean purchases came in Q4 2024, when Victoria Place closed. 79 of 2025's 87 came in the second half, when The Park on Keeaumoku began closing; that building holds 80 Korea-billed units today. In quarters with no tower deliveries, Koreans bought only 2-6 Oahu homes per quarter. History shows the same thing. Japanese purchases fell from 581 in 2018 (the year Ae'o delivered) to 319 in 2019, even though the yen was flat and Japanese arrivals rose. Currency, stock-market wealth and home-country rules affect whether contracts get signed, but the evidence for them is aggregate and circumstantial. The clearest well-timed factor on the Korean side is Seoul's 2020 tax increases on multi-home owners, which came just before the 2021-22 pre-sale wave. Matching tax-roll owners to quarterly purchases is approximate, and buyer-address counts are a floor. With no Ward Village tower due before 2028, recorded Japanese and Korean purchases should fall back toward their non-delivery pace (an inference; other developers' deliveries were not checked). Confidence: high on the timing explanation, medium on the underlying motives.

research.question: Why are Canadians the top foreign buyers on Maui and Hawaii Island, and why did Canadian purchases fall from 106 (2024) to 64 (2025)?
research.answer: Canadians lead foreign buying on Maui and Hawaii Island because of geography and habit. Western Canada has a winter "snowbird" corridor with nonstop flights to Kahului and Kona, while every Japan route lands in Honolulu, which is why Japanese and Korean buyers stay concentrated on Oahu. Canadian visitors are mostly repeat, long-stay winter guests: two-thirds have been before, they average about 3.8 trips and 11 days per stay, and many use condos or timeshares. Maui also already has about 1,600 Canadian-mailing parcels, mostly South Maui vacation-rental condos. Canada was the No. 1 foreign buyer on both islands in every Title Guaranty full-year report from 2015 to 2025. The 2024-to-2025 fall (106 to 64 statewide, -40%; $186.0M to $110.7M) happened almost entirely on the neighbor islands: Maui County went from 39 to 11 and Hawaii Island from 33 to 17, while Oahu rose from 31 to 35. On Maui, foreign purchases on the South Side (Kihei/Wailea/Makena) fell from 34 to 7, roughly the whole county drop. The decline came in two stages. Neighbor-island Canadian closings had already collapsed in early 2025 (Maui Jan–Mar: 2, down from 15), before the travel boycott could affect closings. At that time the Canadian dollar was at its weakest monthly average since 2003, Canadian air seats were already down 9–10%, and Maui's Bill 9 plan to phase out apartment-zoned vacation rentals (proposed May 2024, signed December 2025) was hitting the Kihei condo-plus-rental model Canadians relied on. From mid-2025 the political boycott and deeper seat cuts drove the statewide numbers lower: only 15 Canadian purchases in July–December 2025 versus 43 a year earlier, and 26 in January–June 2026 versus 49. Our reading is that Maui's drop is mostly about Bill 9 and the CAD, and the later statewide drop is mostly about the boycott and fewer flights. The data show the timing but cannot prove causes. Other factors played smaller parts or none: the 2% annual CAD move explains roughly 7–12%; US tax and estate rules did not change; and the WestJet Lihue cancellation is a 2026–27 event on an island where Canadians bought only 1–3 homes a year.

drivers.driver: Structural (why Canadians lead): a Western-Canada snowbird corridor with nonstop flights to Kahului and Kona, repeat long-stay visitors, and an existing Canadian owner base on Maui. Japanese and Korean buyers concentrate on Oahu because Japan's flights all go to Honolulu.
drivers.quantified_effect: Canada made up 39 of 42 foreign purchases in Maui County (93%) and 33 of 45 on Hawaii Island (73%) in 2024. Kahului received about 35% of Canadian nonstop seats in Jan 2026, while every Japan route listed in the Oct 2026 grid lands in Honolulu. 41% of Canadian visitors went to Maui in 2025, against about 26% of all visitors.

evidence.fact: Canada was the No. 1 foreign buyer in Maui County and on Hawaii Island in every Title Guaranty full-year report from 2015 to 2025, and in Jan–Jun 2026. Maui County Canadian purchases by year: 2015 80, 2016 59, 2017 66, 2018 82, 2019 42, 2020 29, 2021 48, 2022 34, 2023 27, 2024 39, 2025 11. Hawaii Island: 29, 17, 36, 44, 37, 21, 48, 38, 28, 33, 17.
evidence.value: Maui 2024: Canada 39 of 42 foreign; Hawaii Island 2024: 33 of 45
evidence.source: Title Guaranty Hawaii, Buyer Statistics Q4 editions 2015–2025 (Maui and Hawaii Island PDFs)

evidence.fact: Statewide 2025 foreign buyers were Japan 213, Korea 87 and Canada 64. Oahu accounted for Japan 202 and Korea 87. On the neighbor islands Canada led: Hawaii Island 17 (Japan 10) and Maui County 11.
evidence.source: Title Guaranty Hawaii, Buyer Statistics Q4 2025

evidence.fact: January 2026 scheduled Canada–Hawaii nonstops: 277 flights and 52,311 seats. Kahului had 18,245 seats (Vancouver 12,547, Calgary 4,480, Edmonton 1,218); Honolulu 24,194; Kona 7,436 (Vancouver 4,876, Calgary 2,262, Kelowna 298); Lihue 2,436.
evidence.value: Kahului 35% / Kona 14% / Lihue 4.7% of Canadian seats

evidence.source: HVCB Air Service Grid, October 2026 (as of 16 Jun 2026)

evidence.fact: Hawaii had 389,241 Canadian air visitors in 2025. By province: British Columbia 44.6%, Ontario 23.3%, Alberta 15.7%. 158,780 visited Maui island (40.8%) and 69,597 Hawaii Island. 65.7% were repeat visitors, averaging 3.8 trips. Average statewide stay was 11.1 days. 87,992 stayed in condos and 35,279 in timeshares.

evidence.fact: Maui County tax-bill mailing addresses: 1,602 parcels go to Canada, 87.3% of the 1,835 foreign-mailing parcels. 1,099 of the foreign parcels are in South Maui (postal Kihei: Kihei, Wailea, Makena), and 1,173 are condo units in the short-term-rental tax class.
evidence.value: 1,602 Canadian-mailing parcels; 60% of foreign parcels in South Maui
evidence.source: Maui County GIS Parcel Fabric (tax parcels with postal mailing fields), aggregated in owners_neighbor.json

drivers.driver: Seasonal buying: Canadian purchases cluster in winter and spring, so a weak 2025–26 snowbird season fed straight into fewer closings. US and Canadian residency rules cap how long snowbirds stay.
drivers.quantified_effect: 59% of 2024 Canadian purchases closed in Jan–Jun (63 of 106). After a winter when Canadian arrivals fell 9–22% month by month, Jan–Jun 2026 purchases were 26, down from 49 (-47%).

evidence.fact: Canadian arrivals to Hawaii by month: January 2025 54,333; March 2025 53,621; June 2025 14,363. Peak winter months bring roughly 4 times as many Canadians as June.
evidence.source: DBEDT monthly visitor statistics press releases, Jan and Jun 2025

evidence.fact: Statewide Canadian purchases by quarter in 2024: Q1 32, Q2 31, Q3 16, Q4 27 (derived from the cumulative Q1, Q2, Q3 and Q4 2024 editions: 32, 63, 79, 106). Maui County: Q1 2024 15 of the year's 39.
evidence.source: Title Guaranty Hawaii, Buyer Statistics Q1–Q3 2024 editions

evidence.fact: Canadian arrivals in the 2025–26 winter versus a year earlier: Oct 2025 -20.3%, Nov 2025 -22.2%, Dec 2025 -14.0%, Jan 2026 -8.7%, Feb 2026 -4.6%, Mar 2026 -11.4%.
evidence.source: DBEDT monthly visitor statistics press releases

evidence.fact: Statewide Canadian purchases: Jan–Jun 2026 26 ($58.3M), against Jan–Jun 2025 49 ($94.9M).
evidence.source: Title Guaranty Hawaii, Buyer Statistics Q2 2026 and Q2 2025 editions

evidence.fact: Substantial presence test: a person becomes a US tax resident with 183 weighted days over 3 years (all current-year days, 1/3 of the prior year's, 1/6 of the year before). Form 8840 claims the closer-connection exception.
evidence.source: IRS, Substantial Presence Test

evidence.fact: BC Medical Services Plan requires being physically present in BC at least six months in a calendar year. Vacation absences of up to seven months are allowed.
evidence.source: Government of British Columbia, MSP eligibility

drivers.driver: The 2025 Canadian pullback from US travel after the tariffs and annexation rhetoric (the 'boycott'). It explains the statewide and Oahu decline from mid-2025 into 2026 better than it explains Maui's early-2025 collapse.
drivers.quantified_effect: Canadian visitors to Hawaii fell 12.7% in 2025, but Canadian purchases fell 40%. Statewide Canadian purchases in Jul–Dec 2025 were 15, down from 43 a year earlier (-65%). Oahu went from 31 in Jan–Jun 2025 to 4 in Jul–Dec 2025 and 8 in Jan–Jun 2026. Our interpretation: if purchases had moved one-for-one with visitors, the visitor drop would account for only about 14 of the 42 lost purchases.

evidence.fact: Canadian air visitors: 389,241 in 2025 against 445,985 in 2024 (sum of provinces). That is -12.7% in the final annual tables; DBEDT's preliminary January 2026 figure was -11.6%. By province: BC -17.6%, Ontario -14.7%, Alberta -8.8%.
evidence.source: DBEDT Annual Visitor Research Reports 2025 and 2024, Table 25

evidence.fact: DBEDT: Canadian arrivals were down 20.3% in October 2025, and 'Impacted by economic and political uncertainty, there have been fewer visitors from Canada in every month of 2025 so far compared to 2024.'
evidence.source: DBEDT October 2025 visitor statistics press release

evidence.fact: Canadian-resident return trips from the US by air fell 24.2% year over year in May 2025, to 488,800 (Statistics Canada, as reported).
evidence.source: BNN Bloomberg (Canadian Press) citing Statistics Canada

evidence.fact: Statistics Canada 'Tourism activity, 2025': Canadian visits to the US were 30,185,000 in 2024 and 23,096,000 in 2025 (about -23.5%). These figures come from a search-engine extract because the page is blocked from this environment.
evidence.source: Statistics Canada, Tourism activity, 2025 (11-627-M)

evidence.fact: A Longwoods survey relayed by DBEDT found 53% of Canadians say US politics and tariffs make them less likely to visit, down from a 63% peak in July 2025. 23% had cancelled US trips in the past six months.
evidence.source: Maui Now, quoting DBEDT/READ

evidence.fact: Canadian purchases by half-year. Oahu: H1 2024 21, H2 2024 10, H1 2025 31, H2 2025 4, H1 2026 8. Statewide: H2 2024 43, H2 2025 15.
evidence.source: Title Guaranty Hawaii, Buyer Statistics (Oahu Q2 2024, Q4 2024, Q2 2025, Q4 2025, Q2 2026)

evidence.fact: Canadian arrivals in Jan–Aug 2026 were 252,906, against 269,169 in Jan–Aug 2025 (-6.0%; sum of monthly releases). July 2026 was +2.7% and August +0.6%, a sign the decline is bottoming out.
evidence.source: DBEDT monthly visitor statistics press releases Jan–Aug 2026

drivers.driver: Weak Canadian dollar. It is a strong long-run reason Canadian buying is far below its 2010–2013 level, but only a small part of the 2025 change.
drivers.quantified_effect: Our regressions of Data Book foreign-buyer counts on CAD/USD for 2008–2025 give elasticities of -3.6 to -6.2 for Maui and -2.9 to -3.5 for Hawaii County. The +2.0% move in the annual average CAD/USD therefore implies roughly -7% to -12%, against an observed -72% (Maui) and -48% (Hawaii Island) for Canadian purchases. The trough months (Dec 2024–Mar 2025) do line up with Maui's Q1 2025 collapse.

evidence.fact: Annual average CAD per USD: 2010–2013 about 0.99–1.03; 2023 1.349; 2024 1.370; 2025 1.397. The January 2025 monthly average of 1.4389 was the highest since April 2003, and the daily peak was 1.4601 on 2025-02-03. The rate was 1.4253 on 2026-10-02.
evidence.source: Federal Reserve H.10 via FRED, series DEXCAUS

evidence.fact: Foreign buyers on Maui averaged 248 a year in 2010–13, when the CAD was near par, and 34 a year in 2022–25. Maui foreign-buyer counts correlate -0.94 with CAD/USD over 2008–2025; Oahu's (Japan-dominated) correlate +0.10. TG Maui Canadian counts for 2015–2025 correlate -0.70.
evidence.source: DBEDT State Data Book 2025, Tables 21.36–21.37 (buyer origin by county), joined with FRED DEXCAUS (our calculation)

evidence.fact: Maui County Canadian closings in Jan–Mar 2025 were 2 ($5.0M), against 15 ($33.1M) in Jan–Mar 2024. Contracts behind Q1 closings were mostly signed between November and February, when the CAD was at a 20-plus-year low and before boycott-era travel data appeared.
evidence.source: Title Guaranty Hawaii, Buyer Statistics Maui Q1 2024 and Q1 2025

drivers.driver: Maui only: Bill 9's phase-out of apartment-zoned (Minatoya-list) vacation rentals, together with a weak Maui condo market, broke the 'Kihei condo used in winter, rented the rest of the year' model many Canadians bought into.
drivers.quantified_effect: Foreign purchases on Maui's South Side fell by 27 (34 to 7), about 96% of the county's 28-purchase Canadian decline (Canada was 39 of 42 foreign buyers in 2024). The average Canadian purchase on Maui rose from $2.53M to $4.35M, meaning mid-priced condo buyers dropped out.

evidence.fact: Bill 9 was introduced by Mayor Bissen in May 2024 and signed in December 2025. It ends vacation-rental use in apartment districts by Jan 1, 2029 (West Maui) and Jan 1, 2031 (rest of the county). The Minatoya list covers about 7,000 units, and 94% of affected units are owned by non-residents. Owner lawsuits are pending (Malter v. Maui County).
evidence.source: Maui Now

evidence.fact: Maui South Side (Kihei, Wailea, Makena) foreign buyers: 2023 20, 2024 34, 2025 7; Jan–Jun 2024 20 vs Jan–Jun 2025 3. South Side total sales: 435 (2024 restated) to 309 (2025). Other-US buyers there: 179 to 113.
evidence.source: Title Guaranty Hawaii, Buyer Statistics Maui Q4 2025 and Q2 2025 (district panels)

evidence.fact: Average price of Canadian purchases in Maui County: $98.7M / 39 = $2.53M (2024) and $47.8M / 11 = $4.35M (2025). Hawaii Island: $1.74M to $2.18M.
evidence.source: Title Guaranty Hawaii, Buyer Statistics Q4 2024 and Q4 2025 (our division)

evidence.fact: Maui island condo sales fell from 852 (2024) to 702 (2025). The average of monthly condo medians fell from about $911K to about $708K, and was about $660K in Jan–Aug 2026.
evidence.source: DBEDT monthly island home sales series (report dataset page_data.json)

evidence.fact: Maui conveyance-tax records: purchases by buyers not eligible for the owner-occupant rate fell from 1,431 in FY2024 to 1,166 in FY2025 (-18.5%), then 1,173 in FY2026. Owner-occupant purchases were 959, 881 and 896.
evidence.source: Maui County Real Property Tax sales data file (processed by Hawaii Appleseed)

evidence.fact: 1,173 Maui County condo units in the short-term-rental tax class (class 11) have foreign mailing addresses. That is 8.8% of 13,269 such units and 64% of all foreign-mailing parcels.
evidence.source: Maui County GIS parcel fabric joined to PARCELINFO tax class

drivers.driver: Shrinking airline capacity from Canada, including WestJet dropping Vancouver–Lihue
drivers.quantified_effect: Seats from Canada were already down 9–10% in Jan–Mar 2025 (schedules set before the boycott), 17.9% in Nov 2025 and 22.2% in Aug 2026. Lihue had 2,436 of 52,311 Canadian seats in Jan 2026 (4.7%), and Kauai Canadian purchases went from 3 to 1, so the Lihue cut explains essentially none of the 2025 decline. It matters for winter 2026–27 and later.

evidence.source: DBEDT monthly visitor statistics press releases

evidence.fact: In its 14 Jun 26 vs 26 Jul 26 schedule filings, WestJet cancelled 10 US routes for winter 2026–27, including the seasonal Vancouver–Lihue service (4 weekly) from 07 Dec 2026.
evidence.source: AeroRoutes

evidence.fact: WestJet confirmed that Vancouver–Lihue, flown since December 2009, is out of the 2026–27 schedule, and Calgary–Lihue is absent too, leaving Kauai with no Canadian nonstop. Maui stays year-round and Kona service resumes from Oct 23, 2026.
evidence.source: Beat of Hawaii

evidence.fact: Kauai Canadian purchases: 3 ($5.4M) in 2024, 1 ($51.1K) in 2025, 2 ($8.9M) in Jan–Jun 2026.
evidence.source: Title Guaranty Hawaii, Buyer Statistics Kauai

drivers.driver: US tax, estate and immigration rules for Canadians. They shape how Canadians own (winter-only use, ownership structures, withholding when they sell) but did not change between 2024 and 2025, except for a new registration rule for long stays.
drivers.quantified_effect: Not measurable from the data. FIRPTA, estate tax and treaty terms were unchanged between 2024 and 2025. The April 2025 alien-registration rule mostly affects 30-day-plus land arrivals and long-stay snowbirds.

evidence.fact: Buyers from foreign sellers must withhold 15% of the amount realized under FIRPTA.
evidence.source: IRS, FIRPTA Withholding

evidence.fact: The estate of a nonresident non-citizen must file Form 706-NA if US-situated assets exceed $60,000. Under the Canada–US treaty (Art. XXIX B), Canadian residents can claim a share of the full US unified credit prorated to their worldwide estate (adviser summaries).
evidence.source: IRS, Some nonresidents with U.S. assets must file estate tax returns; treaty proration per SF Tax Counsel

evidence.fact: Hawaii's HARPTA requires buyers to withhold 7.25% of the amount realized when buying from a nonresident seller (secondary summary; the official form page is tax.hawaii.gov/forms/a1_b3_6harpta/).
evidence.source: LegalClarity summary of HARPTA

evidence.fact: DHS interim final rule 'Alien Registration Form and Evidence of Registration' (90 FR 11793) took effect April 11, 2025. Law-firm summaries say Canadians staying 30 days or more without an I-94 must register.
evidence.source: Federal Register

counter_evidence: Timing problem for the boycott story: Maui's Canadian closings had already fallen to 2 in Jan–Mar 2025 (from 15), and neighbor-island Canadian closings were 18 in Jan–Jun 2025 against 42 in Jan–Jun 2024. Most of those contracts predate the February 2025 tariff fight, so the boycott cannot be the main cause of Maui's drop.

Size mismatch: Canadian visitors to Hawaii fell about 12.7% in 2025, much less than Canadian air trips to the US overall (about -22% to -27% in mid-2025 months per StatCan). Yet Hawaii purchases fell 40%. Hawaii-specific factors such as Bill 9, Maui condo weakness and seat cuts, or a much higher sensitivity among buyers than among tourists, are needed to explain the gap.

Nationally, Canadian buying did not collapse. NAR estimates Canadians bought 10,700 US homes in Apr 2025–Mar 2026 versus 10,900 a year earlier, with dollar volume down from $6.2B to $5.2B (reported, RISMedia, 2026-07-29). NAR's 'foreign buyer' count includes Canadians living in the US on visas, so it is not a pure snowbird measure.

Oahu moved the other way in 2025 (31 to 35), propped up by an unusual Jan–Mar 2025 cluster of 22 Canadian purchases averaging about $623K. Without it the statewide 2025 decline would look even steeper, and one project or bulk buyer can swing these small counts.

A general second-home slowdown hit all nonresident buyers. Statewide other-US buyers fell 13% (3,799 to 3,314), California buyers 27%, other-US buyers on Maui 21% and on Hawaii Island 24%. Japanese buyers fell 20% (267 to 213), while Korean buyers more than doubled (40 to 87). The Canadian drop (-40%) is about three times the mainland drop, but part of it is shared with everyone else: high rates, insurance and HOA costs, and Maui's post-fire market.

Mean reversion: 2024 was a rebound year (Maui 27 to 39, Hawaii Island 28 to 33). Maui's Canadian purchases had already fallen from 82 (2018) to 27 (2023) as the CAD stayed weak, so part of the 2025 low continues a long decline.
The CAD effect is small for 2025. The annual average weakened only 2.0%, which our elasticity estimates translate into about a 7–12% drop, far short of what happened.
Kauai and the WestJet Lihue cut: Canadians bought only 3 Kauai homes in 2024 and 1 in 2025, and the cancellation starts Dec 7, 2026. It is irrelevant to the 2025 decline.

Measurement limits: Title Guaranty classifies buyers by its own method, probably mailing address, which it does not document. Canadians who buy through US LLCs or US addresses, or who live in the US, would count as US buyers, so a shift in how Canadians title property could look like a decline. Counts are small (Maui County 11 in 2025), so single deals matter.
US tax, estate and FIRPTA rules did not change between 2024 and 2025, so they cannot explain the drop. They only explain why Canadians use homes in winter and hold them carefully.
research.for_brokers: Canadian demand on the neighbor islands has settled at a low base rather than vanished: Maui, Hawaii Island and Kauai together had 18 Canadian closings in Jan–Jun 2025 and 18 in Jan–Jun 2026, against 42 in Jan–Jun 2024. Budget for that level, not a rebound, for winter 2026–27. Seats from Canada were down 22% in August 2026, WestJet is cutting 10 US routes, Kauai loses its only Canadian nonstop from Dec 7, 2026, and the CAD is still weak (1.4253 on Oct 2, 2026). The Canadians still buying are higher-end: the average Canadian purchase on Maui was $4.35M in 2025, against $2.53M in 2024. Lead with resort- or hotel-zoned product that can still be rented legally after Bill 9, not Minatoya-list apartment condos, whose rental use ends Jan 1, 2029 (West Maui) or Jan 1, 2031 (South Maui) unless rezoned or overturned in court. The bigger near-term opportunity is listings. Maui County has about 1,600 Canadian-mailing parcels, 60% of foreign-owned parcels sit in South Maui, and about 1,170 foreign-mailing units are short-term-rental condos facing Bill 9. Expect Canadian sellers, and start FIRPTA (15%) and HARPTA withholding-certificate applications early so escrow does not stall. Canadian buyers act in winter (59% of 2024 purchases closed Jan–Jun), so time showings and price changes for December–March, and watch DBEDT's monthly Canada arrivals (July–August 2026 were flat to slightly up) and Title Guaranty's quarterly country tables as leading signals. Reach Canadian buyers through listing platforms and BC/Alberta brokerages, keep campaigns about the property, and have any country-targeted marketing reviewed for fair-housing compliance.
research.for_locals: Canadians were never a large share of island home buying: 11 of 1,247 Maui County sales and 17 of 3,675 Hawaii Island sales in 2025. Their retreat does little for affordability overall but matters in a few places. It is concentrated in South Maui condos, where foreign purchases fell from 34 to 7 and total South Side sales fell about 29%, while Maui condo prices softened (average monthly median about $911K in 2024, about $708K in 2025). Together with Bill 9 pushing apartment-zoned vacation rentals back toward long-term use by 2031, that could open more Kihei and West Maui condos to residents. Those units often carry high HOA and insurance costs, and the lawsuits and Bill 88 hotel rezonings could keep some of them as rentals. Local buyers already took a bigger share of sales in 2025: 73% on Maui (up from 70%) and 67% on Hawaii Island (up from 60%). The flip side is the visitor economy. Canadian visitors fell about 13% in 2025, they are long-staying winter guests concentrated on Maui and Kona, and Kauai loses its direct Canada flights this winter. Families who depend on hotel, condo-rental, activity and restaurant jobs in Kihei, Kaanapali, Kona and Lihue should expect softer winter seasons until Canadian travel recovers.

challenge.question: Why are Canadians the top foreign buyers on Maui and Hawaii Island, and why did Canadian purchases fall from 106 (2024) to 64 (2025)?

verdicts.driver: Structural: a Western-Canada winter corridor with nonstop flights to Kahului and Kona, repeat long-stay visitors and an existing Canadian owner base on Maui, while Japanese and Korean buyers concentrate on Oahu because all Japan flights land in Honolulu.
verdicts.reason: Re-checked against local Title Guaranty (TG) data (new/tg.json and the Q1 to Q3 editions in ca_tg24). In 2024 Canada was 39 of 42 foreign buyers in Maui County and 33 of 45 on Hawaii Island. In 2025 it was 11 of 16 and 17 of 33. The older Q4 editions I sampled (2015, 2016, 2019, 2021, 2023) rank Canada No. 1 by count on both islands. The October 2026 HVCB grid (ca_dl/air/oct.txt) confirms that all 347 Japan flights land in Honolulu. DBEDT's 2025 annual report (files.hawaii.gov/dbedt/economic/tourism/annual-reports/2025-annual-visitor.xlsx, posted 2026-09-28) confirms 389,241 Canadian visitors, 40.8% to Maui, 65.7% repeat and 22.6% staying in condos. Maui was 2,531,472 of roughly 9.6M total arrivals, about 26%. The owner roll confirms 1,602 Canadian-mailing parcels (87.3% of 1,835 foreign). The structural story holds with two nuances. First, Canada leads by count but not always by dollars: on Hawaii Island in 2025 Japan's 10 purchases ($38.1M) beat Canada's 17 ($37.1M), and Japanese buyers are active on the Kohala Coast. Second, Canada leads on the neighbor islands partly because foreign buying there is tiny (16 foreign sales in Maui County in 2025), not only because Canadian demand is large.
verdicts.corrected_wording: Canada leads foreign buying by number of sales on Maui and Hawaii Island because Japan's much larger buyer base (213 statewide in 2025) is almost entirely on Oahu, where all Japan flights land. Canadian winter visitors, by contrast, over-index on Maui: 40.8% of Canadian visitors went there against about 26% of all visitors. They are mostly repeat, long-stay guests, and about 1,600 Maui County parcels already mail tax bills to Canada. By dollar volume, Japan matched or beat Canada on Hawaii Island in 2025.
fact_errors: 'Canada was the No. 1 foreign buyer' holds by count only. By dollar volume on Hawaii Island in 2025, Japan had $38.1M against Canada's $37.1M (TG Q4 2025).

verdicts.driver: Seasonal buying: Canadian purchases cluster in winter and spring, so the weak 2025-26 snowbird season fed straight into fewer closings (Jan-Jun 2026: 26 vs 49).
verdicts.reason: The seasonality is real but modest. 59% of 2024 Canadian closings fell in Jan-Jun (63 of 106), against 50% of all statewide sales (8,368 of 16,716; TG Q2 and Q4 2024). It does not explain the decline. The whole Jan-Jun 2026 drop (49 to 26) was on Oahu (31 to 8), where a one-off cluster of 22 Canadian purchases in Jan-Mar 2025 (TG Oahu Q1 2025, $13.7M) did not repeat. On the snowbird islands, Canadian closings were unchanged: 18 in Jan-Jun 2025 and 18 in Jan-Jun 2026 (Maui 8 to 7, Hawaii Island 9 to 9, Kauai 1 to 2). That held even though Canadian arrivals fell 4.6% to 22.2% each month from Oct 2025 to Mar 2026 (DBEDT monthly releases, files.hawaii.gov/dbedt/economic/tourism/monthly-highlights/press-release-2025-10.pdf through press-release-2026-03.pdf). The IRS 183-day and BC MSP six-month rules are real limits on how long snowbirds stay, but they did not change.
verdicts.corrected_wording: Canadian closings lean toward the first half of the year (59% in Jan-Jun 2024, against 50% for all buyers), so showings and price changes matter most from December to March. Seasonality affects when Canadians buy, not how many. The weak 2025-26 winter did not reduce neighbor-island Canadian closings, which held at 18 in Jan-Jun of both 2025 and 2026. The statewide Jan-Jun 2026 drop came entirely from Oahu's one-off early-2025 cluster not repeating.
fact_errors: The Jan-Jun 2026 drop (49 to 26) is attributed to a weak snowbird season, but it was entirely Oahu (31 to 8). Neighbor islands were flat at 18.

verdicts.driver: The 2025 Canadian pullback from US travel after the tariffs and annexation rhetoric (the 'boycott'), said to explain the statewide and Oahu decline from mid-2025 better than Maui's early collapse.
verdicts.reason: The core facts check out. DBEDT shows Canadian visitors down 12.7% in 2025 (389,241 against 445,985). StatCan's 'Tourism activity, 2025' (www150.statcan.gc.ca/n1/pub/11-627-m/11-627-m2026029-eng.htm, 2026-09-25) shows Canadian visits to the US falling from 30,185,000 to 23,096,000, with holiday trips down 21.5%. May 2025 air return trips fell 24.2% to 488,800 (BNN Bloomberg, 2025-06-10). The researcher placed the effect in the wrong places, though. (1) Statewide Canadian closings were flat in Jan-Mar 2025 (31 against 32). The whole statewide drop came in Apr-Dec: 18, 8 and 7 against 31, 16 and 27, consistent with the travel pullback that began in February-March 2025. (2) Oahu is a weak test: its 31 to 4 move mostly reflects the end of the one-off Q1 2025 cluster, and Oahu's second half fell only from 10 to 4. (3) The pullback matters on Maui and Hawaii Island too. Maui's second-half closings fell from 17 to 3. Hawaii Island lost 12 of its 16 in Apr-Dec. South Maui sales to Hawaii buyers rose in the second half of 2025 (101 to 109) while Canadian buying stayed down. (4) It works through willingness to own US property, not through visitor numbers. Canadian visitors to Maui fell only 4.4% (DBEDT 2025 annual report) while Canadian purchases there fell 72%. In an August 2025 Royal LePage poll, 54% of Canadian owners of US property planned to sell within 12 months, and 62% of them cited the US administration (Global News, globalnews.ca/news/11350508/canadian-property-owners-in-us/, Aug 2025, reported). (5) The political shock began with the 25% tariff threat on 2024-11-25 (Global News, globalnews.ca/news/10887991/trump-25-per-cent-tariff-canada-mexico/) and the 'Governor Trudeau' taunts on 2024-12-10 (CBC). So 'before the boycott' does not mean 'before the political shock'. HTA's 2026 Canada plan says Hawaii held up 'considerably better than continental U.S.' (hta.hawaii.gov/wp-content/uploads/2026/06/canada-2026-brand-marketing-plan.pdf, June 2026).
verdicts.corrected_wording: The political shock that began with the November 2024 tariff threat, and became a broad Canadian pullback from US travel and property from February 2025, is the best fit for the statewide decline. All of the statewide drop came in Apr-Dec 2025, along with most of Hawaii Island's drop and half of Maui's. It worked through Canadians' willingness to own US property more than through visitor numbers: Canadian visitors to Maui fell only 4.4% while Canadian purchases there fell 72%. Oahu's swings are dominated by one early-2025 cluster and say little about the boycott.
