fact_errors: Jan-Aug 2026 Canadian arrivals were -5.0% per DBEDT's own year-to-date figure (252,907 vs 266,309, press-release-2026-08.pdf), not -6.0% (252,906 vs 269,169).
The Longwoods '53% less likely' figure could not be re-verified: the Maui Now page is blocked from this environment and no other source surfaced. Treat it as unverified.
'Explains Oahu better than Maui' is backwards. Oahu's 31-to-4 move is mostly the end of a one-off Q1 2025 cluster of 22, while Maui lost 14 Canadian closings in the second half of 2025 (17 to 3).

verdicts.driver: Weak Canadian dollar: a strong long-run reason Canadian buying is far below 2010-2013 levels, but only a small part of the 2025 change.
verdicts.reason: The rate figures are correct (FRED DEXCAUS, fred.stlouisfed.org/series/DEXCAUS, through 2026-10-02). Annual averages were 1.3494 (2023), 1.3699 (2024) and 1.3973 (2025). January 2025's monthly average of 1.4389 was the highest since April 2003. The daily peak was 1.4601 on 2025-02-03, and the rate was 1.4253 on 2026-10-02. The 'strong long-run' claim overreaches. The Maui level correlation of -0.94 is driven by trend; in year-to-year changes it falls to -0.57 (Data Book foreign counts) and to -0.43 for TG Maui Canadian counts outside the COVID years. In 2024 the CAD weakened 1.5% while Maui Canadian purchases rose 44% (27 to 39). In Jan-Jun 2026 the CAD averaged about 2.3% stronger than in Jan-Jun 2025 (1.377 against 1.409), yet Canadian buying did not recover. The 2010-13 high also coincided with the post-crash bottom in US prices. The Data Book series breaks between 2024 and 2025: Maui 2024 shows 1,625 sales and 49 foreign, against 1,471 and 42 in TG's FY2024 edition, while 2025 matches TG. That mix of bases affects the regression. Finally, the January 2025 trough was itself partly caused by the November 2024 tariff threat, so currency and politics cannot be separated in the Q1 2025 data.
verdicts.corrected_wording: The weak Canadian dollar raises the cost of a Hawaii home and of its carrying costs for Canadians. It is a plausible background reason that buying is below its 2010-2013 level, when the dollar was near par and US prices were near their post-crash low. It is not what moved 2025: the annual average weakened only 2%, the January 2025 low partly reflected the tariff threat, and purchases did not recover in 2026 when the dollar was about 2% stronger.
fact_errors: The elasticities (-3.6 to -6.2) come from level regressions on trending series that use Data Book counts, which switch basis between 2024 (sum of earlier editions) and 2025 (TG Q4 edition). They overstate the currency effect.
The 'r = -0.94' refers to all foreign buyers on Maui, not Canadians. For TG Canadian counts in year-to-year changes, the correlation is about -0.4 to -0.6.

verdicts.driver: Maui only: Bill 9's phase-out of apartment-zoned (Minatoya-list) vacation rentals, plus a weak Maui condo market, broke the 'Kihei condo used in winter, rented the rest of the year' model.
verdicts.reason: Partly supported. TG's Maui district panels (Q4 2025 edition) show South Side Canadian purchases falling from 33 ($89.5M) to 6 ($32.4M), which is 27 of Maui's 28 lost. Canadian visitors to Maui fell only 4.4%, so something specific to Maui property is needed. Bill 9 facts check out: proposed by Mayor Bissen in May 2024 (council Bill 9 of 2025) and signed December 15, 2025. The deadlines are Jan 1, 2029 for West Maui and Jan 1, 2031 elsewhere, though some reports say 2030 for South Maui (KHON, khon2.com/maui-county-news/bill-9-officially-passes-maui-county-council-phasing-out-thousands-of-short-term-rentals/, Dec 2025, reported). About 6,100 to 7,000 units are affected. The original 2024 proposal had much nearer deadlines, mid-2025 for West Maui and Jan 2026 elsewhere (reported), which makes the uncertainty in late 2024 and early 2025 more relevant. But the evidence does not isolate Bill 9. (a) The first-half 2025 South Side collapse hit every buyer group: total sales 256 to 147, Hawaii buyers 121 to 80, other-US 115 to 64. Maui's Jan-Mar 2025 total was 267 against 399, and Hawaii buyers fell from 272 to 184 (TG Q1 2025). That looks like a broad condo or investor shock, also fed by rising short-term-rental property tax. Maui's TVR-STRH rate was a flat $11.85 per $1,000 in FY23-24, and the FY27 tiers are $13.00, $15.00 and $17.00 (Maui County resolution 26-69, mauicounty.gov/DocumentCenter/View/161952, adopted 2026-05-15). (b) Canadian closings on Maui were still 12 in Oct-Dec 2024, after the May 2024 proposal. (c) Hawaii Island has no Bill 9, yet its Canadian purchases fell 48%. (d) Maui's condo market recovered in 2026 (Jan-Aug condo sales 466 to 545, up 17%) while Canadian closings did not. (e) The average-price inference is fragile. Maui's 2025 Canadian dollar volume is dominated by Apr-Jun 2025: 6 deals worth $40.8M, including 3 South Side deals worth $30.5M in the first half. The lost South Side deals averaged about $2.1M ((89.5M - 32.4M) / 27), closer to Wailea than budget Kihei. Nothing shows that they were Minatoya-list units. (f) The 1,173 foreign-mailing units are in the short-term-rental tax class (class 11, about 13,269 condo units). Only about 6,108 of those units are Minatoya-list, so the number facing Bill 9 is unknown and probably much lower.
verdicts.corrected_wording: Maui's drop is almost entirely South Maui Canadians (33 to 6). About half of it came in Jan-Jun 2025, when a South Maui condo slump hit every buyer group. That slump coincided with the Bill 9 phase-out threat (first proposed in May 2024 with 2025-26 deadlines), rising short-term-rental property-tax rates and falling condo prices. The data show a Maui-specific property shock but cannot attribute it to Bill 9 alone. The other half came in Jul-Dec 2025, after the South Maui market had recovered for local buyers, which points to Canada-specific causes.
fact_errors: 'Average price rose $2.53M to $4.35M, meaning mid-priced condo buyers dropped out' is not shown. A handful of high-value deals ($40.8M across 6 closings in Apr-Jun 2025) drive the 2025 average, and the lost South Side deals averaged about $2.1M.

'About 1,170 foreign-mailing units are STR condos facing Bill 9' is wrong. They are class-11 short-term-rental units. Minatoya-list units make up only about 6,108 of the 13,269 class-11 condo units, so far fewer than 1,170 foreign units are likely affected.
'94% of affected units owned by non-residents' could not be re-verified; the source page is blocked.

verdicts.driver: Shrinking airline capacity from Canada, including WestJet dropping Vancouver-Lihue.
verdicts.reason: Rated weak, which is correct. The seat figures match the DBEDT releases: Jan 2025 52,101 seats (-9.2%); Mar 2025 56,607 (-10.4%); Nov 2025 40,328 (-17.9%); Dec 2025 49,000 (-8.6%); Jan 2026 51,095 (-1.9%); Aug 2026 11,399 (-22.2%). WestJet's cancellation of Vancouver-Lihue from Dec 7, 2026 (4 weekly) is confirmed by AeroRoutes (aeroroutes.com/eng/260727-wsnw26us, 2026-07-27) and Daily Hive. Kauai Canadian purchases went 3, 1, 2. Seat cuts also overstate the loss of access. In January 2025 seats fell 9.2% but Canadian arrivals rose 0.6%. In August 2026 seats fell 22.2% but arrivals rose 0.6%, and 13,636 of the 24,041 Canadian visitors came on flights from the US mainland (DBEDT press-release-2026-08.pdf). Seat cuts look more like airlines responding to weaker demand than an independent cause.
verdicts.corrected_wording: Fewer nonstop seats from Canada (down 9% to 22% from a year earlier through 2025-26) mostly follow weaker demand rather than cause it, and Canadians increasingly connect through the mainland: arrivals were up 0.6% in August 2026 despite 22% fewer direct seats. WestJet's Vancouver-Lihue cut starts December 7, 2026, on an island where Canadians bought 1 to 3 homes a year, so it explains none of the 2025 decline.

verdicts.driver: US tax, estate and immigration rules for Canadians: they shape how Canadians own but did not change between 2024 and 2025, apart from a new registration rule.
verdicts.reason: Correctly rated weak, but 'did not change' is inaccurate. The One Big Beautiful Bill Act (signed 2025-07-04) set a permanent, inflation-indexed $15M estate exemption from 2026 instead of letting it roughly halve. Because the treaty prorates the unified credit, this made US ownership more favorable for Canadians (Morgan Lewis, morganlewis.com/pubs/2025/08/estate-tax-alert-new-15-million-federal-exemption-becomes-law, Aug 2025, reported). The proposed Section 899 'revenge tax' would have hit Canadian investors in US real estate in May-June 2025; it was withdrawn before enactment (CRE Finance Council, crefc.org, June 2025, reported). The DHS registration rule (effective 2025-04-11) mainly reaches visa-exempt land arrivals staying 30+ days without an I-94. Air arrivals with an I-94 are already treated as registered, per law-firm summaries (e.g. Pryor Cashman, 2025, reported), so it barely touches Hawaii snowbirds, who fly in. FIRPTA at 15% and HARPTA at 7.25% are unchanged.
verdicts.corrected_wording: US tax and immigration rules shape how Canadians use and hold Hawaii homes (winter-only stays, ownership structures, FIRPTA and HARPTA withholding when they sell) but do not explain the 2025 drop. The one lasting 2025 change, a permanent $15M estate exemption from 2026, made ownership more favorable. The Section 899 tax threat of May-June 2025 was dropped. The April 2025 registration rule mainly affects land arrivals, not Canadians who fly to Hawaii.
fact_errors: 'Estate tax and treaty terms were unchanged between 2024 and 2025' is wrong: OBBBA (July 2025) made the $15M exemption permanent from 2026, which helps Canadians through treaty proration.
The registration rule 'mostly affects long-stay snowbirds' overstates its relevance to Hawaii. Air arrivals with an I-94 are treated as already registered.

missing_drivers: Timing breakdown that changes the story (TG cumulative editions in ca_tg24 and new/tg.json). Statewide Canadian closings by quarter were 32, 31, 16, 27 in 2024; 31, 18, 8, 7 in 2025; 13, 13 in Jan-Jun 2026. The statewide fall was entirely in Apr-Dec 2025. On the neighbor islands, 17 of the 46 lost purchases (37%) showed in Jan-Mar 2025 and 29 (63%) in Apr-Dec. Maui split about evenly (-13 in Q1, -15 later). Hawaii Island lost 12 of its 16 after March.

A Maui-wide, and especially South Maui, condo slump in Jan-Jun 2025 that hit local buyers as well. Maui Jan-Mar 2025 total sales were 267 against 399, with Hawaii buyers 184 against 272. South Side first-half sales fell from 256 to 147, with Hawaii buyers 121 to 80 (TG Q1 2025 and Q2 2025 district panels). Maui condo sales then recovered in Jan-Aug 2026 (+17%) while Canadian buying did not.

Rising carrying costs for vacation-rental condos. Maui's TVR-STRH property-tax rate went from a flat $11.85 per $1,000 (FY23-24) to tiers of $12.50, $14.00 and $15.55 (FY26) and $13.00, $15.00 and $17.00 (FY27), per Maui County resolution 26-69 (mauicounty.gov/DocumentCenter/View/161952, adopted 2026-05-15) and the county's Final Budget Handout. These add to insurance and HOA pressure, which was not quantified here.

Canadian housing wealth and economy. The Greater Vancouver benchmark price fell 4.5% year over year by December 2025 (condos -5.3%), and 2025 sales were the lowest in more than two decades (GVR via CTV, ctvnews.ca/vancouver/article/vancouver-area-saw-least-home-sales-in-more-than-two-decades-in-2025-board/, Jan 2026, reported). BC residents are 44.6% of Canadian visitors to Hawaii, and many buyers draw on home equity.

An ownership-sentiment channel distinct from travel volume. A Royal LePage poll (Aug 2025) found 54% of Canadian owners of US property planned to sell within 12 months, 62% of them citing the US administration (globalnews.ca/news/11350508/canadian-property-owners-in-us/, reported). Canadian visitors to Maui fell only 4.4% in 2025 while Canadian purchases there fell 72%.

The political shock predates the 'boycott'. Trump's 25% tariff threat came on 2024-11-25 and the 'Governor Trudeau' taunts on 2024-12-10, so contracts behind Q1 2025 closings were already signed during political and currency stress. The CAD trough was partly a result of the threat.

Substitution to other destinations and domestic property. Canadian overseas trips rose 10.2% in 2025 to 14.27M, Mexico 2.66M (StatCan Tourism activity 2025, 2026-09-25), and media reports describe a 'buy Canadian' rebound in Canadian recreational property (reported).

Lumpy small counts. Oahu's 22 Canadian purchases in Jan-Mar 2025 (average about $623K) and 15 in Apr-Jun 2024 dominate Oahu's series. Maui's 2025 Canadian dollar volume is dominated by 6 closings worth $40.8M in Apr-Jun 2025.

Measurement issues. TG does not document how it assigns buyer origin, and some counted deeds look like timeshare or fractional interests (e.g. a $51.1K Kauai Canadian purchase in 2025). The Hilo 2024 'CA = 232' anomaly inflates the 2024 baseline for other-US buyers. Excluding Hilo, other-US buyers fell only about 8% statewide (3,520 to 3,226), so the Canadian decline (-40%) was about five times the mainland decline, not three times.
challenge.final_answer:
Canadians are the top foreign buyers on Maui and Hawaii Island mainly because foreign buying there is small, and Japan's much larger buyer base (213 purchases statewide in 2025) is almost entirely on Oahu, where every Japan flight lands. Canada's winter visitors, by contrast, lean toward Maui and Kona. In 2025, 40.8% of Hawaii's 389,241 Canadian visitors went to Maui, compared with about 26% of all visitors. Two-thirds of them had been before, and about 1,600 Maui County properties already send their tax bills to Canada, many of them South Maui condos. Canada has led foreign purchases by count on both islands in every year checked since 2015, though on Hawaii Island in 2025 Japan slightly beat it by dollar value.

The 2025 drop, from 106 to 64 purchases ($186.0M to $110.7M), happened on the neighbor islands. Maui County went from 39 to 11, Hawaii Island from 33 to 17 and Kauai from 3 to 1. Oahu rose from 31 to 35 only because of a one-time cluster of 22 Canadian purchases in early 2025. Statewide, Canadian closings were flat in January to March 2025 (31 vs 32), and the whole decline came from April to December.

Two explanations fit the data best:
- **A Maui property-market shock.** Almost all of Maui's drop was Canadians in South Maui (33 to 6). In the first half of 2025, South Maui sales fell for every kind of buyer, including locals (256 to 147 sales). That coincided with the Bill 9 plan to end vacation rentals in apartment-zoned condos (first proposed in May 2024, with much nearer deadlines than the final law), higher property-tax rates on short-term rentals and falling condo prices. The data show the shock but cannot pin it on Bill 9 alone.
- **A Canada-specific political shock.** It began with the November 2024 tariff threat and became a broad pullback from US travel and property from February 2025. Canadian trips to the US fell 23.5% in 2025, and in an August 2025 poll 54% of Canadian owners of US property said they planned to sell. Canadian buying on Maui stayed low in late 2025 and 2026 even after South Maui and Maui condo sales recovered for other buyers.

The pullback shows up in willingness to own a home in the US, not in visitor numbers. Canadian visitors to Maui fell only 4.4% while Canadian purchases there fell 72%.

Other factors did little:
- **Weak Canadian dollar:** background only. It weakened just 2% on average in 2025, its January 2025 low was partly caused by the tariff threat, and purchases did not recover in early 2026 when it was about 2% stronger.
- **Winter seasonality:** affects when Canadians buy, not how many. Neighbor-island closings held at 18 in January to June of both 2025 and 2026.
- **Fewer flights:** mostly a response to weaker demand. Canadians are increasingly connecting through the mainland.
- **US tax rules:** the one lasting 2025 change, a larger estate-tax exemption from 2026, actually favors Canadians.
- **WestJet Lihue cancellation:** starts in December 2026, on an island where Canadians bought 1 to 3 homes a year, so it explains none of the 2025 drop.

For brokers, Canadian demand on the neighbor islands has held at about 18 closings per half-year since early 2025, with no sign of a rebound yet. For local families, the drop is too small (11 of 1,247 Maui sales in 2025) to change affordability island-wide, though it matters in South Maui condos.

The counts are small, and Title Guaranty does not say how it decides where a buyer is from. So the where and when are solid, but confidence in the causes is low to medium.

research.question: Why did the mainland buyer share on Maui fall from about 52% (2010) and 42% (2015) to 25% in 2025, with most of the drop by 2019?
research.answer: Mainland buyers did not leave Maui in proportion to the headline drop. The fall from 52% to 25% is three separate stories, and only the last one is a clear, real pullback. First, 2010 was a bust-era spike. Pre-sold resort condos such as Honua Kai were closing, and prices that had fallen 16% drew bargain hunters. Mainland purchases fell from 1,768 (2010) to 1,090 (2015) while local purchases stayed near 1,390, which brought the share back to about 42%. Second, almost all of the 2015–2019 drop happened in a single quarter. The mainland share was 38.6% in Q2 2018 and 29.1% in Q3 2018, and it never recovered. That break shows up only on Maui and only in condos. Other data covering the same period shows no such break. Maui County's conveyance-tax records show buyers without a homeowner exemption steady at 55–56% of home sales from FY2018 to FY2020. MLS condo sales rose, mainland in-migration held steady, and visitor arrivals set a record 3.07M in 2019. After mid-2018, the Title Guaranty/DBEDT count of Maui condo sales fell below the MLS count, and it has stayed 23–47% below it. No other county shows that. UHERO's own Title Guaranty-based tables count 1.7–2.0 times as many Maui condo sales for 2024–25, with 55–59% of those buyers from out of state. On that basis the out-of-state share is about 36–41%, not the published 27–31%. Our read: the published series stopped capturing much of Maui's vacation-rental condo market around July 1, 2018. That is when the county's new short-term-rental property-tax class took effect, and it was designed to move about 10,800 STR-eligible condos out of the hotel class. Title Guaranty does not publish its method, so this is unconfirmed. Third, the slide from 34.5% (2021) to 25.3% (2025) is real, and other data confirms it. Mortgages for second-home purchases on Maui fell from about 328 (2019) to 87 (2025). Mainland purchases fell 70% from 2021, against 54% for local purchases. The causes were 6.6–7% mortgage rates and record prices, then the August 2023 Lahaina fire, Bill 9's phase-out of about 6,100 apartment-zoned vacation rentals (85% owned out of state; signed Dec 15, 2025), and a jump in condo insurance and HOA costs. The pullback was concentrated in South Maui condos. The share recovered to about 28% in Jan–Jun 2026, after Bill 88 created a hotel-rezoning path.

drivers.driver: A break in what the published Title Guaranty/DBEDT Maui series measures, starting in Q3 2018 and concentrated in condos, not a retreat of mainland buyers. This accounts for most of the 2015–2019 drop. Timing matches Maui's new short-term-rental property-tax class (effective July 1, 2018); the mechanism is unconfirmed.
drivers.quantified_effect: The quarterly mainland share averaged 40.7% in 2016Q1–2018Q2 and 28.6% in 2018Q3–2019Q4. That 12.1-point step is about 85% of the 14.1-point fall from 2015 (42.4%) to 2019 (28.3%). Rebuilt on other bases, the 2024–25 out-of-state share is about 36–41% (UHERO's Title Guaranty universe), against 27–31% published. If Title Guaranty's ratio of outside buyers to non-homeowner purchases had stayed at its FY2016–18 level, the outside share would be about 41–43%. Read these as a range, not a point estimate.

evidence.fact: Maui mainland purchases by quarter, Title Guaranty via DBEDT: Q2 2018 had 324 mainland of 840 sales (38.6%). Q3 2018 had 186 of 639 (29.1%). Local purchases barely moved (488 to 438). The share stayed between 21.7% and 32.8% through 2019.
evidence.source: DBEDT Quarterly Statistical & Economic Report, 3rd Qtr 2026, Table G-55 (Home sales by origin of buyer, Maui)

evidence.fact: In the same quarter, Title Guaranty's Maui condo count fell from 503 to 303 while its single-family count held (337 to 336). Over the same months, MLS condo sales on Maui fell only from 499 to 410, and MLS condo sales for 2019 (1,617) were above 2017 (1,453).
evidence.value: TG condos -40% vs MLS condos -18% (2018Q2 to Q3)
evidence.source: DBEDT QSER Table G-51 (Maui by type); DBEDT Monthly Economic Indicators (REALTORS Association of Maui MLS), summed by quarter

evidence.fact: Title Guaranty's Maui condo count divided by MLS condo sales was 1.03–1.22 in 2013–2017. It was 0.93 in 2018, 0.77 in 2019, then 0.53–0.72 in 2020–2025 (0.58 in 2025: 405 vs 702). Recorded deeds should outnumber MLS sales: on O'ahu the ratio stayed 1.42–1.72 throughout.
evidence.source: DBEDT QSER G-49/G-51 and Monthly Economic Indicators; computed here

evidence.fact: No comparable step appears in other counties in 2018. Mainland shares by quarter, 2018Q1–Q4: Honolulu 8.5–10.0%, Hawai'i County 36.5–42.7%, Kaua'i 33.2–42.5%.
evidence.source: DBEDT QSER Tables G-53, G-54, G-56

evidence.fact: Maui County conveyance-tax records show home purchases taxed at the higher rate for buyers ineligible for the homeowner exemption (second homes, investors, landlords) held at 56.1% (FY2018), 55.2% (FY2019) and 55.5% (FY2020) of owner plus non-owner home sales. Non-owner purchases fell only 5.8% in FY2019 (2,152 to 2,027). Over the same fiscal years, Title Guaranty's mainland plus foreign count fell 34% (1,223 to 810). Its ratio to non-owner purchases fell from 0.56–0.63 (FY2016–18) to 0.40 (FY2019) and 0.29–0.39 since.
evidence.value: Non-owner share flat at 55–56% while TG outside share fell 42.3% to 32.4% (FY basis)
evidence.source: County of Maui RPT Sales Data File (file dated 2026-09-22), classified by HRS §247-2 schedule by Hawai'i Appleseed; computed here

evidence.fact: UHERO's Housing Factbooks, also built from Title Guaranty deeds with the buyer's deed address, count far more Maui condo sales than the DBEDT series. For 2024: 1,026 condos (59.0% out-of-state) and 904 single-family homes (21.2%), against 617 condos in DBEDT. For 2025: 824 condos (54.5%) and 827 single-family homes (18.1%), against 405 in DBEDT. The implied out-of-state share is 41.3% (2024) and 36.3% (2025), versus DBEDT mainland plus foreign at 30.6% and 26.6%. In Honolulu and Hawai'i County, UHERO's condo counts are below DBEDT's (for example Honolulu 2025: 6,267 vs 7,534), so definitions alone do not explain Maui's 1.7–2.0x gap.
evidence.value: Maui out-of-state share 36–41% (UHERO basis) vs 27–31% (DBEDT basis)
evidence.source: UHERO, The Hawai'i Housing Factbook 2025 and 2026 (Maui County profile pages)

evidence.fact: Same comparison for the 2024 data year: Maui County condominium transactions 1,026 (59.0% out-of-state) and single-family 904 (21.2%).
evidence.source: UHERO, The Hawai'i Housing Factbook 2025

evidence.fact: In October 2017 the council's budget committee advanced a new property-tax class for short-term rentals. It would also take in STRs in hotel-zoned areas and condo units where STRs are allowed, which were then in the hotel and resort class. The Maui Vacation Rental Association counted 10,769 condo owners in the hotel class who would move. The council passed the class on Dec 4, 2017 (5-4). A separate highest-and-best-use condo bill failed.
evidence.source: The Maui News (Oct 29, 2017; Dec 5, 2017)

evidence.fact: The FY2019 rate resolution (Res. 18-83, adopted May 2018, effective July 1, 2018) is the first to list a Short Term Rental class, at $9.28 per $1,000 (Hotel and Resort $9.37). July 1, 2018 is the first day of the quarter in which the Title Guaranty break appears. The county's 2018 tax-rate document was found through search but could not be opened directly.
evidence.source: County of Maui, 2018 Tax Rate (Resolution 18-83)

evidence.fact: Ordinance 5160 (December 2020) classifies condominiums permitted to rent short term as Short-Term Rental even if they are not rented short term. The Title Guaranty/MLS condo ratio fell further, from 0.72 (2020) to 0.60 (2021) and 0.53 (2022). That is consistent with, but does not prove, a second reclassification step.
evidence.source: County of Maui Real Property Tax FAQ (Ordinance 5160)

evidence.fact: Maui's current vacation-rental tax class (TVR-STRH) holds 13,693 parcels. 75.5% have an other-state mailing address and 8.7% a foreign one, against 3.0% non-Hawai'i for owner-occupied parcels. If a series drops this class, it removes the most outside-owned segment of the market.
evidence.source: Maui County GIS parcel fabric (mailing addresses, Oct 4, 2026) joined to 2026 certified roll; computed here

evidence.fact: Demand indicators show no 2018–19 collapse. Households moving into Maui County numbered 2,748 (2017-18), 2,639 (2018-19) and 2,783 (2019-20). Maui visitor arrivals reached a record 3,071,596 in 2019, up 5.4%.
evidence.source: IRS SOI county migration data; Hawai'i Tourism Authority figures via The Maui News

evidence.fact: Neither Title Guaranty nor DBEDT documents how buyer origin is assigned or which deed and property types count. UHERO's data dictionary says origin is the home address the buyer lists on the deed.
evidence.source: DBEDT Data Book 2025 Tables 21.36–21.38 notes; UHERO Factbook 2026 data dictionary

drivers.driver: The 2010 starting point was a bust-era spike: closings of resort condos pre-sold in 2005–06, plus distressed-price bargains. It normalized by 2015.
drivers.quantified_effect: Mainland purchases fell from 1,768 (2010) to 1,090 (2015), a drop of 678, while local purchases held at 1,380 and 1,392. That alone moved the share from 51.7% to 42.4%. Foreign buyers, mainly Canadians, fell from 274 (2011) to 87 (2015) as well.

evidence.fact: Maui mainland buyers: 1,768 of 3,418 sales in 2010 (51.7%), average price $619,190. In 2015: 1,090 of 2,569 (42.4%), average $818,362.
evidence.source: DBEDT QSER 3rd Qtr 2026, Tables G-51/G-55

evidence.fact: Honua Kai (700 units, 512 pre-sold in 2005–06) closed about 150 units in 2009 and 45 in April 2010 alone. Maui condo sales that month were 158, against 41 a year earlier, the most in any month since December 2005.
evidence.source: Honolulu Advertiser (Andrew Gomes), 'Maui condo sales triple from year ago'

evidence.fact: Maui County condo sales rose 39% in 2010 (824 to 1,148) while the median condo price fell 16%. The Realtors association said inventory included many short sales and bank-owned (REO) properties.
evidence.source: Maui Now, reporting Maui Board of Realtors 2010 year-end data

evidence.fact: In 2010 Title Guaranty recorded 2.0 times as many Maui single-family sales as the MLS (1,631 vs 817) and 1.56 times as many condo sales (1,787 vs 1,148), against about 1.0–1.2 in 2015–2017. That points to many non-MLS transfers in the boom-bust years, such as developer closings and distressed transfers.
evidence.source: DBEDT QSER G-51 and Monthly Economic Indicators; computed here

drivers.driver: A real pullback by outside buyers after 2021: high mortgage rates, record prices and outside buyers concentrated at the top of the market. Locals now buy in price bands that second-home buyers used to dominate.
drivers.quantified_effect: From 2021 to 2025, Title Guaranty mainland purchases on Maui fell 70% (1,069 to 316) and local purchases fell 54% (1,975 to 915). The share fell 9.2 points, from 34.5% to 25.3%. HMDA second-home purchase loans fell about 73% from 2019 to 2025. In the conveyance-tax data, the non-owner share of $1–2M sales fell from 66% (FY2016) to 50% (FY2025).

evidence.fact: In 2025, mainland buyers on Maui paid an average of $2,237,541, against $1,102,874 for local buyers. Out-of-state buyers made 25% of sales but 40% of dollar volume.
evidence.source: DBEDT Data Book 2025 Table 21.38; Title Guaranty Buyer Statistics Maui Q4 2025

evidence.fact: Maui County home-purchase loans: 2,010 in 2019, 886 in 2025. The second-residence share fell from 16.3% to 9.8% (about 328 to 87 loans). The investment-property share rose from 18.4% to 24.6% (about 369 to 218). The median borrower income rose from $132K to $217K.
evidence.source: FFIEC/CFPB HMDA Data Browser, Maui County (15009), originated site-built 1–4 unit purchase loans

evidence.fact: The mortgage payment on Maui's median single-family house took 42.4% of median household income in 2019 and 78.2% in 2025 (rates 3.93% and 6.6%).
evidence.source: DBEDT monthly medians; Freddie Mac PMMS rates; ACS income; computed here

evidence.fact: Conveyance-tax data by price band: in $1–2M sales, homeowner-exemption (local owner-occupant) purchases rose from 90 (FY2016) to 312 (FY2025). The non-owner share of that band fell from 66% to 50%, and of $2–4M sales from 83% to 66%. The overall non-owner share was still 57.0% in FY2025 and 56.7% in FY2026.
evidence.source: County of Maui RPT Sales Data File, processed by Hawai'i Appleseed; computed here

evidence.fact: Maui MLS condo median, as an average of monthly medians: $911K in 2024 and $708K in 2025 (-22%). The single-family median was $1.317M and $1.291M.
evidence.source: DBEDT Monthly Economic Indicators (REALTORS Association of Maui)

drivers.driver: Vacation-rental policy risk: the Minatoya-list phase-out (Bill 9), earlier enforcement against illegal rentals, and the partial rescue in Bill 88. This matters mainly for the 2024–2025 condo drop, not for 2018–19.
drivers.quantified_effect: Title Guaranty out-of-state buyers in the South Side district (Kihei–Wailea condo market) fell from 193 (2024) to 113 (2025), -41%, while Hawai'i buyers there fell from 217 to 189 (-13%). Maui's mainland share was lowest in 2025 H2 (22%) and recovered to about 28% in Jan–Jun 2026, after Bill 88 passed.

evidence.fact: Bill 9 passed 5-3 and was signed Dec 15, 2025. It phases out transient vacation rentals in apartment districts by Jan 1, 2029 in West Maui and Jan 1, 2031 elsewhere. Mayor Bissen first proposed it in May 2024.
evidence.source: Maui Now

evidence.fact: 6,127 apartment-zoned units operate as TVRs (8,834 are eligible). 85% of owners have an out-of-state mailing address: 36% California, 12% Washington, 8% Canada. Condo prices are projected to fall 20–40%. TVRs are 21% of all Maui County housing units.
evidence.source: UHERO, An Economic Analysis of the Proposal to Phase Out TVRs in Maui County Apartment Districts

evidence.fact: Title Guaranty Maui district counts, 2024 to 2025: South Side other-US buyers 193 to 113 (share 43.5% to 36.6%). West Side 67 to 84 (32.7% to 46.7%). Central 37 to 36. Up Country 37 to 36. In Jan–Jun 2026 there were 179 other-US buyers of 642 sales (28%).
evidence.source: Title Guaranty Buyer Statistics, Maui Q4 2024, Q4 2025, Q2 2026

evidence.fact: Bill 88 (Ordinance 6008) passed 7-2 in June 2026. It created H-3 and H-4 hotel districts so that about 4,500 Minatoya units could keep renting if rezoned. In late September 2026 the council referred 32 shoreline complexes to the Planning Commission, which had recommended against most of an earlier batch. No property had been rezoned.
evidence.value: About 4,500 units with a possible path
evidence.source: Maui Now

evidence.fact: Earlier enforcement: Maui hired Lodging Rev in May 2018 to find illegal listings. Voters approved higher fines in November 2018, and $20,000 initial plus $10,000-per-day fines took effect in December 2019. There were 180 warnings and 80 violation notices in 2019. This mainly targets unpermitted single-family rentals, not Minatoya condos, so it cannot explain a condo-only drop in Q3 2018.
evidence.source: Maui Now

drivers.driver: The Lahaina fire (August 8, 2023) shrank West Maui stock and visitor demand. It reduced the number of deals more than it changed the outside share.
drivers.quantified_effect: Title Guaranty West Side sales were only 196–205 a year in 2023–2024 and 180 in 2025. The outside share there rose in 2025 (46.7%), so the fire does not explain the 2025 county-wide low.

evidence.fact: PDC/FEMA assessment as of Aug 11, 2023: 2,207 structures damaged or destroyed in the Lahaina fire; 86% of exposed buildings were residential.
evidence.source: Pacific Disaster Center / FEMA, via Maui Now

evidence.fact: UHERO says the 2023 wildfires destroyed more than 3,000 housing units.
evidence.source: UHERO TVR phase-out analysis

evidence.fact: Maui County air visitor arrivals fell from 2.97 million (2022) to 2.53 million (2023).
evidence.source: DBEDT visitor statistics (as used in the report)

drivers.driver: Condo insurance and HOA costs raised the cost of holding second-home and rental condos from 2023.
drivers.quantified_effect: Not quantified for Maui. No official Maui-specific premium series was found.

evidence.fact: Legislative findings: condo master-policy deductibles rose from about $10,000–$25,000 per unit per occurrence to as much as $250,000, and the master-policy market was shrinking.
evidence.source: Hawai'i Legislature, HB 589 (2025) findings

evidence.fact: Act 296 (SB 1044), signed July 7, 2025, reactivated the Hurricane Relief Fund (dormant since after Iniki; reactivated by the Governor in 2024) to cover condo associations denied by two insurers, expanded HPIA, and created a condominium loan program. An agent quoted in the release reported savings of up to 70% on hurricane coverage.
evidence.source: Hawai'i DCCA Insurance Division news release

drivers.driver: A fixed supply of resort condos: no new vacation condo supply to replace sales, while new vacation-ownership supply goes into timeshares, which are not counted as home sales.
drivers.quantified_effect: Maui County visitor units were 21,413 in 2015 and 22,585 in 2025. On Maui island, condo-hotel units fell from 2,882 to 2,709 between 2024 and 2025 while timeshare units rose from 3,602 to 3,978.

evidence.fact: DBEDT Visitor Plant Inventory: Maui island 2025 vs 2024: condominium hotel 2,709 vs 2,882; vacation rental units 7,297 vs 7,290; timeshare 3,978 vs 3,602. Maui County available units 21,773 (2019), 22,585 (2025).
evidence.source: DBEDT 2025 Annual Visitor Research Report, Tables 112 and 114

counter_evidence: The measurement-break mechanism is inferred, not documented. Title Guaranty and DBEDT do not publish how origin is assigned or which property classes count. The match with the July 1, 2018 tax-class change is a timing match only. The enacted December 2017 ordinance text was not reviewed to confirm that hotel-class condos moved in FY2019.

An address-based reclassification could produce the same pattern as a coverage loss. Examples are deeds listing a Hawai'i manager or property address, or LLCs and trusts with local agents. After 2018, Title Guaranty's 'local' count rose above the county's count of homeowner-exemption purchases (ratio 0.93 in FY2016–17, 1.02–1.19 since). That fits either misclassified outside buyers or genuinely more local investor buying.

Real local-for-mainland substitution is possible, because the conveyance-tax 'non-owner' category includes O'ahu and Maui landlords and second-home owners. But a one-quarter, condo-only, Maui-only step that MLS sales and conveyance data do not show is not how buyer behavior usually changes.

MLS and Title Guaranty comparisons are noisy. Kaua'i's Title Guaranty condo count was only 0.74–0.82 of MLS in 2015–2017 with no break in its mainland share. The Maui MLS counts new-project sales, and the condo definitions differ.

UHERO's condo definition is broader (it includes townhomes and duplexes) and drops sales under $50,000. Part of the Maui gap could be definitional, although UHERO's counts are lower than DBEDT's in Honolulu (0.83x) and Hawai'i County (0.82–0.89x).

Real 2018 shocks could explain some of the step: Hurricane Lane and the August 2018 West Maui fires, the start of illegal-rental enforcement (Lodging Rev, May 2018), the higher tax rate for the new STR class, and the federal SALT deduction cap from 2018. The SALT cap applied to every island, and none of these shocks fits a lasting condo-only step that MLS data do not show.
The Lahaina fire did not reduce the outside share in West Maui in 2025 (32.7% to 46.7%), so it is a weak explanation for the 2025 county low.
The 2025 low of 25.3% partly reverses in 2026: 28% in Jan–Jun 2026, once Bill 88 offered a rezoning path. Part of the 2025 drop may be timing driven by policy uncertainty rather than a lasting shift.
The 2010 peak may also include non-market transfers such as lender and REO acquisitions, which a mainland address would classify as 'mainland'. That was not verified.
research.for_brokers: Don't present Title Guaranty's 25% as proof that mainland demand on Maui has dried up. On the county's conveyance-tax records, buyers without a homeowner exemption still made up 57% of Maui home sales in FY2025–26, and 77–92% of sales above $4M. Out-of-state buyers brought 40% of 2025 dollar volume. UHERO's Title Guaranty-based tables put out-of-state buyers at 55–59% of condo purchases. Outside demand has moved up-market and away from apartment-zoned vacation-rental condos, where Bill 9 creates deadline risk (West Maui Jan 1, 2029; elsewhere Jan 1, 2031) and Bill 88 rezoning (about 4,500 units, 32 complexes referred to the Planning Commission in late September 2026, none rezoned yet) is the main swing factor for Kihei and West Maui condo values. Practical steps: check each complex's Minatoya and H-3/H-4 status, and get the master insurance policy, deductible, reserve study and any special-assessment history before pricing a listing. Target California, Washington and Canadian owners of Minatoya units as a source of listings (85% of affected owners live out of state). When you cite buyer-origin numbers, pair Title Guaranty's figures with MLS and conveyance-tax data, because the published Maui series appears to under-count condo buyers since mid-2018.
research.for_locals: Competition from second-home buyers and investors did not fade the way the headline mainland share suggests: they were still more than half of Maui home purchases in every year from FY2016 to FY2026. What changed after 2022 is that outside buyers pulled back from condos that face vacation-rental bans and rising insurance and HOA costs, and condo prices fell (MLS median about -22% in 2025). That opens some entry-level ownership chances for local families, especially in South and West Maui. The risks are real: rising maintenance fees, special assessments, high insurance deductibles, and condo values that will depend on how Bill 9 and Bill 88 rezoning play out. Ask for the association's budget, reserves and insurance details before you buy. Houses remain hard to reach: the payment on a median-priced house took about 78% of median household income in 2025, against 42% in 2019. If Bill 9 conversions go ahead, UHERO estimates up to 6,127 units could return to long-term use, with condo prices 20–40% lower.

challenge.question: Why did the mainland buyer share on Maui fall from about 52% (2010) and 42% (2015) to 25% in 2025, with most of the drop by 2019?

verdicts.driver: A break in what the published Title Guaranty/DBEDT Maui series measures, starting Q3 2018 and concentrated in condos (timing matches Maui's July 1, 2018 short-term-rental tax class), not a retreat of mainland buyers. The researcher credits it with about 85% of the 2015–2019 drop.
verdicts.reason: WHAT HOLDS: There is a break. It shows up only on Maui, it is sudden, and it is in the measurement. Re-read from DBEDT QSER Tables G-51 and G-55 (https://files.hawaii.gov/dbedt/economic/data_reports/qser/G-select-county-tables.xlsx, 3Q-2026 edition): Q2 2018 had 324 mainland of 840 sales (38.6%) and Q3 2018 had 186 of 639 (29.1%). The average for 2016Q1–2018Q2 is 40.7% and for 2018Q3–2019Q4 is 28.6%. Honolulu, Hawai'i County and Kaua'i moved 0–3 points over the same windows. I computed Title Guaranty's quarterly Maui condo count against MLS condo sales (DBEDT MEI series in page_data): it fell from 1.01 (2018Q2) to 0.74 (2018Q3) and stayed at 0.69–0.88 after that. Total sales against MLS fell from 1.06 to 0.90 in the same quarter. UHERO's Title Guaranty-based Factbooks count 1,026 Maui condos for 2024 (59.0% out-of-state) and 824 for 2025 (54.5%), against 617 and 405 in DBEDT (https://uhero.hawaii.edu/wp-content/uploads/2026/05/TheHawaiiHousingFactbook2026.pdf, 2026-05-07). In Honolulu and Hawai'i County, UHERO's condo counts are below DBEDT's (0.82–0.83x). On county conveyance-tax records (Appleseed extract, file dated 2026-09-22), buyers without a homeowner exemption stayed at 54–57% of home sales in FY2016–FY2020. The 10,769 figure is accurate as reported: Tom Croly of the Maui Vacation Rental Association said 10,769 condo owners in the hotel class would move to the new STR class (The Maui News, Oct 2017, https://www.mauinews.com/news/local-news/2017/10/proposed-tax-changes-cause-concern/). The council passed the class 5-4 (The Maui News, 2017-12-05, https://www.mauinews.com/news/local-news/2017/12/tax-rate-for-short-term-rentals-created/). WHAT DOES NOT HOLD: (1) The 85% attribution is too high. I restored Title Guaranty's 2019 condo coverage to its 2017 MLS ratio of 1.03, which adds back about 424 sales. I then gave the added sales an out-of-state share between 55% (UHERO condo share) and 84% (owners in the TVR-STRH class). UHERO's own 2025 excess over DBEDT is 66% out-of-state ((599−332)/404). On those assumptions the 2019 mainland share rises from 28.3% to about 32–36%. That is roughly 4–8 points, or about a quarter to a half of the 14.1-point fall from 2015 to 2019. (2) Title Guaranty's local count jumped before the tax-class change. Local purchases were up 28% year on year in 2018Q1, 36% in Q2 and 28% in Q3, and rose from 1,450 (2017) to 1,768 (2018). Holding local purchases at their 2017 level lifts the 2019 mainland share by about 4 points. Part of the jump tracks extra single-family sales that are not on the MLS: the Title Guaranty/MLS single-family ratio went from about 1.02–1.06 to 1.13–1.16 from 2018Q1. The rest could be real local investors or misclassified outside buyers. Title Guaranty's local count has run above the county's homeowner-exemption purchase count ever since (ratio 0.93 in FY2016–17; 1.02–1.19 since). (3) Coverage did not collapse all at once. Title Guaranty's total against conveyance-tax home sales was 0.72–0.77 in FY2016–18, 0.68 in FY2019–21 and 0.61–0.63 in FY2022–26. (4) The STR-class mechanism rests on timing alone. Condos moved from a $9.37 rate (hotel and resort) to $9.28 (short-term rental), so buyers faced no real tax shock. That fits a measurement explanation but does not prove it, and Title Guaranty does not document its method. Maui County pages could not be re-opened in this session (egress blocked). (5) IRS in-migration does not test second-home demand, because second-home buyers do not change their tax address.
fact_errors: 'That 12.1-point step is about 85% of the 14.1-point fall' is correct arithmetic, but the step is not all measurement. Lost condo coverage explains roughly 4–8 points, and a local-count jump that began in 2018Q1 explains about 3–4 more.

'TG condos −40% vs MLS −18% (2018Q2 to Q3)' compares against a spike quarter. Q2 2018 had 503 Title Guaranty condos, against 401 in Q1 2018 and 405 in Q2 2017. Year on year, Q3 2018 condos were down 10% while MLS condos were up 22%. The clean comparison is the coverage ratio, which fell from 1.01 to 0.74.

'stopped capturing much of Maui's vacation-rental condo market around July 1, 2018' overstates the size. Coverage against conveyance-tax home sales fell about 10% in FY2019 (from about 0.75 to 0.68) and eroded further later.
The 10,769 figure is a Maui Vacation Rental Association estimate quoted in The Maui News (Oct 2017). It is not a county design target.
Steady IRS in-migration is not evidence about second-home demand.
verdicts.corrected_wording: A Maui-only break appears in the published Title Guaranty/DBEDT series in Q3 2018. Title Guaranty's condo count dropped from parity with MLS condo sales to about 75% of them in a single quarter, and the mainland share stepped down from 38.6% to 29.1%. Meanwhile the county's conveyance-tax records show buyers without a homeowner exemption holding at 55–56% of home sales. Lost condo coverage plausibly explains about a quarter to a half of the 2015–2019 fall (roughly 4–8 points). A rise in Title Guaranty-counted local purchases that began in early 2018 explains another 3–4 points. The timing matches the county's July 2018 short-term-rental tax class, but the mechanism is unconfirmed because Title Guaranty does not publish its method.

verdicts.driver: The 2010 starting point was a bust-era spike: resort condos pre-sold in 2005–06 (Honua Kai) were closing and distressed prices drew bargain hunters. It normalized by 2015.
verdicts.reason: Counts verified from QSER G-55. In 2010 mainland buyers made 1,768 of 3,418 purchases (51.7%). In 2015 they made 1,090 of 2,569 (42.4%). Local purchases were 1,380 and 1,392. Foreign buyers fell from 274 (2011) to 87 (2015). The Honolulu Advertiser (2010-05-08, https://archives-new.honoluluadvertiser.com/article/2010/May/08/bz/hawaii5080316.html) confirms 45 Honua Kai closings in April 2010 and about 150 in 2009, and notes that the Maui MLS counts new-project sales. Maui Now (2011-01-12, https://mauinow.com/2011/01/12/maui-sells-more-homes-at-lower-prices-in-2010/) confirms condo sales rose 39% (824 to 1,148) with the median down 16%, and that inventory included 'many short sales and REO' properties. In 2010 Title Guaranty recorded 2.0 times as many single-family sales as the MLS and 1.56 times as many condos. An alternative the researcher did not pursue: lender and REO transfers may have counted as 'mainland purchases.' Maui was described in March 2010 council testimony as the state's foreclosure hotspot. A RealtyTrac count republished by a Maui real-estate blog in May 2011 listed 1,712 bank-owned or pending-foreclosure properties in Maui ZIPs, 581 in Kihei and 450 in Lahaina (reported, unverified). A nonjudicial foreclosure deed to a lender with a mainland address would be classified as mainland. DBEDT's 2008–2015 analysis (dated 2016-07-06, https://files.hawaii.gov/dbedt/economic/data_reports/homesale/Home%20Sales%20in%20Hawaii%20to%20Mainland%20Buyers%20by%20Property%20Type.pdf) shows Texas as 12.1% of mainland single-family purchases. In Title Guaranty's 2025 statewide data, Texas was 5.3% of other-US buyers (175 of 3,314). That gap fits lender and servicer addresses (several large servicers are Texas-based) but does not prove it. Hawai'i's Act 48 (May 2011) curtailed nonjudicial foreclosures.
fact_errors: Maui Now's 2010 MLS single-family count is 812; the researcher's monthly sum gives 817. The difference is immaterial.
verdicts.corrected_wording: The 2010 peak was not a normal year. Pre-sold resort condos were closing, distressed sales were common, and some 'mainland purchases' may have been lender foreclosure transfers to mainland-addressed banks and servicers (unverified). In 2010 Title Guaranty recorded twice as many single-family transfers as the MLS. Mainland purchases fell from 1,768 (2010) to 1,090 (2015) while local purchases held near 1,390, which brought the share to 42%.

verdicts.driver: A real pullback by outside buyers after 2021: high mortgage rates and record prices, with outside buyers concentrated at the top. Locals now buy in price bands that second-home buyers used to dominate.
verdicts.reason: Verified. Title Guaranty mainland purchases fell 70% (1,069 to 316) and local purchases fell 54% (1,975 to 915) from 2021 to 2025. On conveyance-tax records, non-owner purchases fell from 2,813 (FY2022) to 1,166 (FY2025), or −59%, while owner purchases fell 43%. The non-owner share fell from 64.5% to 57.0%. That confirms a relative outside pullback from the 2021–22 peak. The problems: (1) The pullback brought the market back to its pre-pandemic level, not below it. The non-owner share was 57.0% in FY2025 and 56.7% in FY2026, against 57.4% in FY2017 and 54–56% in FY2016–20. (2) HMDA (an/new/hmda.json, FFIEC data browser) shows the non-owner-occupied share of mortgaged purchases flat at 34.7% (2019) and 34.4% (2025). Second-home loans fell from 328 to 87, but investment loans went from 18.4% to 24.6% of the total. Part of the second-home drop is a change in how lenders coded loans. One likely cause is FHFA's second-home upfront-fee increase (announced 2022-01-05, effective 2022-04-01, https://www.fhfa.gov/news/news-release/fhfa-announces-targeted-increases-to-enterprise-pricing-framework). That source could not be re-fetched this session. (3) The price-band evidence reflects inflation, not a retreat. Non-owner purchases in the $1–2M band rose from 173 (FY2016) to 309 (FY2025), while owner-occupants entered the band (89 to 312) as the median house reached about $1.3M. (4) High mortgage rates hit local, mortgage-dependent buyers hardest. Outside buyers paid an average $2.24M and more often pay cash, so rates by themselves would tend to raise the outside share, not lower it. (5) The 78.2% payment-to-income figure for 2025 carries 2024 income forward (income_held=true in page_data). (6) Part of Title Guaranty's 2021–2025 slide may still be coverage loss: its total against conveyance home sales went from 0.67 to 0.62, and its condo count against MLS from 0.60 to 0.58.
fact_errors: 'Out-of-state buyers made 25% of sales but 40% of dollar volume' mixes groups. Mainland buyers alone were 25.3% of sales and about 39.7% of dollars. Mainland plus foreign buyers were 26.6% of sales and about 43% of dollars.
'HMDA second-home purchase loans fell about 73%' is accurate, but non-owner-occupied loans as a whole fell 56%, the same rate as owner-occupied loans (also −56%).
The non-owner share falling from 66% to 50% in the $1–2M band is price inflation moving local owner-occupants into that band. Non-owner purchases in the band rose 79%.
For sales over $4M the non-owner share was 75% (FY2025) and 86% (FY2026), not '77–92%'.
verdicts.corrected_wording: After the 2021–22 pandemic surge, outside buying fell faster than local buying. Title Guaranty mainland purchases fell 70% against 54% for locals, and the conveyance-tax non-owner share fell from 64.5% (FY2022) to 57% (FY2025). That brought it back to its pre-pandemic level, not below it. On these data, mortgage rates and prices squeezed local mortgage borrowers at least as much as cash-rich outside buyers. Part of the remaining Title Guaranty slide may still be coverage erosion.

verdicts.driver: Vacation-rental policy risk (the Bill 9 phase-out of Minatoya-list rentals, earlier enforcement, and Bill 88's partial rescue), mainly behind the 2024–2025 condo drop. The researcher says the share recovered after Bill 88.
verdicts.reason: Verified. Bill 9 passed 5-3 and was signed on 2025-12-15. Phase-out dates are Jan 1, 2029 for West Maui and Jan 1, 2031 elsewhere (Maui Now, https://mauinow.com/2025/12/15/maui-council-passes-bill-9-5-3-on-second-and-final-reading/). UHERO's analysis (2025-03-31, https://uhero.hawaii.edu/wp-content/uploads/2025/03/EconomicAnalysisOfProposalToPhaseOutTVRsMaui.pdf) gives 6,127 operating units and 8,834 eligible, 85% with out-of-state owners (36% California, 12% Washington, 8% Canada), and projects condo prices falling 20–40%. Title Guaranty's South Side district had 193 other-US buyers in 2024 and 113 in 2025. Bill 88 (Ordinance 6008, H-3 and H-4 districts covering about 4,500 units) passed 7-2 in June 2026 (Maui Now, 2026-06-22, https://mauinow.com/2026/06/22/new-hotel-zoning-for-vacation-rentals-passes-maui-council-on-final-vote-7-2/). Thirty-two complexes were referred to the Planning Commission on 2026-09-30 (https://mauinow.com/2026/09/30/maui-council-refers-32-shoreline-condo-complexes-hotel-rezoning-to-maui-planning-commission/). CONTRADICTED: (1) There was no post-Bill 88 recovery. Bill 88 passed at the end of June 2026, after almost all January–June sales had closed. The mainland share was 28.5% in H1 2025 (175 of 613) and 27.8% in H1 2026 (179 of 643), so H1 2026 was slightly lower. The 2025 H2 low (22.2%) is partly seasonal: in 2024, H1 was 29.2% and H2 was 25.1%. In the South Side, the other-US share was 44% in H1 2025 and 36% in H1 2026. (2) West Side (Lahaina–Kaanapali) faces the earliest deadline (2029), yet its outside share rose from 32.7% to 46.7% in 2025, which cuts against Bill 9 as the main deterrent. (3) Policy risk cannot explain 2015–2019. Enforcement (Lodging Rev 2018, fines from Dec 2019) was not re-verified this session, and it targets unpermitted homes rather than condos. (4) The South Side sample is small (113 buyers), and the condo series it comes from is the one with impaired coverage.
fact_errors: 'recovered to about 28% in Jan–Jun 2026, after Bill 88 passed' is wrong. Bill 88 passed in late June 2026, and the H1 2026 share (27.8%) is below H1 2025 (28.5%).
'Maui's mainland share was lowest in 2025 H2 (22%)' is correct, but second halves run lower every year (2024: H1 29.2%, H2 25.1%), so the low is not a policy shock by itself.
verdicts.corrected_wording: Vacation-rental policy risk fits the 2024–25 drop in out-of-state buyers in South Maui condos: other-US buyers fell from 193 to 113 while Hawai'i buyers there fell only 13%. It does not explain the 2015–2019 fall or the West Maui pattern. The data show no rebound after Bill 88: the H1 2026 mainland share (27.8%) was at or below H1 2025 (28.5%).

verdicts.driver: The Lahaina fire (Aug 8, 2023) shrank West Maui housing stock and visitor demand. It reduced the number of deals more than it changed the outside share.
verdicts.reason: The facts check out. UHERO's TVR report says about 3,000 housing units were lost. Maui visitor arrivals were 2.97M in 2022 and 2.53M in 2023 (−14.8%), then 2.39M in 2024 and 2.55M in 2025 (QSER Table G-19). Title Guaranty West Side sales were 205 (2024) and 180 (2025). The outside share there rose in 2025. Note that the rise came partly from local West Side purchases falling (134 to 94), possibly after 2024 replacement buying by fire survivors, so the share is noisy. The 2,207-structure count comes from PDC/FEMA via Maui Now (2023-08-12); it is reported and was not re-checked.
verdicts.corrected_wording: The Lahaina fire cut West Maui housing stock (about 3,000 units) and visitor arrivals (−15% in 2023). That reduced transactions but does not explain the fall in the county-wide outside share. West Side's outside share rose in 2025, partly because local purchases there fell.

verdicts.driver: Condo insurance and HOA costs raised the cost of holding second-home and rental condos from 2023.
verdicts.reason: The facts are confirmed. HB 589 (2025) findings say master-policy deductibles rose from about $10,000–$25,000 to as much as $250,000 per unit (https://data.capitol.hawaii.gov/sessions/session2025/bills/HB589_.HTM). Act 296 (SB 1044) was signed 2025-07-07 and reactivated the Hurricane Relief Fund; an agent quoted 'upwards of 70%' savings (reported) (DCCA, https://cca.hawaii.gov/ins/release-governor-green-enacts-laws-to-stabilize-property-insurance-market-2/). But this was a statewide shock, and condo-heavy O'ahu's mainland share rose from 9.6% (2019) to 16.2% (2023) and was 13.8% in 2025. Hawai'i County and Kaua'i were at about 32% in 2025. No Maui-specific premium data were found. The cost increase may weigh on condo prices, but it does not explain why outside buyers' share fell on Maui.
verdicts.corrected_wording: Higher condo insurance deductibles and fees raised holding costs statewide from about 2022–23. Because other islands' mainland shares held or rose, this is at most a minor factor in Maui's outside-buyer share. It mainly affects condo prices and carrying costs.

verdicts.driver: A fixed supply of resort condos, while new vacation-ownership supply goes into timeshares, which are not counted as home sales.
verdicts.reason: The figures are confirmed from DBEDT's 2025 Annual Visitor Research Report, Table 112 (https://files.hawaii.gov/dbedt/economic/tourism/annual-reports/2025-annual-visitor.xlsx, file dated 2026-09-28). On Maui island, condo-hotel units were 2,709 (vs 2,882), vacation-rental units 7,297 (vs 7,290) and timeshares 3,978 (vs 3,602). These changes are small (hundreds of units). The inventory covers rental-pool units only, and supply levels do not set buyer-origin shares. In the key 2018–19 period, MLS condo resales were high (1,657 and 1,617), so a supply constraint did not limit outside buying when the share fell.
verdicts.corrected_wording: Resort-condo supply has been roughly flat, and new vacation-ownership units go into timeshares, but no evidence links this to the falling outside share. It is not a meaningful driver.

missing_drivers: A jump in Title Guaranty-counted local purchases that began in Q1 2018, before the tax-class change: up 28–36% year on year, and from 1,450 in 2017 to 1,768 in 2018. On its own this cuts the 2019 mainland share by about 4 points. Part of it tracks extra single-family sales that are not on the MLS (Title Guaranty/MLS single-family ratio up from about 1.02 to 1.13–1.16). The rest is unexplained.

How buyer origin is assigned. Origin comes from the deed address, so trusts, LLCs, local agents or managers, and property-address listings can make an outside buyer look local. Since 2018, Title Guaranty's local count has run above the county's homeowner-exemption purchase count.

Foreclosure-era lender and REO transfers in 2009–2012, which may be counted as 'mainland purchases' and would inflate the 2010 baseline. Texas made up 12.1% of mainland single-family buyers in 2008–2015 against about 5% of other-US buyers in 2025. Hawai'i's Act 48 (2011) curtailed nonjudicial foreclosures.
The pandemic remote-work surge and its reversal. The non-owner share of conveyance-tax sales peaked at 64.5% in FY2022, so 2021–22 is an abnormal reference point for measuring the later decline.

Changes in mortgage coding and pricing (for example FHFA's 2022 second-home fees) that moved loans from 'second home' to 'investment' in HMDA. This makes the HMDA second-home series a weak indicator of demand.
Seasonality and small samples. Second-half mainland shares run 3–5 points below first-half shares, and district counts are often under 200.
The near-disappearance of foreign (mostly Canadian) buyers, from 270 in 2010 to 16 in 2025. This lowers the combined out-of-state share but not the mainland share.
challenge.final_answer: Most of Maui's fall from about 52% to 25% is not a mainland exodus. Three separate things stack up. First, 2010 was an abnormal base year. Pre-sold resort condos such as Honua Kai were closing, distressed sales were common, and some 'mainland purchases' may have been bank foreclosure transfers (unverified). By 2015 mainland purchases had fallen from 1,768 to 1,090 while local purchases stayed near 1,390, which brought the share to 42%. Second, between 2015 and 2019 the published Title Guaranty/DBEDT series broke, only on Maui. The mainland share dropped from 38.6% to 29.1% in a single quarter (Q3 2018). In that same quarter, Title Guaranty's condo count fell from roughly matching MLS condo sales to about 75% of them. Yet county conveyance-tax records show buyers without a homeowner exemption steady at 55–56% of Maui home sales. Lost condo coverage plausibly explains a quarter to a half of the 2015–2019 drop (about 4–8 points). A jump in Title Guaranty-counted local purchases that began in early 2018 explains another 3–4 points. That leaves only a few points that could be a real shift. The timing matches the county's July 2018 short-term-rental tax class, but the mechanism is unconfirmed because Title Guaranty does not publish its method. Third, after the 2021–22 pandemic surge, outside buying did fall faster than local buying: Title Guaranty mainland purchases fell 70% against 54% for locals, and the conveyance-tax non-owner share fell from 64.5% to 57%. That only returned the market to its pre-pandemic level. The vacation-rental phase-out (Bill 9) shows up in South Maui condos, where out-of-state buyers fell from 193 to 113. The Lahaina fire, condo insurance costs and resort supply explain little of the share. There was no rebound after Bill 88: the H1 2026 mainland share was 27.8%, against 28.5% in H1 2025. For brokers, Title Guaranty's 25% understates outside demand. By other measures, non-homeowner buyers were still about 57% of Maui home purchases in FY2025–26, and UHERO counts 55–59% of condo buyers as out-of-state. For local families, competition from second-home buyers and investors has returned to its pre-pandemic level rather than faded, and the main opening is in Minatoya-list condos whose rental status is in doubt. Confidence: medium that the headline fall mostly reflects a distorted 2010 base year and a 2018 measurement break; low on the exact cause of the break.

research.question: Why are investors 23–31% of mortgaged purchases on Maui, Kauai and Hawaii Island but 13% on Oahu, and why do VA loans make up 27% of Oahu purchase mortgages?
research.answer: Two things drive the gap: where vacation renting is legal, and who Oahu's other buyers are. On Kauai, Maui and Hawaii Island, legal vacation rentals are a large part of the housing stock. UHERO counts active STRs at 19.9%, 15.2% and 9.0% of homes there, against 2.5% on Oahu. In 2025 they booked about $17.7K, $13.6K and $5.3K of vacation-rental revenue per housing unit, against $1.7K on Oahu (DBEDT revenue figures divided by housing units, computed here). Investor buying follows the same map inside each island. In 2025 HMDA data (grouped by census tract), investment loans were 53% of mortgaged purchases in West Maui, 50% on Kauai's North Shore and 37% in Waikiki. They were 12% in Central Maui and 4–7% in Ewa, Mililani and Pearl City. So the split is resort areas versus everywhere else, not Oahu versus the other islands. Oahu's 2022 90-day rule is a small part of the story. Oahu's investor share was already 10.3% in 2019, before the rule, and it rose to 12.7% by 2025. Oahu's low share is also diluted by a large group of owner-occupants that barely exists elsewhere: the military. DoD counts 43,719 active-duty personnel and 44,123 dependents on Oahu, against fewer than 900 personnel and dependents combined on all neighbor islands. Oahu also has about 76% of the state's veterans. VA loans require the buyer to live in the home. They need no down payment or mortgage insurance and have no loan limit for full-entitlement borrowers. On Oahu in 2025 they carried a median rate half a point below conventional and allowed debt-to-income above 50% (47% of VA loans versus 1% of conventional ones). Hawaii tours run 36 months, and 2026 housing allowances for mid-grade families ($3,663–$4,428 a month) are close to the $4,050–$4,140 principal-and-interest payment on a median Oahu VA loan. So a steady stream of service members buy instead of renting. VA ends up at 27% of Oahu purchase loans, about 2.7 times the national share on a comparable measure. Taking VA loans out lifts Oahu's investor share from 12.7% to 17.2%, which closes about 2–3 points of the 10–18 point gap. Two cautions. HMDA leaves out cash purchases, which are likely more common among out-of-state buyers. And much of the rise in the 'investor' label since 2019 is lenders coding vacation-home purchases as business-purpose investment loans (likely DSCR-style). The combined second-home-plus-investor share hardly changed: 31–40% on the neighbor islands versus 14–16% on Oahu in both years.

drivers.driver: Legal vacation-rental stock and STR revenue are concentrated on the neighbor islands and in Oahu's resort zones (zoning geography)
drivers.quantified_effect: Island ranking on STR share of housing and on vacation-rental revenue per housing unit (Kauai > Maui > Hawaii > Oahu) matches the ranking on investor share of mortgaged purchases (30.7% > 24.6% > 22.8% > 12.7%). Within Oahu, Waikiki has 37% investor loans on 7% of purchase loans (21% of Oahu's investor loans). Oahu excluding Waikiki is 10.8%. Central Maui (12%) looks like Oahu, while West Maui (53%) and South Maui (33%) look like resort markets.

drivers.driver: VA loan terms (no down payment, no mortgage insurance, no limit with full entitlement, residual-income underwriting, lower rate) make VA the cheapest route to ownership for eligible Oahu buyers
drivers.quantified_effect: On Oahu, 61% of VA purchase loans had LTV of 100% or more. VA made up 61% of owner-occupant first-lien loans with 5% or less down, and 39% (172 of 436) of first-lien loans above the $1,209,750 conforming limit. VA's median note rate was 5.875% versus 6.375% for conventional owner-occupant loans. 46.8% of VA loans had DTI of 50% or more, versus 1.3% of conventional owner-occupant loans. VA purchase volume fell 17% from 2019 to 2025, while non-VA fell 25%.

drivers.driver: BAH levels and 36-month PCS rotations create steady military buyer turnover on Oahu
drivers.quantified_effect: Honolulu 2026 BAH with dependents ($3,663 for E-5, $3,912 for E-6, $4,098 for E-7, $4,428 for O-3) covers about 88–107% of principal and interest on the median Oahu VA loan ($4,052, or $4,139 with the 2.15% funding fee financed; computed here). A 36-month tour implies about a third of the roughly 43,700 Oahu personnel rotate each year (about 14,500; our estimate). BAH level itself does not explain the gap between islands: Maui's BAH is higher than Honolulu's.

Investor shares counting only consumer-purpose loans were Kauai 9.8%, Maui 6.9%, Hawaii 5.4% and Oahu 3.5%. The combined second-home-plus-investor share barely moved from 2019 to 2025: Hawaii 30.0% to 31.2%, Kauai 38.5% to 39.9%, Maui 34.7% to 34.4%, Oahu 14.3% to 15.7%.

At the median Oahu condo ($562,400), 70% financing at 7.0% costs about $2,619 a month in principal and interest, against a $2,083 median rent (computed here). Leveraged long-term renting does not cash-flow, so it does not produce a high mortgaged-investor share. Oahu's investor share is highest below $500K (16%), where entry condos sit.

drivers.driver: Conforming loan limits
drivers.quantified_effect: Limits were identical in all four counties in 2025 ($1,209,750), so they cannot explain the investor gap between islands. They matter for VA on Oahu, because full-entitlement VA buyers can borrow above the limit with no down payment. Conventional jumbo share on Oahu fell from 13.3% to 5.8% as the limit rose.

evidence.value: 2025: $1,209,750 in all four counties. 2026: Hawaii, Honolulu and Kauai $1,249,125; Maui $1,299,500.
evidence.source: FHFA Full County Loan Limit Lists 2025 and 2026

evidence.fact: Oahu first-lien purchase loans above the conforming limit, 2025
evidence.source: HMDA 2025 loan-level data, computed here

counter_evidence: HMDA covers only mortgaged purchases, so cash buyers are missing. On Maui, 57% of FY2025 improved residential sales (1,166 of 2,047) went to buyers not eligible for the homeowner exemption, versus 34% non-owner-occupied among mortgaged purchases. The true investor and second-home share on the neighbor islands is likely higher, and the gap with Oahu probably wider (Maui County RPT sales file, processed locally; https://www.mauicounty.gov/DocumentCenter/View/8070/RPT-Sales-Data-File-).

The '23–31% investor' figure partly reflects how lenders label loans, not more investing. Second-home loans shifted into investment/business-purpose coding after 2019, while the combined non-owner share stayed flat (Kauai 38.5% to 39.9%, Maui 34.7% to 34.4%, Hawaii 30.0% to 31.2%, Oahu 14.3% to 15.7%). The 2019 investor-only gap was smaller on Hawaii Island (10.5% vs Oahu 10.3%).

Hawaii Island's 22.8% is not explained by resort zoning alone. Hilo/Puna tracts show 22% investor loans while Hilo ZIP 96720 has only a 2.8% STR share, and 21% of Hawaii County loans under $500K are investor loans. Cheap Puna/Hilo homes, long-term rental investors and DSCR lenders likely contribute.

Maui's 2025 mix reflects the post-Lahaina-fire market. Purchase loan volume was down 56% from 2019 (886 vs 2,010), so composition shifts could move the shares; HMDA cannot separate fire effects from rate effects.

Oahu's VA share is not purely active duty. About 81,000 Oahu veterans (including retirees near Tripler and other VA facilities) also use VA loans, and HMDA cannot tell active-duty borrowers from veterans. The younger age profile (44.6% under 35) suggests a large active-duty share but does not prove it.

The geography of VA loans may partly reflect product rules rather than base proximity. VA requires condo projects to be VA-approved, and secondary guides report 50% owner-occupancy thresholds, which many investor-heavy Waikiki and urban towers may fail. New single-family and townhome supply is concentrated in Ewa/Kapolei. Both could push VA toward those areas regardless of commute (reported: https://www.quickenloans.com/learn/va-loan-condo-approval-process).

BAH levels do not explain the gap between islands. Maui's 2026 E-5 with-dependents BAH ($4,329) is higher than Honolulu's ($3,663), but fewer than 200 active-duty personnel live on Maui. Headcount, not allowance level, is what matters.
The removal of VA from the denominator explains only about 2–3 points of the 10–18 point gap. Most of the gap remains even after excluding VA (Oahu 17.2% vs 25.6–32.4%).

Oahu's 90-day rule may have reduced investor demand at the margin that HMDA cannot detect (for example, buyers shifting to cash or to Waikiki). Oahu's investor share rose from 2019 to 2025 rather than falling, but there is no counterfactual.
Region assignments use approximate tract-centroid boxes, and some tract boundaries changed between Census vintages. Sub-island shares are indicative, not exact.
research.for_brokers: Investor demand follows where vacation renting is legal, not the island name. In resort-zoned and VDA/apartment-district areas (West and South Maui, Princeville/Poipu, Kona, Waikiki, Turtle Bay/Ko Olina), a third to half of mortgaged buyers are investors, and more pay cash. Before marketing a unit as an income property, confirm its legal STR status in writing: Honolulu resort zone or NUC, Kauai VDA or nonconforming use certificate, Maui permit or Minatoya status. Maui apartment-district units face Bill 9 deadlines on Jan 1, 2029 (West Maui) and Jan 1, 2031, with owner lawsuits pending. Most investor financing now runs through business-purpose (DSCR-style) loans at a median 7.0–7.5%, about 0.5–1.0 point above owner-occupant rates, with 25–30% down. Run every STR deal against a long-term-rent fallback, because long-term rent on Oahu and Maui typically does not cover a 70%-financed payment at those rates. On Oahu, the core financed buyer in Ewa/Kapolei (57% VA), Central Oahu (42%), Pearl City/Waipahu/Aiea (36%) and the Windward side (30%) is a VA buyer. Make listings VA-ready: check condo project approval on VA's condo report before listing, expect zero-down offers with financed funding fees and seller-concession requests, and time launches for spring–summer PCS season. VA has no loan cap for full-entitlement buyers: 172 Oahu VA loans in 2025 were above the conforming limit ($1,209,750 in 2025; $1,249,125 in 2026), so VA buyers matter up to about $1.5M. The 36-month rotation also produces a steady supply of military owners who leave and either sell or rent out their homes. Build listing and property-management referral pipelines with PCS-departing owners, and relocation referrals to Washington, Texas, Virginia and other military-heavy states.
research.for_locals: On Oahu, non-military families compete with buyers who can put zero down, skip mortgage insurance, get about half a point lower rates, and qualify at debt-to-income ratios conventional lenders rarely allow. In 2025, 61% of Oahu owner-occupant loans with 5% or less down were VA loans. This competition is strongest in Ewa, Kapolei, Mililani and Pearl City, where more than a third to over half of financed buyers use VA. Urban Honolulu and East Honolulu see much less of it (10–12% VA). Military demand also props up rents near bases, since 2026 BAH for a junior enlisted family is $3,333–$3,663 a month. On the neighbor islands, the toughest competition from investors and second-home buyers is concentrated in resort areas: West Maui (53% investor loans plus 15% second homes), South Maui, Kauai's North Shore and Poipu, and Kona. In Central Maui, Upcountry, West Kauai and Kohala/Waimea, investors are 11–18% of mortgaged buyers, close to Oahu levels. Maui's Bill 9 could return many of about 7,000 apartment-zoned vacation units to long-term use or sale by 2029–2031, which may ease condo prices and rents in Kihei and West Maui. But owners can also keep units for personal use, and the law faces lawsuits. Check state and county first-time buyer programs to offset the down-payment gap that VA buyers do not face.

challenge.question: Why are investors 23–31% of mortgaged purchases on Maui, Kauai and Hawaii Island but 13% on Oahu, and why do VA loans make up 27% of Oahu purchase mortgages?

verdicts.driver: Legal vacation-rental stock and STR revenue are concentrated on the neighbor islands and in Oahu's resort zones (zoning geography)
verdicts.reason: Re-checked from local files. County investor shares come from the raw HMDA 2025 loan-level CSV: Hawaii 22.8%, Honolulu 12.7%, Kauai 30.7%, Maui 24.6%. UHERO STR shares come from an/new/uhero.json county rows: Kauai 19.9% (6,052), Maui 15.2% (10,972), Hawaii 9.0% (8,207), Honolulu 2.5% (9,284); Waikiki 96815 has 5,463 STRs, 58.8% of Oahu's. DBEDT vacation-rental YTD demand and ADR are in the Dec-2025 report text (vr2025_12.txt), and the revenue-per-unit results reproduce: $17.7K, $13.6K, $5.3K, $1.7K. All match. New test (data, computed 2026-10-08): 47 ZIPs with at least 25 loans (9,537 loans), joining the hmda_tract.json ZCTA rollup to UHERO ZIP STR shares, loan-weighted. STR share alone explains R²=0.63 of investor share; an Oahu dummy adds about nothing (coefficient -2.0 pts, R² 0.638). Adding VA share lifts R² to 0.70. Decomposing each island's gap with Oahu (inv = 0.159 + 0.777·STR − 0.198·VA): the STR term accounts for 10.7 of Maui's 11.9 points, 19.2 of Kauai's 18.2 and only 6.4 of Hawaii Island's 11.1. Three limits. (1) STR share is partly an outcome of past investor buying, and resort amenities drive both, so zoning cannot be isolated as the cause. (2) The pattern breaks on Hawaii Island. Pahoa-Kalapana CCD is 47.6% investor (n=82) and Keaau-Mountain View 19.7% (n=615), at 4.9–7.9% STR shares. Hawaii County Ordinance 2018-114 bars new unhosted STVRs in residential and agricultural zones unless grandfathered (prior project verification, ev/decades_result.json). (3) Ala Moana/Ward ZIP 96814 is 29.5% investor (n=573) at a 1.4% STR share. One tract there (36.03) holds 134 of 391 loans as investor loans, about 16% of all Oahu investor loans, unrelated to STR use. The sub-region boxes are approximate. For example, the researcher's 'Kohala/Waimea 11%' excludes Waikoloa (South Kohala CCD 26.3%, n=217; Waikoloa ZIP 32%).
fact_errors: The claim that the split is 'resort areas versus everywhere else' does not hold on Hawaii Island. Non-resort Puna and Hilo run well above Oahu's non-resort areas: Pahoa-Kalapana CCD 47.6%, Keaau-Mountain View 19.7%, Hilo 18.6%, at STR shares of 2.8–7.9%.
The claim also misses a large non-STR investor cluster on Oahu: 96814 Ala Moana/Ward, 29.5% investor loans at a 1.4% STR share.
verdicts.corrected_wording: Across 47 ZIP codes, the share of homes used as short-term rentals explains nearly two-thirds of the variation in investor share of mortgaged purchases. Once it is accounted for, being on Oahu makes no difference. Resort ZIPs run 29–54% investor (Lahaina, Kihei, Princeville, Koloa/Poipu, Kona, Waikoloa, Waikiki), while non-resort towns on every island run 3–12% (Kahului, Wailuku, Kalaheo, Mililani, Ewa, Waipahu). Exceptions are Puna and Hilo on Hawaii Island (19–48%) and Ala Moana/Ward on Oahu (29.5%), where investor buying is not tied to STRs. Because STR stock partly reflects past investor buying and resort amenities, this shows association with vacation-rental geography, not a clean zoning effect.

verdicts.driver: Military and veteran population concentrated on Oahu creates a large VA owner-occupant pool, which also dilutes Oahu's investor share
verdicts.reason: VA counts are confirmed. Raw HMDA 2025 gives Honolulu 1,830 of 6,746 loans (27.1%), 31.9% of owner-occupant loans, against Hawaii 10.8%, Kauai 5.3% and Maui 4.7%; Oahu was 25.1% in 2019. FFIEC aggregation API (2026-10-08) gives Honolulu 24.7% vs national 9.24% (617,940 of 6,687,105): https://ffiec.cfpb.gov/v2/data-browser-api/view/nationwide/aggregations?years=2025&loan_purposes=1&loan_types=1,2,3,4. DEERS Table 1.22 (as of 2026-03-31; local DB2025_section01.xlsx) gives Oahu 43,719 personnel plus 44,123 dependents, and 874 combined on all other islands. Investor share with VA excluded is confirmed at 17.2% Oahu vs 25.6–32.4% elsewhere. New context (FFIEC API, 2026-10-08, same all-applications measure): Honolulu's 24.7% is ordinary for a military-host county. Anchorage is 24.6%, Pierce WA 16.1%, San Diego 13.7%, El Paso CO 35.4%, Virginia Beach 37.5%, and base-dominated counties run 50–62% (Onslow NC 62.1%, Cumberland NC 51.6%, Bell TX 51.0%). So the VA share is a headcount effect. Veterans alone do not explain it. Veterans per resident are 7.9% on Oahu vs 6.2–6.3% on Hawaii Island and Kauai (FY2023 Table 10.30 over UHERO populations). Active duty is 4.4% of Oahu's population vs at most 0.2% elsewhere. The dilution effect is real but secondary. Removing VA closes only 1.7–3.3 points (16–28%) of the 10–18 point gap, and the ZIP model's VA term is 3.3–4.6 points.
fact_errors: The veteran count is FY2022. The Data Book's latest, FY2023, is Honolulu 79,391 of 104,765 (75.8%), not 81,293.
The headline framing that military buyers are one of 'two things' driving the investor gap overstates them. Taking VA loans out explains roughly a fifth of the gap.
verdicts.corrected_wording: VA loans are 27% of Oahu purchase loans because about 43,700 active-duty members and 44,100 dependents live on Oahu, against fewer than 900 people combined on all other islands. Honolulu's VA share (24.7% of 2025 purchase applications) is typical of U.S. military-host counties. It is in line with Anchorage (24.6%) and below Virginia Beach (37.5%) and El Paso County, Colorado (35.4%). These owner-occupant VA buyers dilute Oahu's investor share only modestly. Removing them lifts it from 12.7% to 17.2%, which closes 2–3 of the 10–18 point gap.

verdicts.driver: VA loan terms (no down payment, no mortgage insurance, no limit with full entitlement, residual-income underwriting, lower rate) make VA the cheapest route to ownership for eligible Oahu buyers
verdicts.reason: Re-computed from raw HMDA 2025 (Oahu). VA median loan is $685K. VA median rate is 5.875% vs 6.375% for conventional owner-occupant loans. 46.8% of VA loans with a reported DTI were at 50% or more (848 of 1,813), vs 1.3% of conventional owner-occupant loans. VA made up 61.4% of owner-occupant first-lien loans with LTV of 95% or more (1,095 of 1,783). 172 of 436 first-lien loans above the conforming limit were VA, the smallest at $1.215M. VA count fell 17% from 2019 to 2025 (2,205 to 1,830) vs 25% for non-VA (6,581 to 4,916).
