New: owner-occupant VA share is flat at 31–35% in every price band from under $500K up to $1.5M, then 25% at $1.5–2M and 11% above $2M. VA buyers are not confined to entry-level homes. The VA program rules (no limit with full entitlement since Jan 1, 2020; funding fees) could not be re-fetched because va.gov is blocked to this session. An earlier project adjudication confirmed the no-limit rule (ev/adjudications.json). Caveat: the terms are national, so they explain why eligible buyers choose VA over conventional or FHA loans. They do not explain why Oahu's share is high; headcount does. The residual-income figure comes from a lender (Veterans United) and is reported, not official.
fact_errors: '61% of VA purchase loans had LTV of 100% or more' is 61.4% of the 1,552 VA loans that report LTV. Counting all 1,830 VA loans, the share is 52%, because 278 have no LTV.
verdicts.corrected_wording: For eligible buyers, VA is the cheapest way to buy on Oahu. Of VA loans that report a loan-to-value ratio, 61% financed 100% or more of the value. The median VA rate was 5.875% vs 6.375% for conventional owner-occupant loans. 47% of VA borrowers had debt-to-income of 50% or more, vs 1% of conventional ones. VA also finances above the conforming limit with no down payment: 172 of 436 Oahu loans above $1,209,750 in 2025 were VA. VA's share of owner-occupant purchases holds at 31–35% from under $500K up to $1.5M.

verdicts.driver: BAH levels and 36-month PCS rotations create steady military buyer turnover on Oahu
verdicts.reason: The 2026 BAH figures are confirmed in the local DBEDT Data Book Table 10.27 (DB2025_section10.xlsx, rates effective 2026-01-01). Honolulu with dependents: E-5 $3,663, E-6 $3,912, E-7 $4,098, O-3 $4,428. Maui E-5 is $4,329. The payment math reproduces. $685K at 5.875% gives $4,052 P&I, or $4,139 with the 2.15% funding fee financed, so BAH covers 88–109% of P&I. ACS 2024 PUMS confirms 22.2% of interstate in-migrants were active duty (page_data.json, n=554). Problems: (1) The 36-month tour source cited is a DoD civilian-personnel memo (CAP 53-23), which covers civilian employees, not service members. The military tour length (Joint Travel Regulations) could not be re-verified: web search was exhausted and media.defense.gov is blocked to this session. (2) BAH is set from local market rents, so it roughly equals rent by design. BAH that covers 88–109% of P&I alone, before property tax, insurance and HOA dues, shows that buying costs about as much as or more than renting for E-5 to E-7. It does not by itself show that buying beats renting; expected equity or keeping the home as a rental would have to do that. (3) The roughly 14,500-a-year rotation counts all personnel, including junior members in barracks. The family pool is closer to the 16,107 spouses on Oahu (Table 1.22), so about a third of that rotates each year (rough estimate). (4) Table 10.25 shows about 14,000 all-rental units in military CDPs. These house families on base. The table shows there is no on-base ownership, not that families are pushed off base. (5) BAH levels cannot explain the gap between islands: Maui's BAH is higher, but fewer than 200 personnel live there. (6) The idea that departing military owners become landlords gets little support from the owner roll (an/new/owners_oahu.json). Mainland-mailing owners are 4.4% of parcels in Mililani 96789 (49% VA) and 5.6% in Ewa 96706 (52% VA), vs 7.4% Oahu-wide. Makakilo/Kapolei 96707 is the exception at 10.7%.
fact_errors: The 36-month tour is sourced to a civilian-employee tour-length memo (CAP 53-23), not to military tour rules.
BAH covers 88–109% of principal and interest, not 88–107%; O-3 without a financed fee is 109%. That comparison also leaves out taxes, insurance and HOA dues.
On-base housing does not 'push' families into the private market. It houses many of them; it only rules out owning on base.
verdicts.corrected_wording: Steady military turnover keeps feeding VA buyers. 22% of people who moved to Hawaii from another state in the past year were active duty (ACS 2024). 2026 housing allowances for mid-grade families ($3,663–$4,428) roughly match principal and interest on a median Oahu VA loan, before taxes, insurance and HOA dues. Because the allowance is set at local rents, buying is not clearly cheaper than renting each month. The appeal is zero-down equity. Allowance levels do not explain the difference between islands.

verdicts.driver: The lending channel and how lenders label loans (DSCR/business-purpose investor loans; vacation homes recoded from second home to investment after 2022 GSE fees)
verdicts.reason: The occupancy-coding shift is confirmed from raw HMDA. Combined second-home-plus-investor share in 2019 to 2025: Hawaii 30.0% to 31.2%, Kauai 38.5% to 39.9%, Maui 34.7% to 34.4%, Oahu 14.3% to 15.7%. Investor-only 2019 shares were Hawaii 10.5%, Oahu 10.3%, Kauai 19.2%, Maui 18.4%. Correction on 'business-purpose = DSCR': Regulation Z commentary deems any credit to acquire non-owner-occupied rental property business-purpose. That is comment 3(a)-4, eCFR Title 12 Part 1026 Supplement I, version 2025-12-01, retrieved 2026-10-08: https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-12/chapter-X/part-1026/appendix-Supplement%20I%20to%20Part%201026. So the 75–81% BP share is largely a legal default. A better DSCR proxy is business-purpose with income not relied on. Under that proxy, 2025 investment loans were 44% DSCR-like on Hawaii Island, 33% on Kauai, 31% on Oahu and 25% on Maui, vs 4–10% in 2019. These loans add 10.0 points to the investor share of Hawaii and Kauai, 6.1 to Maui and 3.9 to Oahu. Without them, investor shares are Hawaii 12.9%, Kauai 20.7%, Maui 18.5% and Oahu 8.8%; in 2019 they were 10.0, 18.4, 16.8 and 9.3. So Oahu's whole rise from 10.3% to 12.7% is DSCR-like lending. For Hawaii Island this channel is a main driver. Its investor-only gap with Oahu was zero in 2019. In 2025, one business-purpose bridge lender, Temple View Capital Funding, LP (GLEIF: https://api.gleif.org/api/v1/lei-records/549300RYTR2RVL4SFJ90, retrieved 2026-10-08), made 77 of the county's 405 investor loans. All 77 were business-purpose, at a median 10.5% rate and $415K median value, with 55 in two Puna tracts (210.13 and 211.08). Oahu's top investor lenders are local banks (Bank of Hawaii, First Hawaiian, American Savings, Central Pacific, Hawaiian Financial FCU), plus non-QM lenders (Citadel Servicing, Conventus, HomeXpress). The FHFA second-home fee rests on NAHB (reported) and is plausible but not shown to cause the recoding.
fact_errors: The 75–81% business-purpose share does not indicate DSCR loans. Reg Z deems all non-owner-occupied rental purchase credit business-purpose. The DSCR-like share (no income relied on) is 25–44% of investment loans.
'This changes the level of the label more than the gap between islands' is wrong for Hawaii Island. Its investor-only share equaled Oahu's in 2019 (10.5% vs 10.3%).
verdicts.corrected_wording: Part of the 23–31% investor figure is a labeling and lending effect. Since 2019, lenders moved vacation-home loans from 'second home' to 'investment', so the combined non-owner share barely changed (Oahu 14–16%; neighbor islands 30–40%). Meanwhile, lenders that don't verify income grew from about 1% to 4–10% of all purchase loans. Without those loans, 2025 investor shares are Kauai 21%, Maui 19%, Hawaii Island 13% and Oahu 9%. On Hawaii Island, one bridge lender charging about 10.5% made 77 of 405 investor loans, mostly in Puna.

verdicts.driver: Long-term rental demand (large on Oahu, but thin returns for leveraged buyers)
verdicts.reason: Confirmed for Oahu, Maui and Kauai. UHERO county rows give Honolulu 40.2% renters, $2,083 median rent and a $562,400 condo median. A 70%-financed condo at 7.0% costs $2,619 P&I, before HOA dues, which would widen the shortfall. Oahu's investor share by value is under $500K 16%, $500–750K 9%, $750K–1M 9%, $1–1.5M 14%, $1.5–3M 19%, $3M+ 24%, all confirmed. At ZIP level, Oahu suburbs give gross yields of 3–4% on asking rents (Mililani $2,800 on $988,500; Ewa $3,300 on $1.0M), and investor shares there are 3–6%. The dismissal is too broad for Hawaii Island, though. In Puna, cheap homes do cash-flow. Hawaiian Beaches 96778 has a $250K median SF price, $1,600 asking rent (7.7% gross yield), and $1,164 P&I at 70% LTV and 7%. Volcano yields 6.6% and Mountain View 5.4%. These ZIPs show 17–25% investor loans at only 5–8% STR shares. So long-term-rental economics (and flipping) is a plausible contributor to Hawaii Island's share, while the data still do not support it for Oahu vs Maui and Kauai.
verdicts.corrected_wording: Long-term rental demand does not explain Oahu's low investor share. At Oahu prices, a 70%-financed condo or house does not cover its payment from rent, and investor shares in Oahu suburbs are 3–6%. The exception is Puna on Hawaii Island. There, $250K–450K homes rent for $1,350–1,750, gross yields reach 5–8%, and investor loans are 17–25% of purchases despite few legal vacation rentals.

verdicts.driver: Oahu's 90-day STR minimum (Ordinance 22-7)
verdicts.reason: Confirmed as a weak driver. Oahu's investor share was already 10.3% in 2019. The rise to 12.7% in 2025 is entirely DSCR-like lending: without business-purpose loans with no income relied on, Oahu fell from 9.3% to 8.8%. Waikiki, the main investor zone, is resort-zoned and so is not covered by the 90-day rule. Dates come from earlier project verification (ev/decades_result.json): signed 2022-04-26; effective 2022-10-23; preliminary injunction by Judge Watson 2022-10-13 (Hawaii Public Radio, 2022-10-21, reported); December 2023 ruling barring application to existing 30–89 day rentals (Courthouse News, 2023-12-21, reported). Those dates could not be re-fetched in this pass: the search budget was exhausted and the HPR and VRMA sites are blocked to this session. Bill 9 evidence needs correction. From prior project adjudication (ev/adjudications.json, brief/audit_result.json): Mayor Bissen signed Bill 9 on 2025-12-15 after a 5-3 vote, with deadlines of Jan 1, 2029 for West Maui and Jan 1, 2031 elsewhere. The county counted 6,208 Minatoya-listed units operating as STRs (May 29, 2024); about 7,000 is the size of the whole list. Bill 88 (Ordinance 6008, effective 2026-06-22, 7-2 vote) creates H-3/H-4 hotel zones covering about 4,500 of those units (Maui Now 2026-06-22, Civil Beat 2026-06; reported). In September 2026 the Maui Planning Commission recommended against most of the first rezoning batch.
fact_errors: The Bill 9 unit count should be about 6,200 operating STRs (county 6,208; UHERO 6,172). About 7,000 is the size of the whole Minatoya list.
The researcher's for-brokers and for-locals text omits Bill 88 (Ordinance 6008, June 22, 2026). It gives about 4,500 units a hotel-zoning path that may keep them renting rather than selling.
The 90-day timeline omits the Oct 13, 2022 preliminary injunction.
verdicts.corrected_wording: Oahu's 90-day minimum is not why Oahu's investor share is low. The share was already 10.3% in 2019, and the investor hot spot, Waikiki, is resort-zoned and unaffected. Outside lenders that don't verify income, Oahu's investor share actually slipped from 9.3% to 8.8% between 2019 and 2025.

verdicts.driver: Conforming loan limits
verdicts.reason: Confirmed from the local FHFA files cll2025.xlsx and cll2026.xlsx. The 2025 one-unit limit was $1,209,750 in all four counties. For 2026 it is $1,249,125 in Hawaii, Honolulu and Kauai and $1,299,500 in Maui. Identical 2025 limits cannot explain the 2025 investor gap. Also confirmed: 172 of 436 Oahu first-lien loans above the limit were VA, and the conventional jumbo share fell from 13.3% to 5.8%, mainly because the limit rose.
verdicts.corrected_wording: Conforming loan limits were the same on every island in 2025 ($1,209,750), so they do not explain the investor gap. They matter on Oahu only because VA buyers with full entitlement can borrow above the limit with no down payment. 172 of the 436 Oahu purchase loans above the limit in 2025 were VA.

missing_drivers: Cash buyers. HMDA covers only mortgaged purchases. On Maui, conveyance-tax schedule 2 (buyer ineligible for the homeowner exemption) applied to 57% of FY2025 improved residential sales (1,166 of 2,047), vs 34% non-owner among mortgaged buyers. The share was 54–65% in every fiscal year from FY2016 to FY2026 (local Maui RPT sales extract, dl/appl2/maui_sales_totals_fy2016_2026.csv). Oahu's all-buyer out-of-state shares are low (UHERO: 8.6% SF, 16.5% condo, 2025), so the true gap is probably wider than HMDA shows.

Non-QM, bridge and fix-and-flip lender growth. Business-purpose loans with no income relied on rose from 0.5–1.6% of purchase loans in 2019 to 3.9–10.0% in 2025. One bridge lender, Temple View Capital Funding, made 77 of Hawaii County's 405 investor loans (median rate 10.5%), concentrated in Puna.

Price-to-rent and cash-flow geography. Puna is the one area where leveraged long-term renting or flipping pencils out: Hawaiian Beaches yields 7.7% gross and Volcano 6.6%. It explains part of Hawaii Island's share without resort zoning; Hawaii County Ordinance 2018-114 bars new unhosted STVRs in residential and agricultural zones unless grandfathered.

New condo tower closings in Ala Moana/Ward. ZIP 96814 is 29.5% investor loans (n=573) at a 1.4% STR share, and tract 36.03 alone holds 134 investor loans. That is about 16% of Oahu's investor loans, unrelated to vacation-rental zoning.

Resort amenities as a common cause. Beaches, climate and resorts drive both where resort and STR zoning was drawn and where second-home buyers want to own. STR share is also partly a result of past investor buying, so zoning cannot be cleanly isolated as the cause.

New single-family and townhome supply, plus VA condo-approval rules, shaping where VA buyers buy. Oahu VA share is 46–48% in tracts with a median housing age of 20 years or less, vs 14% in tracts over 50 years old. Within Ewa/Kapolei it is 64% in newer tracts vs 46% in older ones. Base proximity and new supply overlap and cannot be separated here.
Maui's post-fire market composition. Maui purchase loans fell 56% from 2019 (2,010 to 886), and Lahaina-area supply and insurance shocks change the mix of buyers in ways HMDA cannot isolate.

Maui Bill 88 (Ordinance 6008, effective June 22, 2026), a hotel-zoning path for about 4,500 Minatoya units. It changes the outlook for apartment-district investors relative to Bill 9 alone (reported, prior project verification).
challenge.final_answer: In 2025 mortgage records (HMDA), investment-property loans were 30.7% of home-purchase loans on Kauai, 24.6% on Maui and 22.8% on Hawaii Island, against 12.7% on Oahu. VA loans were 27.1% of Oahu purchase loans, against 5–11% on the other islands. The investor gap mostly follows where vacation renting happens, not the island line. Across 47 ZIP codes, the share of homes used as short-term rentals explains nearly two-thirds of the variation in investor share, and once it is accounted for, being on Oahu makes no difference. Resort areas (Lahaina, Kihei, Princeville, Poipu, Kona, Waikoloa, Waikiki) run 29–54% investor loans; non-resort towns on every island (Kahului, Wailuku, Mililani, Ewa, Waipahu) run 3–12%. Resort amenities and past investor buying are tangled up with zoning, so this is an association, not proof that zoning alone causes it. The military answers the VA question but explains only a small part of the investor gap. About 43,700 active-duty members and 44,100 dependents live on Oahu, against fewer than 900 people combined on all other islands. VA's terms make it their default loan: no down payment, no mortgage insurance, no loan cap with full entitlement, looser debt limits and rates about half a point lower. Honolulu's VA share is normal for a U.S. military town: 24.7% of 2025 purchase applications, about the same as Anchorage (24.6%) and below Virginia Beach (37.5%) and Colorado Springs' El Paso County (35.4%). Taking VA loans out lifts Oahu's investor share only to 17.2%, which closes 2–3 of the 10–18 points. Three cautions matter. First, the 'investor' label shifted. Since 2019, lenders have recoded vacation-home loans from 'second home' to 'investment', and lenders that don't verify income grew from about 1% to 4–10% of purchase loans. The combined second-home-plus-investor share barely moved: 14–16% on Oahu and 30–40% on the neighbor islands. Second, Hawaii Island is a different story. Its investor-only share equaled Oahu's in 2019 (10.5% vs 10.3%). Much of its 2025 gap sits in Puna, where $250K–450K homes can pay for themselves as long-term rentals, and one bridge lender charging about 10.5% made 77 of the county's 405 investor loans. Third, HMDA leaves out cash buyers. On Maui, 57% of FY2025 home sales went to buyers not eligible for the homeowner exemption, against 34% of mortgaged buyers, so the real gap with Oahu is probably wider. Oahu's 90-day rental minimum, military housing allowances and conforming loan limits explain little of the difference between islands. (Not re-checked in this pass: military tour lengths, the Honolulu court rulings and Maui Bills 9 and 88. Web search was exhausted and those sites were blocked, so those points rest on earlier project verification.)

research.question: Affordability: Why did the payment on a median house rise from about 40% of local income in 2019 to 66–78% in 2025? This splits the change into rates, prices and income using the report's data, then explains the structural drivers of Hawaii prices: supply, outside demand, short-term rental (STR) conversion, and condo insurance and HOA costs.
research.answer:
The report measures the monthly principal and interest on a 30-year loan with 20% down on the county's median single-family price, divided by median household income from the Census American Community Survey (ACS). On that measure Oahu rose from 41.0% (2019) to 66.2% (2025), Maui from 42.4% to 78.2%, Kauai from 37.0% to 76.3%, and Hawaii Island from 25.6% to about 46%.

We split each change among the three inputs, averaged over the order they are applied (a Shapley split). From 2019 to 2025, higher prices added about 19 points on Oahu, 32 on Maui and 33 on Kauai. Higher mortgage rates (3.93% to 6.60%, which raises the payment on every borrowed dollar by 35%) added 16 to 18 points. Income growth of 20 to 25% took back 10 to 14 points. So over the full period prices did slightly more than rates, and the two arrived in sequence. Prices jumped in 2020–22, when rates were near 3%, listings fell below two months of supply and wealthier mainland movers arrived. Rates then jumped in 2022–23, and prices did not fall back. From 2021 to 2025 Oahu's price-to-income ratio was flat (−1%), so rates explain almost all of the increase since 2021.

Hawaii's structural constraints were not a new shock after 2019:
- Building permits averaged about 3,840 a year in 2019–25, the same as in 2010–18 and about half of 2006's level.
- The state's Urban land-use district grew by only 295 acres and is 4.9% of all land.
- The housing stock grew 3%.
- Hawaii's 2019–25 price growth (+47% on the Federal Housing Finance Agency (FHFA) index) was below the typical state (+61%).

What these constraints do is set a very high starting point: 40% of income in 2019, against the usual 30% guideline. Slow permits (a median of 394 days for a single-family permit on Oahu), construction costs rising faster than incomes, and very little land zoned for housing also stopped prices from falling when rates doubled.

Mainland buyers and vacation rentals mainly explain the high neighbor-island price levels and the 2021 spike. They do not explain the 2022–25 squeeze: the out-of-state buyer share was 21% in 2019 and 22% in 2025.

The 2023–26 condo insurance and HOA spike is not in the 66–78% figure at all. It adds about 6 to 10 points of income for an Oahu condo buyer. It also lowers condo prices: Maui condos fell 22% in 2025, and Oahu condos have been flat in nominal terms since 2022.

Two measurement choices push the headline up: 2025 income is held at its 2024 level, and the price is the single-family median. Together they overstate the burden for a typical first-time local buyer by a few points, while the exclusion of taxes, insurance and dues understates it.

drivers.driver: The 2020–22 price run-up: the largest single piece over 2019–2025, concentrated before rates rose
drivers.quantified_effect: Shapley split of the 2019→2025 change: price +19.3 pts on Oahu (of +25.2), +31.8 on Maui (of +35.8), +33.0 on Kauai (of +39.4), +13.8 on Hawaii Island (of +20.1). At 2019 prices, the 2025 share would have been 46.0% Oahu, 45.7% Maui, 41.7% Kauai. Price-to-income rose 20% on Oahu (9.0x to 10.8x), 37% on Maui (9.3x to 12.8x) and 53% on Kauai (8.1x to 12.5x). Almost all of that came by 2021–22: from 2021 to 2025 price-to-income moved −1% Oahu, −3% Maui, −11% Kauai, +8% Hawaii Island.

evidence.source: DBEDT Monthly Economic Indicators (report page_data ext.afford)

evidence.fact: Months of supply (annual average) collapsed in 2021, then rebuilt. Oahu 4.0 (2019), 1.8 (2021), 5.4 (2025). Maui 4.4, 1.7, 11.3. Kauai 5.6, 2.4, 6.3. Hawaii Island 5.6, 1.4, 5.5.
evidence.source: Report page_data ext.mos (Realtor.com listings ÷ DBEDT sales)
Moku repeat-sales index from City and County of Honolulu sales records (report page_data moku_index)

evidence.fact: FHFA all-transactions house price index, 2019 vs 2025 annual averages: Hawaii +46.6%, 7th-lowest of 51 (50 states + DC). The median state was +60.9%. From 2021 to 2025 Hawaii was +30.6%.
evidence.source: FHFA House Price Index, state all-transactions (our calculation)

drivers.driver: Mortgage rates: the dominant factor since 2021, applied to Hawaii's very high price base
drivers.quantified_effect: The payment per borrowed dollar is +34.9% at 6.60% vs 2019's 3.93%, and +52.3% vs 2021's 2.96%. Shapley contribution for 2019→2025: +15.9 pts Oahu, +17.9 Maui, +16.6 Kauai, +10.5 Hawaii Island. For 2021→2025: +22.9, +27.6, +27.9, +15.1 pts, the largest factor on every island. At the 2019 rate, 2025 shares would have been 49.1% Oahu, 58.0% Maui, 56.6% Kauai. Near 6.6%, each 1-point rate move changes the payment by about 10–11%.

evidence.fact: Freddie Mac 30-year fixed, annual average of weekly readings: 3.93% (2019), 2.96% (2021), 5.33% (2022), 6.79% (2023), 6.72% (2024), 6.60% (2025). The weekly rate was 7.28% on Oct 1, 2026, up from a 6.05% February 2026 average.
evidence.source: Freddie Mac Primary Mortgage Market Survey (PMMS) via report page_data

evidence.fact: UHERO says the 2025 improvement in affordability was driven primarily by lower interest rates. Rates peaked at 7.8% in October 2023, fell below 6% in February 2025, and were back to 6.4% by the end of March 2026.
evidence.value: Rates were the main driver of the 2025 improvement
evidence.source: UHERO, The Hawaii Housing Factbook 2026, pp. 4 and 11

evidence.fact: Same formula at the Oct 1, 2026 rate of 7.28% with 2026 year-to-date medians, income held at 2024: Oahu about 74.5%, Maui about 81.3%, Kauai about 87.6%, Hawaii Island about 49.2%.
evidence.source: Our calculation from report page_data (PMMS, DBEDT, ACS)

drivers.driver: Income growth offset the squeeze; actual buyers were increasingly drawn from the top of the income distribution
drivers.quantified_effect: ACS median household income, 2019→2024: Oahu +20.3% ($87,470 to $105,205), Maui +25.3%, Kauai +19.7%, Hawaii Island +12.5%. That offset 10.0, 13.8, 10.3 and 4.2 pts respectively. Measured against actual Oahu borrowers' incomes instead, the single-family payment went from about 32% (2019) to about 44% (2025).

evidence.fact: ACS 1-year median household income: Oahu $87,470 (2019) to $105,205 (2024). 2025–26 use 2024 income because no later release was used. 2020 is interpolated.
evidence.source: Census ACS 1-year B19013 (report page_data ext.afford / acs)

evidence.fact: Financed home-purchase originations fell 28% statewide (13,797 to 9,875) and 56% on Maui (2,010 to 886). Median borrower income rose from $119K to $166K. Honolulu owner-occupant first-lien borrowers went from $112K to $158K (+41%).
evidence.source: FFIEC/CFPB HMDA Data Browser, 2019 vs 2025 (local hmda.json)

evidence.fact: Affording the median single-family home takes just over 180% of state median income, which roughly one in five households earns. The median condo takes about 110%, down from a 140% peak.
evidence.value: About 1 in 5 households can afford the median single-family home
evidence.source: UHERO, The Hawaii Housing Factbook 2026, p. 4

drivers.driver: Chronic supply constraints: land-use law, entitlement and permit delays, infrastructure. They set the high 2019 level and stopped prices falling, but were not a new shock after 2019.
drivers.quantified_effect: Level effect, not quantified as a 2019→25 share. Permits averaged about 3,836 a year in 2019–25 vs about 3,815 in 2010–18, roughly half of 2006's 7,549. The housing stock grew 3.0% from 2019 to 2025. The Urban district gained 295 acres from 2019 to 2025 (3,235 since 2006). Honolulu single-family permits took a median 394 days in H1 2025. Permit delays added about 7% to private project costs.

evidence.fact: State Land Use Commission Urban district: 200,898 of 4,112,388 acres (4.9%) in 2025, against 200,603 in 2019. Oahu is 26.3% urban, Maui 5.2%, Kauai 4.2%, Hawaii Island 2.1%.
evidence.source: DBEDT State of Hawaii Data Book 2025, Tables 6.02–6.03 (Land Use Commission, HRS ch. 205)
Census Building Permits Survey (FRED HIBPPRIV) via report page_data

evidence.fact: Housing units statewide: 557,614 (July 2019) to 574,520 (July 2025). Maui fell from 73,631 (2023) to 70,070 (2024) after the Lahaina fire.
evidence.source: DBEDT Data Book 2025, Table 21.20 (Census population estimates)

evidence.fact: Median permit processing in 2025: Honolulu 394 days for single-family and 585 for multifamily (H1 2025, still trending up). Kauai single-family 309 days (+37%). Maui standard permits 379 days (fire-recovery permits 83). Hawaii County 127 days. UHERO says Hawaii's average processing time is more than triple the national average.
evidence.source: UHERO, The Hawaii Housing Factbook 2026, pp. 9–10

evidence.fact: Honolulu private-sector permit delays beyond 180 days cost $202M in 2022–23, 7% of permit value. In 2023 DPP received about 19,700 applications, issued about 14,800 and carried about 5,000 over. DPP had about a 25% staff vacancy rate in June 2024. Hawaii's Wharton land-use regulation index is 1.7, the highest in the nation.
evidence.source: DBEDT READ, Assessing the Cost of Building Permit Delays in Honolulu: 2022–2023

evidence.fact: UHERO ranked Hawaii the most heavily regulated state for homebuilding, with permit delays three times the national sample. By county: Hawaii County 1st, Maui 6th, Kauai 9th, Honolulu 11th. Bonham cautioned this is correlation, not proven cause.
evidence.source: Hawaii Business Magazine, on UHERO brief

evidence.fact: After the Red Hill fuel contamination, the Board of Water Supply told senators a moratorium on new construction was possible and sent developers letters saying water availability could not be promised. Later 2022 reporting said projects could proceed.
evidence.source: Civil Beat

drivers.driver: Construction costs: imported materials, shipping and a small labor pool. Costs rose faster than incomes.
drivers.quantified_effect: The Honolulu single-family construction cost index rose 28.3% from 2019 to 2025 (290.7 to 372.9) and high-rise costs rose 26.2%, against +20.3% for Oahu median income. Hawaii's year-over-year cost growth was 5.4–5.9% in 2025–26 vs 4.4–4.5% nationally. No official Hawaii-specific estimate of the Jones Act shipping premium or union wage premium was found.

evidence.fact: Honolulu construction cost index for a single-family residence: 290.7 (2019), 313.0 (2021), 345.0 (2023), 372.9 (2025, preliminary). High-rise: 264.2 to 333.4.
evidence.source: DBEDT Data Book 2025, Table 21.09 (First Hawaiian Bank / DBEDT QSER)

evidence.fact: Accepted construction value per new one-family unit, state average: $394,104 (2019) to $531,472 (2025).
evidence.source: DBEDT Data Book 2025, Table 21.03

evidence.fact: Hawaii construction costs rose 5.40% year over year vs a 4.50% national average. RLB cites geographic isolation, reliance on imported materials and a limited labor pool. Q2 2026: +5.93%.
evidence.source: Rider Levett Bucknall, Construction Cost Report – Hawaii

drivers.driver: Outside demand: mainland and foreign buyers and wealthier in-movers. It drove the 2020–22 spike and the neighbor-island price level, not the 2022–25 squeeze.
drivers.quantified_effect: Out-of-state share of recorded sales statewide: 21.3% (2019), 24.2% (2021), 25.9% (2023), 22.0% (2025). Share of dollars: 27.1%, 34.2% (2021), 30.4% (2025). Maui's out-of-state share fell from 30.2% to 26.6%. Maui in-movers' adjusted gross income (AGI) per tax return jumped from $71K (2018–19) to $192K (2021–22), then fell back to $90K (2022–23), with mover counts roughly flat. Out-of-state buyers were only 8.6% of 2025 single-family sales in Honolulu County, the base of the Oahu metric.

evidence.fact: Average 2025 purchase price, mainland vs local buyers: statewide $1,259,806 vs $818,264; Maui $2,237,541 vs $1,102,874; Kauai $2,013,208 vs $985,714.
evidence.value: Mainland buyers pay 1.5–2x what locals pay
evidence.source: Title Guaranty via DBEDT Data Book 2025, Tables 21.37–21.38 (report page_data tg)

evidence.value: Maui in-mover AGI per return nearly tripled in 2021–22
evidence.source: IRS SOI migration data (report page_data irs20)

evidence.fact: 2025 out-of-state buyer share, single-family / condo: state 16.6% / 24.3%; Honolulu 8.6% / 16.5%; Maui 18.1% / 54.5%; Kauai 28.6% / 44.1%; Hawaii County 24.9% / 49.3%.
evidence.source: UHERO Housing Factbook 2026 DataBook (Title Guaranty deeds)

drivers.driver: STR and second-home conversion: raises neighbor-island price levels. STR counts changed little, and the 2022–26 restrictions are pushing condo prices down.
drivers.quantified_effect: About 34,500 active STR listings in 2025 (33,600 in 2024): 20% of housing units on Kauai, 15% Maui, 9% Hawaii County, 2.5% Honolulu. 36,808 vacant seasonal-use units statewide (6.4% of the stock), 16.5% in Maui plus Kauai. UHERO estimates a full Maui Bill 9 phase-out cuts condo prices 20–40%. A national study finds +1% listings raises house prices 0.026%. Neither is a measured Hawaii single-family effect.

evidence.fact: Vacation rentals rose to about 34,500 in 2025 from 33,600 in 2024. Bill 9 sets a phase-out of about 7,000 apartment-zoned (Minatoya List) STRs: West Maui in 2029, countywide in 2031. That could grow Maui's housing stock by up to 13%. Maui condo prices in 2025 were 11% below 2023 (Minatoya List units −16%, state excluding Maui −4%).
evidence.value: 20–40% estimated condo price drop under full phase-out
evidence.source: UHERO, The Hawaii Housing Factbook 2026, pp. 12–13

evidence.fact: Maui condo median, average of monthly values: $911,479 (2024), $708,229 (2025), $659,769 (2026 year to date). Maui single-family median held at about $1.29M in 2025.
evidence.source: DBEDT Monthly Economic Indicators (report page_data islands)

evidence.fact: Vacant 'seasonal, recreational or occasional use' units: 36,808 of 572,824 statewide. Maui plus Kauai: 16,831 of 102,295. Oahu: 11,898 of 377,848.
evidence.source: Census ACS 2024 PUMS (report page_data pums.vacancy)

evidence.fact: In the median owner-occupancy ZIP, a 1% increase in Airbnb listings raises rents 0.018% and house prices 0.026%. The effect is larger where fewer homes are owner-occupied.
evidence.source: Barron, Kung & Proserpio, Marketing Science

evidence.fact: Honolulu Ordinance 22-7 (Bill 41) set a 90-day minimum outside resort areas. A federal judge enjoined it for rentals already operating at 30–89 days, and the December 2023 summary judgment made that permanent.
evidence.value: The 90-day rule is only partly in force
evidence.source: Skift / Courthouse News

drivers.driver: The 2023–26 condo insurance, HOA, reserve and fire-safety cost spike. It is excluded from the 66–78% metric, adds 6–10 points to an Oahu condo buyer's real burden, and pushes condo prices down.
drivers.quantified_effect: Oahu median condo ($508,058 in 2025): principal and interest is 29.6% of median income. Adding the ACS Honolulu median HOA fee ($526) makes it 35.6%; adding the February 2026 listing median ($882) makes it 39.7%. In 2019 the condo payment was 22.2% before dues. Each $100 a month of dues removes about $15,700 of borrowing power at 6.6%. A $300 increase is about $47,000, roughly 9% of the median Oahu condo price, which fits Oahu condos being flat in nominal terms since 2022 (index +0.4% vs houses +4.8%).

evidence.fact: 42% of Hawaii homeowners pay HOA/AOAO fees, vs 25% nationally. Hawaii's median fee of $470 is the 2nd-highest state; Honolulu's is $526 and Hawaii County's $135. The median Oahu listing in February 2026 advertised $882. Special assessments are excluded from these figures.
evidence.source: UHERO Factbook 2026, pp. 5–6 (ACS 2024 HOA question; Oahu listings)

evidence.fact: Aggregate property insurance premiums in Hawaii rose 13.4% in 2024, the largest increase in at least a decade, vs 9.7% nationally. UHERO calls this a lower bound and cites reports of some condo policies rising more than 1,000%.
evidence.source: UHERO Factbook 2026, p. 7 (Hawaii Insurance Commissioner annual reports; BLS PPI)

evidence.fact: Legislative findings: master-policy deductibles rose from $10,000–25,000 per unit to as much as $250,000. 375–390 buildings renewed with less than 100% hurricane coverage. Only three insurers write condo hurricane coverage. More than 700 Oahu condo buildings predate 1990. One Waikiki building's premium went from $235,000 to about $1.2M on the secondary market. Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac will not buy loans in buildings with more than $10,000 per unit of unfunded repairs.
evidence.value: Deductibles up to 10x; premiums up to ~5x (example)
evidence.source: Hawaii Legislature SB1044 SD2, Section 1 findings (citing Insurance Associates)

evidence.fact: House Consumer Protection committee: condo master and unit-owner insurance options were shrinking even before the August 2023 Maui fire.
evidence.source: House Standing Committee Report 254 on HB253 HD1

evidence.fact: SB1044 was enacted as Act 296. It lets the Hawaii Property Insurance Association (HPIA) write condo property coverage for a limited time (at most 60 months for high-rises), revives the Hawaii Hurricane Relief Fund (HHRF) with a flat recording fee of up to $44, and seeds a condo repair loan program with $20M in bonds plus $5M.
evidence.source: Insurance Business

evidence.fact: Gov. Green issued a fourth emergency proclamation relating to condominium insurance stabilization.
evidence.source: Hawaii Department of Defense / HI-EMA news releases

evidence.fact: Associations must budget from a reserve study reviewed by an independent preparer at least every three years. They must fund at least 50% of estimated replacement reserves (percent-funded plan) or 100% (cash-flow plan). In counties over 500,000 people (Honolulu), budgets must include fire and life-safety costs.
evidence.source: HRS §514B-148 (current)

evidence.fact: Sprinkler retrofits under Honolulu's post-Marco Polo high-rise law: Marco Polo cost $6M, about $10,500 per unit (2021). Kahala Towers was estimated at $17,000–21,500 per unit.
evidence.source: Civil Beat

counter_evidence: The report says 'Higher rates did most of that.' That is true for 2021→2025: on Oahu, rates added +22.9 of the +22.5 pts while prices (+7.8) and income (−8.2) roughly cancelled. It is not true for 2019→2025, where prices added +19.3 pts vs +15.9 for rates on Oahu, and roughly twice the rate effect on Maui and Kauai. Suggested wording: prices jumped first (2020–22), then rates (2022–23) did most of the rest.

2025 and 2026 hold income at its 2024 level. If 2025 income grew 3.5%, the 2025 shares would be about 64.0% (Oahu), 75.6% (Maui) and 73.8% (Kauai). UHERO, which uses rising incomes, reports affordability improving in both 2024 and 2025; the report shows Oahu worsening from 64.7% to 66.2% over 2024→2025.

The metric uses the single-family median, but most Oahu first purchases are condos: an Oahu condo's principal and interest was 29.6% of median income in 2025. Median household income also includes renters and retirees. On the incomes of actual Oahu borrowers (HMDA), the single-family payment was about 44%, not 66%. On the other hand, excluding taxes, insurance and dues understates the true cost.

The neighbor-island inputs are noisy. Maui and Kauai medians rest on thin sales (707 and 423 single-family sales in 2025) and shift with the price mix. ACS 1-year income is volatile (Maui $83,691 in 2023 vs $101,192 in 2024). Using the ACS 5-year income ($97,161) would put Maui's 2025 share at 81.5%.

The 2019→2025 deterioration is mostly national, not Hawaii-specific. Hawaii's FHFA price growth (+46.6%) ranked 7th-lowest of 51. The rate shock was the same everywhere. Hawaii-specific factors explain the high starting level more than the change.
Supply did not get worse after 2019: permits averaged about 3,836 a year in 2019–25 vs about 3,815 in 2010–18. Supply limits therefore explain why prices did not fall, not why they rose.
Outside demand did not rise over the period: the statewide out-of-state share was 21.3% in 2019 and 22.0% in 2025, and Maui's fell from 30.2% to 26.6%. It cannot explain the 2022–25 squeeze.

STR policy has been pushing condo prices down (Maui condos −22% in 2025; Minatoya List units −16% vs 2023), and STR counts barely changed. On the condo side, STRs helped affordability over this window.
Insurance and HOA increases are partly priced into lower condo values, so UHERO's condo affordability improved (110% of median income needed, down from 140%), even as monthly carrying costs rose.

Other explanations not measured here: (a) the mortgage rate lock-in effect, where owners with sub-3% loans kept inventory low through 2022–23 (Oahu months of supply 2.0 in 2022 and 3.4 in 2023); (b) the Lahaina fire, which destroyed units (Maui's estimated housing stock fell from 73,631 to 70,070) and drove Maui's 2024 peak ($1.317M); (c) steady military and VA demand (VA loans 25.1% to 27.1% of Honolulu purchase loans); (d) changes in price mix as sales volume fell 28%, with sales tilting toward higher-income buyers.
research.for_brokers:
Price buyers on payment, not price. Near 6.6%, each 1-point move in rates changes the payment by about 10–11%. The jump from 6.49% (the 2026 year-to-date average) to 7.28% (Oct 1) cut buying power by about 8%. On the report's formula, that pushes Oahu toward about 75%, Maui about 81% and Kauai about 88% of median income. Expect local, rate-sensitive buyers to keep thinning out; mainland buyers, who pay 1.5–2x local prices, are less sensitive to rates. Rate buydowns and seller credits work better than equivalent price cuts.

Prices have been sticky because of supply, not demand. Permits are flat at about 3,800 a year, Honolulu single-family permits take a median 394 days, and construction costs are up 28% since 2019. So do not expect single-family values to correct the way they would in a market that builds easily. Correction risk sits in condos.

For any condo listing, collect the following up front:
- The insurance certificate: full hurricane coverage or not, and the master deductible per unit.
- The reserve study and its percent funded (HRS 514B-148 requires a floor).
- Any pending special assessments.
- Fire and life-safety evaluation status for Oahu high-rises.
- Eligibility for Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac loans: underinsured buildings, or buildings with more than $10K per unit of unfunded repairs, can lose conventional financing. That shrinks the buyer pool to cash buyers.

Quote HOA dues in loan terms: each $100 a month removes about $15,700 of borrowing power at 6.6%.

Maui condos face both Bill 9 (deadlines in 2029 and 2031, lawsuits pending) and insurance pressure. Listings there are a source of motivated sellers but are hard to finance. UHERO's 20–40% estimate for a full phase-out is the downside case.
research.for_locals:
The headline 66–78% compares one median single-family house to one median household. It overstates the burden for a typical first purchase and leaves out taxes, insurance and dues. Even so, UHERO finds only about one in five households earns enough for the median single-family home (more than 180% of median income). Nearly half can afford the median condo, before HOA costs.

The biggest change since 2021 is the mortgage rate. A 1-point drop in rates is worth roughly a 10% price cut, so when rates fall, refinancing or buying can help more than haggling over price. In 2020–22, though, prices also rose faster than local pay, so lower rates alone will not bring back 2019 conditions.

A condo's sticker price understates what it costs to own. Dues of $526–882 a month add 6 to 10 points of income on Oahu. Before buying, ask for:
- The master insurance policy, including whether hurricane coverage is full and the per-unit deductible. Buy HO-6 loss-assessment coverage to match that deductible.
- The reserve study and how fully funded it is.
- Any planned special assessments, including fire-sprinkler or plumbing work, which has cost $10K–22K per unit in older Honolulu towers.

The state's 2025 Act 296 backstop (HPIA/HHRF) and the new condo repair loan program are stopgaps, not fixes.

Hawaii Island is still around 45% of income. Maui condo prices are falling as vacation-rental rules tighten, which could open entry-level ownership there, but check insurability first.

The lasting fix is more housing, which depends on permit speed and zoning. Urban-zoned land has barely grown since 2019 (+295 acres), and a Honolulu single-family permit took a median 394 days in early 2025.

challenge.question: Affordability: Why did the payment on a median house rise from about 40% of local income in 2019 to 66–78% in 2025? The change is split into rates, prices and income, then checked against the structural drivers: supply, outside demand, short-term rentals, and condo insurance and HOA costs.

verdicts.driver: The 2020–22 price run-up was the largest single piece over 2019–2025 and came before rates rose
verdicts.reason: I recomputed the formula and the Shapley split from page_data ext.afford and the numbers match exactly. For 2019 to 2025, price added +19.3 points of Oahu's +25.2, +31.8 of Maui's +35.8, +33.0 of Kauai's +39.4 and +13.8 of Hawaii Island's +20.1. For 2021 to 2025 on Oahu, price added only +7.8 against +22.9 from rates. Oahu's price-to-income ratio went from 9.02x to 10.80x, and from 2021 to 2025 it fell 0.6%. The Moku repeat-sales index for Oahu houses rose 46% (114.8 to 167.4), which matches the DBEDT median (+43.9%), so Oahu is not distorted by changes in the mix of homes sold. FHFA all-transactions (downloaded 2026-10-08 from https://www.fhfa.gov/hpi/download/quarterly_datasets/hpi_at_state.csv) confirms Hawaii at +46.6%, 7th-lowest of 51, against a median state of +60.9%. Two limits apply. FHFA is built from conforming loans and leaves out jumbo and cash purchases. Maui and Kauai single-family medians rose 71% and 83%, faster than the typical state, but they rest on 707 and 423 sales in 2025 and move with the mix of homes sold.
fact_errors: 'Over the full period prices did slightly more than rates' holds only for Oahu (19.3 vs 15.9). On Maui and Kauai the price effect was about twice the rate effect (31.8 vs 17.9; 33.0 vs 16.6).
'Prices jumped in 2020–22, when rates were near 3%': rates averaged 3.11% in 2020 and 2.96% in 2021, but 5.33% in 2022 (Freddie Mac PMMS).
verdicts.corrected_wording: Higher prices were the largest piece from 2019 to 2025: about 19 of Oahu's 25-point rise and 32–33 of the 36–39-point rises on Maui and Kauai. Almost all of it came in 2020–22, while rates were near 3% and listings fell below two months of supply. On Oahu the rise (+44–46%) was in line with the rest of the country or below it. Maui's and Kauai's single-family medians (+71% and +83%) rose faster than the typical state's (+61% on FHFA), but they rest on thin sales.

verdicts.driver: Mortgage rates: the dominant factor since 2021, applied to Hawaii's very high price base
verdicts.reason: The Freddie Mac PMMS history file (https://www.freddiemac.com/pmms/docs/PMMS_history.csv, downloaded 2026-10-08) gives annual averages of 3.94% (2019), 2.96% (2021), 6.72% (2024) and 6.60% (2025). The payment per borrowed dollar rises 34.9% from 2019 and 52.3% from 2021. The Shapley rate effects check out: +15.9, +17.9, +16.6 and +10.5 points for 2019→2025, and +22.9 Oahu, +27.6 Maui, +27.9 Kauai for 2021→2025. A rate shock adds more percentage points in Hawaii because the starting share was already high: a 35% rise on a 41% base is about 14 points. That supports the 'high base' framing. One cited fact is wrong. UHERO's text (Factbook 2026, p.11) says rates 'fell below 6% in February 2025'. PMMS shows 6.76–6.89% that month; the first reading below 6% was 5.98% on 2026-02-26. The 2025 annual average was only 0.13 points below 2024, so in the report's annual metric rates barely moved in 2025. Most of the decline came in late 2025 to early 2026. The latest PMMS reading is 7.40% (2026-10-08), not 7.28%. At 7.40%, with 2026 year-to-date medians and 2024 income, the shares are about 75.4% Oahu, 82.3% Maui, 88.7% Kauai and 49.8% Hawaii Island.
fact_errors: Rates did not fall below 6% in February 2025 (PMMS 6.76–6.89%). The first sub-6% reading was 5.98% on Feb 26, 2026. UHERO's Factbook 2026 p.11 contains this date error and the research repeated it.
The 'latest' weekly rate is out of date: PMMS was 7.40% on 2026-10-08 (7.28% was the Oct 1 reading).
The 2026 year-to-date average from weekly PMMS is 6.46%. The 6.49% figure averages monthly means and counts the single October week as a full month.
verdicts.corrected_wording: Mortgage rates rose from 3.9% (2019 average) to 6.6% (2025), which raises the payment on every borrowed dollar by 35%. That added 16–18 points on Oahu, Maui and Kauai, and almost all of the increase since 2021. Rates peaked at 7.79% in October 2023, first dipped below 6% on Feb 26, 2026, and were 7.40% on Oct 8, 2026. At today's rate the same formula gives about 75% on Oahu, 82% on Maui and 89% on Kauai.

verdicts.driver: Income growth offset the squeeze; actual buyers were increasingly drawn from the top of the income distribution
verdicts.reason: The ACS figures match page_data: Oahu $87,470 to $105,205 (+20.3%), Maui +25.3%, Kauai +19.7%, Hawaii Island +12.5%. The income offsets were −10.0, −13.8, −10.3 and −4.2 points. The local HMDA file confirms 13,797 to 9,875 originations statewide, Maui 2,010 to 886, and Honolulu owner-occupant first-lien median income $112K to $158K. Payment ÷ borrower income does compute to about 32% (2019) and 44% (2025). Three caveats. (1) Maui's ACS 1-year income swings: $80,754 in 2019, $76,273 in 2021, $94,760 in 2022, $83,691 in 2023, $101,192 in 2024. Maui's income offset therefore depends on which endpoints are used. (2) HMDA borrower income is selected: rising unaffordability screens out lower-income buyers. The 44% figure describes who still buys, not how affordable housing is for residents. HMDA also covers condo loans, while the payment in that ratio is for a single-family home. (3) 2025 income is held at the 2024 level. The ACS 2025 1-year release (normally September) may now exist; census.gov was unreachable from this environment, so this was not verified.
fact_errors: 'Income growth of 20 to 25%' leaves out Hawaii Island (+12.5%).
Treating HMDA borrower income as a cleaner denominator is circular, because buyers are selected by affordability.
verdicts.corrected_wording: Median household income rose about 20% on Oahu and Kauai (2019–2024) and 12.5% on Hawaii Island. That took back about 10 points on Oahu and Kauai and 4 on Hawaii Island. Maui's apparent +25% rests on a volatile survey estimate. Financed purchases fell 28% statewide and 56% on Maui, and the median borrower's income rose about 40%. Lower-income households were priced out, so the people still buying are a narrower, higher-income group.

verdicts.driver: Chronic supply constraints (land-use law, permit delays, infrastructure) set the high 2019 level and stopped prices falling, and were not a new shock after 2019
verdicts.reason: The level facts check out. DBEDT Data Book 2025 Table 6.02 (https://files.hawaii.gov/dbedt/economic/databook/db2025/DB2025_section06.xlsx) gives Urban district acreage of 200,603 (2019) and 200,898 (2025), +295 acres, 4.9% of land. Table 6.03 gives Oahu 26.3%, Maui 5.2%, Kauai 4.2% and Hawaii Island 2.1%. UHERO Factbook 2026 pp.8–9 confirms the 394-day Honolulu single-family median and that Hawaii's processing time is more than triple the national average. The DBEDT READ permit-delay report (May 2025, https://files.hawaii.gov/dbedt/economic/reports/building_permit_delays.pdf) confirms $202M, 7%, 19,700/14,800/5,000, about 25% DPP vacancies and a Wharton index of 1.7. However, the claim that supply did not change after 2019 overstates the evidence. Census housing-unit estimates (Data Book Table 21.20) show stock growth slowing from 0.77% a year (2010–19) to 0.50% a year (2019–25), or 0.87% to 0.58% excluding Maui. The 2010–18 permit average is lifted by a 5,416 outlier in 2015. Permits averaged 4,237 in 2017–19 and 3,739 in 2020–25. ACS households rose 6.0% (465,299 to 493,151, 2019–2024) while housing units rose 2.4%, though the ACS was reweighted after the 2020 Census. The DBEDT 7% delay cost counts only construction inflation during the delay. Its private-permit universe averaged 97–104 days, with only 20% over 180 days, which differs from UHERO's 394-day new single-family median. Urban-district acreage is a crude gauge, because county zoning and infrastructure are often what binds.
fact_errors: 'Permits ... the same as in 2010–18' holds only as a raw average inflated by 2015 (5,416). Permits fell from about 4,240 a year in 2017–19 to about 3,740 a year in 2020–25.
'The housing stock grew 3%' is accurate but is slower than before: 0.50% a year vs 0.77% a year in 2010–19.

'Permit delays added about 7% to private project costs' is DBEDT's estimate of construction-inflation cost on private permits in 2022–23, not a full cost of delay. Those permits averaged about 100 days, not 394.
verdicts.corrected_wording: Hawaii's supply limits are mainly a long-standing condition rather than a 2019–25 shock. They explain why a median house already took 40% of income in 2019, and they helped keep prices from falling when rates rose. Supply growth did slow after 2019, however: the housing stock grew 0.5% a year against 0.8% a year in 2010–19, and permits dipped from about 4,200 to about 3,700 a year. Meanwhile the number of households grew faster than the number of homes, as average household size shrank.

verdicts.driver: Construction costs (imported materials, shipping, small labor pool) rose faster than incomes
verdicts.reason: Data Book 2025 Table 21.09 confirms the Honolulu single-family construction cost index at 290.7 (2019), 357.3 (2024) and 372.9 (2025, preliminary), and high-rise at 264.2 to 333.4. Table 21.03 confirms $394,104 to $531,472 per new one-family unit. The research, however, set a 6-year cost change (2019–2025, +28.3%) against a 5-year income change (2019–2024, +20.3%). Over the same years (2019–2024) the index rose 22.9% against 20.3% for income, so costs only slightly outpaced incomes. The index values from 2020 on are preliminary. Accepted value per unit swings with unit size and mix (Honolulu $440,714 in 2024, $676,235 in 2025). The RLB figures (+5.40%/+5.93%) could not be re-verified because rlb.com was blocked. Construction costs mainly limit new supply and set a replacement-cost floor; they do not directly set resale prices.
fact_errors: The comparison of the 2019–2025 cost index (+28.3%) with 2019–2024 income (+20.3%) mixes periods. Over the same years the index rose 22.9%.
verdicts.corrected_wording: Honolulu building costs rose about 23% from 2019 to 2024 (construction cost index, preliminary), slightly faster than Oahu median income (+20%). That discourages new building and keeps a floor under prices, but it is a modest and indirect contributor to the 2019–25 jump in payments. No official Hawaii estimate of the Jones Act or union-wage premium was found.

verdicts.driver: Outside demand (mainland and foreign buyers, wealthier in-movers) drove the 2020–22 spike and neighbor-island price levels, not the 2022–25 squeeze
verdicts.reason: Title Guaranty / DBEDT shares in page_data recompute as stated statewide: 21.3% (2019), 24.2% (2021), 25.9% (2023), 22.0% (2025). Maui fell from 30.2% to 26.6%. The IRS figures for Maui in-mover income check out ($71.1K to $191.9K to $90.1K per return), and UHERO's DataBook confirms Honolulu single-family out-of-state at 8.6% in 2025. The Maui conveyance-tax file supports the 2021–22 timing: purchases by buyers without a homeowner exemption peaked at 64.5% of residential sales in FY2022 and were back to about 57% in FY2025–26 (55% in FY2019). That file classifies buyers by the 2026 exemption roll. But the statewide count masks increases elsewhere. Honolulu's out-of-state share rose from 12.9% (2019) to 17.1% (2025), peaking at 20.0% in 2023, and Oahu is the island the 66% headline is based on. Statewide, the out-of-state share of dollars rose from 27.1% to 30.4%. The mainland average price rose 53% ($824K to $1.26M), against 31% for locals. On Maui the mainland average more than doubled ($1.05M to $2.24M) even as the count share fell. 'Mainland buyers pay 1.5–2x' does not hold on Oahu ($940,974 vs $865,054, 1.09x). Origin is the buyer's mailing address, so military buyers arriving on transfer and recent movers are ambiguous.
fact_errors: 'Outside demand did not rise over the period' is wrong for Oahu: the out-of-state share went from 12.9% (2019) to 17.1% (2025), peaking at 20.0% (2023). Statewide, the out-of-state share of dollars rose from 27.1% to 30.4%.
'Mainland buyers pay 1.5–2x what locals pay' holds statewide (1.54x) and on Maui and Kauai (about 2.0x), not on Oahu (1.09x).
verdicts.corrected_wording: Outside money mainly explains why neighbor-island prices are so high and why prices spiked in 2021–22. On Maui, purchases by non-owner-occupants and the incomes of in-movers peaked in 2021–22 and then fell back. By count, the statewide out-of-state share is back near 2019 (22%). On Oahu it rose from 13% to 17%, mostly in condos (single-family 8.6% in 2025), and out-of-state buyers pay much more per purchase on Maui, Kauai and the Big Island. It is a secondary driver of the 2022–25 squeeze, not a non-factor.

verdicts.driver: STR and second-home conversion raises neighbor-island price levels; counts changed little; 2022–26 restrictions are pushing condo prices down
verdicts.reason: UHERO Factbook 2026 pp.12–13 confirms about 34,500 listings in 2025 vs 33,600 in 2024; 20% of units on Kauai, 15% Maui, 9% Hawaii and 2.5% Honolulu; Bill 9's roughly 7,000 Minatoya units with phase-outs in 2029 and 2031; up to 13% of Maui's housing stock; a 20–40% condo price estimate; and Maui −11% and Minatoya −16% vs 2023, against −4% for the rest of the state. PUMS vacancy matches page_data: 36,808 seasonal statewide and 16,831 of 102,295 on Maui plus Kauai. Skift (2024-01-04, https://skift.com/2024/01/04/hawaiian-judge-rules-for-home-owner-rentals/) confirms the permanent injunction against Ordinance 22-7 for existing rentals. Corrections: UHERO says listings 'continued to gradually increase following the pandemic-era decline', with growth concentrated on Maui and Kauai, so 'changed little' is too strong and no 2019 baseline is given. The −22% Maui condo figure averages DBEDT monthly medians from 2024 to 2025 on only 702 sales. The 2024 median ($911K) was itself elevated, and 2025 vs 2023 is −15% on DBEDT and −11% on UHERO's deed data. The national elasticity cited (+0.026% price per +1% listings, Barron, Kung & Proserpio 2021; re-fetch blocked) suggests a small effect per listing. It does not measure Hawaii's level effect. Restrictions, not rentals themselves, are what lowered condo prices.
fact_errors: 'STR counts changed little' understates the change. UHERO reports a gradual post-pandemic rise (33,600 to 34,500 in 2025, concentrated on Maui and Kauai).
Maui condo −22% is the change in averaged monthly DBEDT medians from 2024 to 2025 on thin sales. UHERO's deed-based comparison is −11% vs 2023, and −16% for Minatoya List units.
'On the condo side, STRs helped affordability' should say STR restrictions, not STRs.
verdicts.corrected_wording: Vacation rentals and second homes take a large share of the housing on Kauai (about 20% of units) and Maui (15%), which helps explain those islands' high price levels. Listings have crept up since the pandemic. Restrictions are now pushing the other way: Maui condo prices in 2025 were 11% below 2023 (16% for apartment-zoned STR buildings), and UHERO estimates a full Bill 9 phase-out could cut those condo prices 20–40%.

verdicts.driver: 2023–26 condo insurance, HOA, reserve and fire-safety cost spike: excluded from the 66–78% metric, adds 6–10 points for an Oahu condo buyer, pushes condo prices down
verdicts.reason: Most of the cited facts check out. UHERO pp.5–7 gives 42% vs 25% paying HOA fees, $470 (2nd-highest state), Honolulu $526, Hawaii County $135, an $882 listing median, and +13.4% premiums in 2024 vs 9.7% nationally. SB1044 SD2 findings (https://cca.hawaii.gov/ins/files/2025/03/SB1044_SD2_.pdf) give deductibles rising from $10–25K to $250K, 375–390 buildings, three insurers, more than 700 pre-1990 buildings and $235K to about $1.2M. These are legislative findings that cite Insurance Associates and Hawaii Business. The SB1044 CD1 text (https://data.capitol.hawaii.gov/sessions/session2025/bills/SB1044_CD1_.HTM) gives a 60-month cap for high-rises, a fee of at most $44 per document, $20M in GO bonds plus $5M, and an effective date of July 1, 2025. The act number (296) was not verified. HRS 514B-148 is verified, as are HI-EMA's Jan 31, 2025 fourth proclamation and Civil Beat's $10,500 (Marco Polo) and $17,000–21,500 (Kahala Towers) per unit. My recalculation gives Oahu condo P&I of 29.6% (2025) vs 22.2% (2019), and dues add 6.0 points ($526) or 10.1 points ($882). The problem is attribution. The 6–10 points are the whole dues bill, not the 2023–26 increase. UHERO says the Census asked about HOA fees for the first time in 2024, so there is no 2019 baseline. $526 is the median across all Honolulu owners who pay HOA or AOAO fees, not condos only, and UHERO notes the $882 listing median overweights new buildings. Oahu condos being flat since 2022 (index +0.4%, houses +4.8%) is consistent with dues being capitalized into prices. It is also consistent with higher rate sensitivity among condo and first-time buyers, the 2022 90-day rental minimum cutting investor demand, and rising condo days on market. The Honolulu fire law (2018) allows a fire and life-safety evaluation as an alternative to sprinklers.
fact_errors: The '6–10 points' is the level of total HOA/AOAO dues, not the effect of the 2023–26 spike. The increase since 2019 is not measured, because the ACS HOA question began in 2024.

HRS 514B-148(b) requires funding at least 50% of the estimated replacement reserve assessments (or 100% under a cash-flow plan). It is not a 50% 'percent-funded' ratio. Whether this floor tightened after 2019 was not verified; the section's history lists amendments in 2022, 2023 and 2025.
Honolulu's post-Marco Polo law does not mandate sprinkler retrofits. Sprinklers are one way to pass the required fire and life-safety evaluation.
The $10,000-per-unit unfunded-repair rule for Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac comes from legislative findings citing press. It was not checked against the agencies' selling guides.
verdicts.corrected_wording: Condo ownership costs more than the mortgage alone. HOA/AOAO dues of $526 (Honolulu median among payers) to $882 (median Oahu listing) add about 6–10 points of income on top of a 30% condo payment. Insurance premiums rose 13.4% statewide in 2024, with far larger jumps for some older towers, so part of today's dues is new. How much of the increase dates from 2023–26 has not been measured. Higher carrying costs probably help explain why Oahu condo prices have been flat since 2022, alongside higher rates and the 90-day rental minimum.

missing_drivers: Rising cash (non-mortgage) purchases. As a rough proxy, HMDA purchase loans (FFIEC, local hmda.json) were 69% of Title Guaranty recorded sales in 2019 and 58% in 2025; Kauai fell from 68% to 53% and Hawaii County from 57% to 48%. That puts the non-financed share at roughly 31% rising to 42%. Buyers who are not limited by a monthly payment help explain why prices held when rates doubled. The proxy is rough: HMDA counts loans and TG counts deeds.

Households grew faster than homes. ACS households rose from 465,299 (2019) to 493,151 (2024), +6.0%, while Census housing units rose 2.4% (Data Book 2025 Tables 1.47 and 21.20), even though population fell 1.7% from 2019 to 2025. Average household size fell from 2.95 to 2.85. The ACS was reweighted after the 2020 Census, so the size of the gap is uncertain.

Mortgage rate lock-in. Owners holding sub-4% loans kept listings scarce while sales fell: Oahu had 1.8–2.0 months of supply in 2021–22 and 3.4 in 2023. No Hawaii-specific measure of the share of locked-in loans was found.
The Lahaina fire. Maui's housing units fell by 3,561 (−4.8%) from 2023 to 2024 (Data Book Table 21.20), and the Maui single-family median peaked at $1.317M in 2024.

Selective out-migration may lift measured median income. IRS data show Oahu losing 2,367–4,648 more tax returns than it gained each year from 2016 to 2023, so part of the ACS income gain may come from who leaves rather than from pay raises.
Equity-rich local buyers, not only outsiders. The average purchase price paid by local buyers on Maui rose 70% ($648K to $1.10M) and statewide 31% from 2019 to 2025 (Title Guaranty/DBEDT).

Military and VA demand. VA loans rose from 25.1% to 27.1% of Honolulu purchase loans (HMDA). Some 'out-of-state' Oahu buyers may be military families arriving on transfer. BAH changes were not checked.
Costs left out of the metric for houses too: single-family homeowner and hurricane insurance (hurricane cover costs 2–3x a conventional premium, per SB1044 findings), plus property tax.

Measurement: 2025 income is held at the 2024 level. The ACS 2025 1-year release (normally September) may now be out; this was not verified because census.gov was unreachable. A 3.5% income gain would lower 2025 shares by about 2–3 points.
challenge.final_answer: The report's own formula checks out: principal and interest on a 30-year loan with 20% down on the county's median single-family price, divided by median household income. On it, Oahu went from 41% of income in 2019 to 66% in 2025, Maui from 42% to 78%, Kauai from 37% to 76%, and Hawaii Island from 26% to 46%. Two things drove the rise, in sequence. First, prices jumped in 2020–22, while rates were near 3%, listings had nearly vanished and wealthier mainland buyers and in-movers were active. Higher prices account for about 19 of Oahu's 25-point rise and 32–33 points on Maui and Kauai. Second, mortgage rates rose from about 3.9% to 6.6% between 2022 and 2023, raising the payment on every borrowed dollar by 35%. That added about 16–18 points, and prices did not fall back. Since 2021, rates explain nearly all of Oahu's increase. Income growth of about 20% (12.5% on Hawaii Island) took back roughly 10–14 points on the three most expensive islands. Hawaii's long-standing limits explain why the starting point was already 40% of income and why prices held when rates rose: slow permits (a median of 394 days for an Oahu single-family permit), very little urban land and high building costs. So does a rising share of all-cash buyers, roughly 31% to 42% of recorded sales by a rough proxy. Supply did tighten somewhat after 2019. The housing stock grew about 0.5% a year, down from 0.8%, while the number of households grew faster than the number of homes. Outside buyers mainly explain the high neighbor-island prices and the 2021–22 spike. Statewide their share of sales is back near 2019 levels, but on Oahu it rose from 13% to 17%, and the out-of-state share of purchase dollars rose statewide. Vacation rentals raise price levels on Kauai and Maui, where they are 15–20% of homes. New limits on them are now pulling Maui condo prices down (11% below 2023). Condo dues and insurance are not in the 66–78% figure. Dues alone add about 6–10 points of income for an Oahu condo buyer, and insurance premiums rose 13.4% statewide in 2024. How much of that cost is new since 2023 has not been measured. The headline also holds 2025 income at its 2024 level, which overstates the burden by 2–3 points, and leaves out taxes, insurance and dues, which understates it. At the October 8, 2026 rate of 7.40%, the same formula gives about 75% on Oahu, 82% on Maui and 89% on Kauai.

research.question: Why do departing Hawaii households go to Las Vegas, Texas, Phoenix, Seattle–Tacoma and Portland, and why is the interior West (Denver, Salt Lake City, Boise) the fastest-growing exit?
research.answer: Departing Hawaii households tend to land where three things meet: housing they can afford, work, and people they already know. For O'ahu there is a fourth: wherever the military sends them. Las Vegas is the clearest case. In IRS migration records, Clark County is the #1 destination from every island (about 1,650 tax-filing households a year in 2019–23). Las Vegas also stands out because the flow runs one way: about 2.4 households leave Hawaii for it for every one that comes back. It has no state income tax, and asking prices run about $259 per square foot against $705 in Honolulu. Nevada has the densest Native Hawaiian community of any state we checked (26,628 people in 2020). Behind that sits 50 years of Boyd Gaming marketing to Hawaii: Hawaii guests still fill about 75% of room nights at the California Hotel, and 734,000 airline seats ran between Las Vegas and Hawaii in 2025. Texas, Seattle–Tacoma and Colorado Springs are shaped heavily by military rotation. About 18% of O'ahu's departing households go to counties dominated by large bases, and those households are noticeably larger than average. Phoenix and Portland look like cost-plus-network destinations. Oregon's 9.9% top income tax shows that taxes are a secondary factor: for a typical departing household, the monthly housing-payment gap with Las Vegas (about $3,700) is far larger than the yearly state income tax gap (about $2,000–3,400). Measured from 2004–08, the interior West grew fastest: departures rose 75% to Denver and 68% to Salt Lake City. Those economies added jobs fastest (Utah +15% and Idaho +17% since 2019, against Hawaii −2.4%). They have direct flights. Their Native Hawaiian, Pacific Islander and Latter-day Saint communities grew fastest (Native Hawaiian population +74% to +100% in Colorado, Utah and Idaho, 2010–20). They are not cheap: their prices rose fastest, so the cost gap with Hawaii shrank. Treat the 'fastest-growing' label with care. Measured from 2011–14 instead, Las Vegas (+60%) and Phoenix (+36%) grew faster than Salt Lake City (+35%) and Denver (+30%). The interior-West numbers are small (roughly 180–360 households a year), Boise is too small to measure as a metro, and part of Colorado's growth is Army moves to Colorado Springs.

drivers.driver: Housing-cost gap: departing households trade Hawaii's prices for cheaper mainland housing, especially in Las Vegas, Phoenix and Texas
drivers.quantified_effect: Our calculation: Oahu's single-family median (2026 year-to-date average $1,193,750) means a $6,030/month principal-and-interest payment at 6.49% with 20% down. The Las Vegas listing median ($464,900) means about $2,348/month, a gap of about $3,680/month or $44,000/year. That is about 11–18 times Hawaii's state income tax at the same household income. Price per square foot: Honolulu is 2.7x Las Vegas and Phoenix, 3.6x Dallas, 4.2x Houston and San Antonio, 2.3–2.7x Portland, Denver, Salt Lake City and Boise, and 1.65x Seattle. Departing households are lower-income than those who stay ($70.4k vs $89.9k average AGI on O'ahu, 2022–23), which fits a cost push. The gap does not explain the interior West's growth, because its prices rose fastest after 2019.

evidence.fact: Asking price per square foot, September 2026: Urban Honolulu $705; Las Vegas $259; Phoenix $264; Dallas–Fort Worth $198; Houston $169; San Antonio $170; Seattle–Tacoma $427; Portland $303; Denver $279; Salt Lake City $262; Boise $301; Provo $220; Colorado Springs $231
evidence.source: Realtor.com Residential Data, RDC_Inventory_Core_Metrics_Metro.csv (listing data, not sales)

evidence.fact: Oʻahu single-family median sale price, 2026 year-to-date average; its payment (20% down, 30-year loan at 6.49%) takes about 68.8% of Oʻahu's ACS median household income
evidence.source: Report dataset (DBEDT/Honolulu Board of REALTORS monthly medians; Freddie Mac PMMS; ACS), ext.afford

evidence.fact: Average adjusted gross income per return, Honolulu County, 2022–23: households that moved to other US states vs households that stayed
evidence.source: IRS SOI county-to-county outflow file 2022–23, computed here

evidence.fact: BEA overall regional price parity, 2024 (US = 100): Hawaii 110.0; Nevada 100.0; Texas 97.1; Arizona 100.7; Washington 107.0; Oregon 103.4; Colorado 103.1; Utah 98.9; Idaho 95.5
evidence.value: Hawaii 10–15 points above NV, TX, AZ, UT and ID
evidence.source: BEA Regional Price Parities via FRED (series HIRPPALL, NVRPPALL, etc.)

evidence.fact: Change in asking price per square foot, Sept 2019 to Sept 2026: Honolulu +29%; Las Vegas +49%; Phoenix +46%; Seattle +43%; Denver +33%; Salt Lake City +62%; Provo +64%; Boise +71%. The Honolulu-to-Salt Lake City ratio fell from 3.4x to 2.7x, and Honolulu-to-Boise from 3.1x to 2.3x
evidence.value: The interior West's relative gap with Honolulu narrowed the most
evidence.source: Realtor.com RDC_Inventory_Core_Metrics_Metro_History.csv, computed here

evidence.fact: FHFA all-transactions house price index, 2019Q4 to 2026Q2: Hawaii +54%; Nevada +59%; Arizona +69%; Utah +68%; Idaho +77%; Colorado +46%; Texas +54%; Washington +56%; Oregon +46%
evidence.source: FHFA House Price Index, state all-transactions, computed here

evidence.fact: In Kamehameha Schools' interview study (186 respondents, 229 moves; not a random sample), economic conditions were the most common reason for leaving in every decade. Among moves driven by economics, high cost of living was a factor in 71% in the 2010s, and housing/homeownership rose about 30 points as a reason
evidence.value: 71% of economics-driven moves in the 2010s cited cost of living
evidence.source: Kamehameha Schools, 'Why Residents Leave Hawaiʻi: A Look at Economic Conditions Across the Decades' (Hawaiʻi in Motion)

drivers.driver: Las Vegas as the 'ninth island': an established diaspora, decades of casino marketing to Hawaii, and a dense air bridge
drivers.quantified_effect: Las Vegas draws the most departures of any metro (about 1,656 households a year in 2019–23, up 32% from 2004–08 and 60% from 2011–14). It is also the most one-directional corridor: 2.41 households leave for every one that arrives, against 1.27–1.48 for Denver, Salt Lake City, Seattle, Portland, Phoenix and Texas. Net loss to Las Vegas is about 968 households a year. Clark County is #1 from every island, including the neighbor islands, which send almost no military moves (Maui 7.2%, Hawaiʻi Island 5.7%, Kauaʻi 4.7%, Oʻahu 5.8% of departing households). So the draw is mainly civilian. Jobs still matter: departures to Las Vegas fell 38% when Nevada's job market crashed (2006–07 to 2009–10), while Hawaii's total departures fell only 8%.

evidence.fact: Hawaii patrons made up about 75% of occupied room nights at the California Hotel, 37% at Fremont and 45% at Main Street Station in 2025. Boyd owns a Hawaii travel agency and has marketed to Hawaii customers and travel agents since the Cal opened in 1975, offering 'affordable all-inclusive packages'
evidence.source: Boyd Gaming Corp. Form 10-K for FY2025 (company filing)

evidence.fact: Total air seats from Las Vegas to Hawaii in 2025, of which 468,537 were to Honolulu (+23.4%). That is more than Phoenix (570,896) or Denver (520,202)
evidence.source: DBEDT 2025 Annual Visitor Research Report, Table 100 & 101

evidence.fact: Native Hawaiians (alone or in combination) living in Nevada, 2020 Census, up from 16,339 in 2010. Our calculation: 8.6 per 1,000 residents, against 5.6 in Alaska, 4.0 in Washington, 3.6 in Oregon and Utah, and 2.4 in California. Statewide, 53% of all Native Hawaiians (362,893 of 680,442) live outside Hawaii
evidence.source: State of Hawaii Data Book 2023, Table 1.37 (from Census 2020 Detailed DHC-A)

evidence.fact: Average households a year leaving Hawaii for Las Vegas (Clark County), 2019–20 to 2022–23, against 689 a year arriving from there; average AGI of households heading to Las Vegas $64.3k
evidence.source: IRS SOI county-to-county migration, computed here (county pairs with 20+ returns)

evidence.fact: Hawaii departures to Las Vegas fell from 1,379 households (2006–07) to 855 (2009–10) as Nevada's unemployment rate averaged 13.2% in 2010 (Hawaii 6.7%)
evidence.value: −38% to Las Vegas vs −8% to all states
evidence.source: IRS SOI migration (computed here); BLS LAUS via FRED (NVUR, HIUR)

evidence.fact: A UNLV historian dates the Hawaii–Las Vegas link to the 1970s California Hotel marketing and Sam Boyd's charter flights. A local Hawaiian civic club leader says migration 'continues' and that many moved for economic reasons
evidence.source: KTNV Las Vegas, 'Why is Las Vegas considered the 9th island for Hawaiians?'

drivers.driver: Military reassignment: permanent change-of-station moves from Oʻahu's bases drive a large share of departures to Texas, Seattle–Tacoma, Colorado Springs, San Diego and the DC area
drivers.quantified_effect: In 2019–23, 17.7% of Oʻahu's departing households (about 3,830 a year) went to counties dominated by large military installations (our list of about 40 such counties, San Diego excluded), up from 13.9% in 2004–08. For the neighbor islands the figure is 0–1.6%. These households are larger (2.1–2.7 people per return vs 1.98 for all leavers). Pierce County (Joint Base Lewis-McChord) is about 35% of Seattle–Tacoma departures. Bexar, Bell and El Paso counties in Texas are about a third of departures to Texas. El Paso County, Colorado (Colorado Springs) took 365 households a year, more than the Denver core (359).

evidence.fact: Active-duty personnel permanently assigned in Hawaii, September 30, 2024: 44,604 across all services (DoD 43,108, of which Army 18,410, Navy 12,668, Marines 6,485, Air Force 5,382; Coast Guard 1,496)
evidence.source: State of Hawaii Data Book 2024, Table 10.02 (from DMDC)

evidence.fact: Share of Oʻahu's departing tax-filing households going to counties dominated by large military installations (e.g., Pierce and Kitsap WA; El Paso CO; Bexar, Bell and El Paso TX; Cumberland and Onslow NC; Montgomery TN; Anne Arundel MD; Norfolk and Virginia Beach VA)
evidence.value: 17.7% in 2019–23 (≈3,826/yr) vs 13.9% in 2004–08; Maui 1.5%, Hawaiʻi Island 1.6%, Kauaʻi 0%
evidence.source: IRS SOI county-to-county outflows, computed here

evidence.fact: People per departing return, 2019–23: El Paso CO 2.56; Bexar TX 2.38; Bell TX 2.57; El Paso TX 2.69; Pierce WA 2.12; against Clark NV 1.91, Los Angeles 1.50, King WA 1.61 and an all-destination average of 1.98
evidence.value: Base counties average 2.1–2.7 people per return
evidence.source: IRS SOI county-to-county outflows, computed here

evidence.fact: Households a year leaving for El Paso County, Colorado (Fort Carson area), against Denver's seven core counties
evidence.source: IRS SOI county-to-county outflows, computed here

evidence.fact: DoD overseas tour-length guidance lists Hawaii at 36 months for both accompanied and unaccompanied tours. The document could not be retrieved directly; seen via search excerpt. If tours average about 3 years, roughly 14,000–15,000 service members rotate out each year (our arithmetic)
evidence.source: DoD CTD for CAP 68-22(I), OCONUS tour lengths correction

drivers.driver: Job markets and real incomes: leavers go where jobs have grown and costs are lower relative to pay; the interior West, Nevada, Texas and Arizona led
drivers.quantified_effect: Nonfarm jobs, August 2026 vs the 2019 average: Hawaii −2.4%; Idaho +17.2%; Utah +15.0%; Nevada +13.9%; Texas +12.9%; Arizona +11.4%; Colorado +6.5%; Washington +5.2%; Oregon +0.5%. The fastest-growing exits match the fastest job growth, except Portland. UHERO estimates that 10% lower price-adjusted income predicts about 0.17 percentage points more out-migration across metros.

evidence.value: Hawaii is the only state shown still below 2019
evidence.source: BLS Current Employment Statistics via FRED (HINA, IDNA, UTNA, NVNA, TXNA, AZNA, CONA, WANA, ORNA)

evidence.fact: UHERO: more residents left Hawaii for the continent than arrived in 23 of the past 25 years. Hawaii is 'simultaneously priced out and left behind', and in urban Honolulu incomes have fallen below the national average. Across 384 metros, higher prices push people out and higher incomes pull them in; 10% lower price-adjusted income predicts about 0.17 percentage points more out-migration
evidence.source: UHERO, 'Are people leaving Hawaiʻi because of high prices or low incomes?' (from 'Beyond the Price of Paradise')

evidence.fact: Average annual net domestic migration rate, 2021–2025 (per 1,000 residents): Idaho +13.6; Arizona +6.9; Nevada +5.4; Texas +5.0; Utah +3.0; Colorado +0.4 (−2.0 in 2025); Washington −0.6; Oregon −0.3; Hawaii −7.6
evidence.source: US Census Bureau, Vintage 2025 state population estimates (NST-EST2025-ALLDATA)

evidence.fact: Unemployment rate, 2025 annual average: Hawaii 2.3%; Nevada 5.3%; Colorado 4.0%; Utah 3.5%. Hawaii's problem is pay and opportunity relative to cost, not joblessness
evidence.source: BLS LAUS via FRED (HIUR, NVUR, COUR, UTUR)

drivers.driver: Family, community and church networks: Native Hawaiian, Pacific Islander and Latter-day Saint communities already on the mainland make some destinations easier to move to; strongest in Las Vegas and Utah
drivers.quantified_effect: Native Hawaiian population growth 2010–2020 was fastest in the interior West: Idaho +99.9%, Utah +80.1%, Colorado +74.1%, against Nevada +63%, Washington +56%, Oregon +59% and California +27%. That matches the ranking of fastest-growing exits. Departures to Utah County (Provo, home of BYU) nearly doubled (82 → 158 a year, +91%). Households heading to Salt Lake City have the lowest average AGI of any major corridor ($51.4k), which fits younger, larger, network-led moves more than affluent remote workers.

evidence.fact: Native Hawaiians (alone or in combination), 2020, with change since 2010: Utah 11,753 (+80.1%); Colorado 9,873 (+74.1%); Idaho 3,840 (+99.9%); Washington 31,061 (+56.4%); Texas 23,234 (+76.1%); Oregon 15,446 (+58.9%); Arizona 13,839 (+44.9%); California 95,165 (+27.0%)
evidence.source: State of Hawaii Data Book 2023, Table 1.37 (from Census 2020 Detailed DHC-A)
