evidence.fact: Utah's Pacific Islander share of population is 1.6% (close to 50,000 people), third among states after Hawaii and Alaska; the share is 2.4% in Salt Lake County and 2.0% in Utah County. More than a quarter of the nation's Tongan population lives in Utah
evidence.source: Kem C. Gardner Policy Institute, University of Utah, 'Insight: Utah's Pacific Islander Community' (2016–20 ACS)

evidence.fact: Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints membership in Hawaii (about 5% of residents by our arithmetic against the 2025 Census estimate of 1,432,820)
evidence.source: Church Newsroom, Facts and Statistics: Hawaii

evidence.fact: Households a year leaving Hawaii for Salt Lake County, Utah County and Ada County (Boise)
evidence.source: IRS SOI county-to-county outflows, computed here (20-return threshold; Ada drops below it in some years)

evidence.fact: Kamehameha Schools' interview study found 'social and environmental conditions (e.g., to be closer to family who live outside of Hawaiʻi) increased as a reason to leave in the 2010s'
evidence.source: Kamehameha Schools, Hawaiʻi in Motion infographic

evidence.fact: Air seats to Hawaii from Salt Lake City rose 32.4% to 218,865 in 2025 (Honolulu +32.2%). Denver had 520,202 seats (Honolulu +18.4%). Boise had no scheduled service in DBEDT's 2025 seat table
evidence.source: DBEDT 2025 Annual Visitor Research Report, Table 100

drivers.driver: State income taxes: zero or low-tax destinations (Nevada, Texas, Washington, Arizona) offer some savings, but this is a secondary, marginal factor
drivers.quantified_effect: Our calculation under Hawaii's 2025 brackets (standard deduction and exemption only): at the $64.3k average AGI of households heading to Las Vegas, Hawaii income tax is about $2,073 (married filing jointly) to $3,357 (single), or 3.2–5.2% of income. That is about 5–8% of the roughly $44,000 a year housing-payment gap. Counter-signal: Portland departures rose 55% even though Oregon's 8.75% rate starts at $11,050 and its top rate is 9.9%. Within the Portland metro, however, the Washington side (Clark County, WA, which has no wage income tax) grew fastest (61 → 179 a year, +194%) against Multnomah County (+20%), which fits a modest tax or price sorting effect at the margin. Hawaii's 2024 tax cut (Act 46) roughly doubles the standard deduction in 2026, so this gap is narrowing.

evidence.fact: State individual income tax rates as of January 1, 2025: Hawaii 1.40% to 11% across 12 brackets (7.6% above $48,000 and 11% above $325,000, single); Nevada and Texas none; Washington taxes only capital gains; Arizona 2.5% flat; Colorado 4.4% flat; Utah 4.55%; Idaho 5.695%; Oregon 4.75% to 9.9% (8.75% above $11,050, 9.9% above $125,000, single)
evidence.source: Tax Foundation, '2025 State Income Tax Rates and Brackets' (think tank compilation of state statutes)

evidence.fact: Act 46 (HB 2404) cuts Hawaii individual income tax by raising the standard deduction and widening brackets in stages. The standard deduction rises to $8,000 single / $16,000 joint for 2026–27 (per DOTAX/EY summaries); the 2027+ steps were partly revisited in the 2026 session
evidence.source: Hawaii Session Laws 2024, Act 46; EY Tax News summary

evidence.fact: Households a year leaving Hawaii for Portland metro counties, 2004–08 vs 2019–23: Multnomah 171 → 206; Washington Co. OR 145 → 200; Clark Co. WA 61 → 179
evidence.source: IRS SOI county-to-county outflows, computed here

counter_evidence: The 'interior West is the fastest-growing exit' finding depends on the baseline. Against 2004–08, Denver (+75%) and Salt Lake City (+68%) lead. Against 2011–14 (after the IRS method change), Las Vegas (+60%) and Phoenix (+36%) grew faster than Salt Lake City (+35%) and Denver (+30%). State-level IRS data for 2011–14 vs 2020–23 agree: Nevada +57%, Utah +55%, Idaho +39%, Colorado +29%. Las Vegas's slower long-run growth reflects its 2008–11 bust, when Hawaii departures there fell 38%.

Small numbers: the interior-West corridors are roughly 180–360 households a year, and part of their 2004–08 → 2019–23 growth is mechanical. Total departures rose 21% over the same span; the IRS 2011–12 method change added about 5%; and county pairs below 20 returns are suppressed. Salt Lake City departures have fallen each year since 2020–21 (200 → 181 → 155). Boise cannot be measured reliably at metro level (Ada County alone is 32–90 a year, with zero years).

Part of the Colorado and Texas 'exit' is military reassignment, not household choice. El Paso County, CO (Colorado Springs) grew +114% and now exceeds the Denver core. Bexar, Bell and El Paso TX are about a third of departures to Texas. Military moves inflate gross departures, and many of those households plan to return or keep Hawaii homes.

Churn rather than flight: inflows from Denver (+89%), Seattle–Tacoma, Portland and Phoenix also rose, and out/in ratios for those metros are only 1.27–1.48. Some 'leavers' to these metros are likely mainland-born residents (or military) returning home. Las Vegas (2.41) is the only strongly one-way corridor.

Cost alone cannot explain the interior West: Boise, Provo and Salt Lake City prices per square foot rose 62–71% since 2019 (Honolulu +29%), narrowing the gap, yet departures there rose. Interior-West listing medians ($565k–$610k) are above Las Vegas, Phoenix and Texas.

Taxes are not first-order. Oregon has one of the highest income tax rates (9.9% top), yet Portland is a top-five landing market whose departures rose 55%. California (13.3% top) remains Hawaii's largest two-way partner. The tax gap at typical leaver incomes is about 5–8% of the housing-payment gap.

Hawaii's job market is not slack (2.3% unemployment in 2025, vs Nevada 5.3%). The job pull is about growth, pay and opportunity relative to cost (UHERO's 'left behind'), not escaping unemployment, and Las Vegas departures fall when Nevada's job market weakens.

National trend: the same Sun Belt and Mountain West states drew domestic migrants from everywhere (Census Vintage 2025). Hawaii's leavers may partly be following national flows rather than reacting to Hawaii-specific factors. Remote work after 2020 is a plausible extra driver for Denver and Boise, but we did not test it.

Data limits: IRS SOI covers tax filers only, by filing address, through early 2023 (2022–23 is the latest county-to-county release). It misses non-filers (some retirees) and 2023–2026 events (Maui fire aftermath, the rate shock). It identifies households that move, not home sellers. The interview and poll evidence on motives (Kamehameha Schools, n=186) is not a random sample. No dataset here gives the age of movers, so a retiree effect in Las Vegas and Phoenix is unmeasured.
research.for_brokers: Treat the landing list as a referral map with three different motives. (1) Las Vegas, the one-way corridor (about 1,650 households a year, 2.4 out for every 1 in): build a standing referral relationship with a Las Vegas agent and expect steady, cost-driven local sellers from every island. It also works in reverse: Nevada buyers made 134 Hawaii purchases in 2025 (Title Guaranty), and the Oʻahu tax roll shows 985 Oʻahu parcels with Las Vegas mailing addresses, a pipeline of absentee owners who may list. (2) Military-driven corridors (Seattle–Tacoma/Pierce, Texas: San Antonio, Killeen, El Paso; Colorado Springs; DC; San Diego): these follow permanent-change-of-station orders, which tend to bunch in summer. Market sell-or-rent decisions to Oʻahu owners near the bases ahead of the move season, and partner with agents near the receiving installations. (3) Interior West and Pacific Northwest (Denver, Salt Lake City/Provo, Boise, Portland, Seattle): these are two-way churn corridors with growing but small flows (about 180–360 households a year to Denver and Salt Lake City). Colorado (136) and Utah (105) were also top buyer-origin states in 2025, so a partner agent there can refer in both directions. When pitching a move, lead with the housing payment gap (about $3,700 a month vs Las Vegas at today's rates), not taxes, which are about $2,000–3,400 a year at typical incomes and shrinking after Hawaii's 2026 standard-deduction increase. Fair housing: target by geography and referral relationships, never by race, ancestry or religion, even though Native Hawaiian, Pacific Islander and Latter-day Saint networks help explain the Las Vegas and Utah flows.
research.for_locals: Families leaving Hawaii mostly follow money, work and ʻohana. The math is stark: a median Oʻahu house now carries about $6,000 a month in principal and interest, against roughly $2,300 for a Las Vegas or Phoenix median home. State income tax savings are much smaller, about $2,000–3,400 a year for a household earning around $64,000, and Hawaii's 2026 tax cut narrows them further. Before choosing a destination, weigh more than price. (a) Jobs: Utah, Idaho, Nevada, Texas and Arizona have added 11–17% more jobs since 2019 while Hawaii is still below 2019. But Nevada's unemployment is higher (5.3% vs 2.3%), and Las Vegas jobs swing hard in downturns (13% unemployment in 2010). (b) The interior West is no longer cheap: Boise, Salt Lake City and Denver asking prices ($565k–$610k) rose fastest since 2019. (c) Community: Las Vegas, Utah, Washington and Oregon have large and growing Native Hawaiian and Pacific Islander communities, which many movers say is what makes a move stick. (d) Coming back is hard: Honolulu prices per square foot rose about 29% since 2019, so if you might return, consider renting out rather than selling, mindful of losing the homeowner exemption and of landlord obligations. For military families, much of the 'leaving' is orders-driven and temporary. Many keep their Oʻahu homes, which keeps some inventory off the market.

challenge.question: Why do departing Hawaii households go to Las Vegas, Texas, Phoenix, Seattle–Tacoma and Portland, and why is the interior West (Denver, Salt Lake City, Boise) the fastest-growing exit?

verdicts.driver: Housing-cost gap: departing households trade Hawaii's prices for cheaper mainland housing (Las Vegas, Phoenix, Texas)
verdicts.reason: The push is real and well supported. In the Kamehameha Schools interviews, high cost of living was cited in 71% of economics-driven moves in the 2010s (KSBE infographic, Dec 2022, checked in saved copy). UHERO finds that for Honolulu 'prices have been the dominant factor' (https://uhero.hawaii.edu/are-people-leaving-hawai%CA%BBi-because-of-high-prices-or-low-incomes/, 2026-03-19). Honolulu households that moved to another state had lower average AGI than those who stayed: $70.4k vs $89.9k (IRS 2022-23 county outflow file, Honolulu 'Different State' vs 'Non-migrants' rows, recomputed). Every major destination is far cheaper. The researcher's quantification is overstated, though, and the cost gap does not explain timing or which corridors grow. FHFA all-transactions index: Las Vegas prices fell 61% from 2006Q2 to 2012Q1 while Honolulu fell 4% (FRED ATNHPIUS29820Q / ATNHPIUS46520Q, retrieved 2026-10-08). So the gap was widest in 2009–12, yet departures to Las Vegas were at their 20-year low then (850–950 a year). Since 2019, Las Vegas prices rose faster than Honolulu's (FHFA +67% vs +48%; Realtor.com price per sq ft +49% vs +29%), so the gap narrowed, yet departures to Las Vegas set records. Cost sets the level of out-migration; jobs and networks shape where and when.
fact_errors: The $3,680/month gap compares O'ahu's single-family SALE median ($1,193,750) with Las Vegas's all-property-type LISTING median ($464,900). On a like-for-like basis (Realtor.com listing medians, Sept 2026: Urban Honolulu $675,000 at a median 912 sq ft vs Las Vegas $464,900 at 1,796 sq ft), principal and interest is about $3,410 vs $2,348, a gap of about $1,060/month. The ~$3,700 figure holds only single-family to single-family.

Typical leavers (AGI $64–70k) are mostly not buyers of O'ahu single-family homes, so rent is the more relevant comparison. Zillow ZORI, Aug 2026 (reported): Urban Honolulu $3,020; Las Vegas $1,742; Phoenix $1,722; Salt Lake City $1,641; Dallas $1,659; Houston $1,643; San Antonio $1,422; Denver $1,922; Boise $1,919; Portland $1,818; Seattle $2,278. The Honolulu–Las Vegas rent gap is about $1,280/month (about $15,300/yr). Source: https://files.zillowstatic.com/research/public_csvs/zori/Metro_zori_uc_sfrcondomfr_sm_month.csv, retrieved 2026-10-08.
'11–18 times Hawaii's income tax' does not reproduce: $44,160 ÷ $3,357 = 13x and ÷ $2,073 = 21x. That is also what the researcher's own '5–8%' figure implies.
verdicts.corrected_wording: High housing costs are the main reason households leave, and every top destination is much cheaper. At August 2026 asking rents, a Honolulu renter pays about $1,300 a month more than in Las Vegas or Phoenix (about $15,000 a year). For a single-family buyer the payment gap is about $3,700 a month. The gap does not explain which corridors grew or when. Las Vegas departures bottomed in 2009–12, when its homes were cheapest relative to Hawaii, and peaked after 2019, when its prices were rising faster than Honolulu's.

verdicts.driver: Las Vegas as the 'ninth island': established diaspora, decades of casino marketing, dense air bridge
verdicts.reason: This is the best-supported destination-specific driver, and the strongest support is new. In the IRS state-to-state inflow files, returns moving from Hawaii to Nevada rose 54% from 2011–14 to 2019–23, while all U.S. returns moving into Nevada rose only 19%. Hawaii's share of Nevada's domestic in-movers went from 1.99% to 2.58% (https://www.irs.gov/pub/irs-soi/stateinflow1112.csv through stateinflow2223.csv, retrieved 2026-10-08). No other large destination shows a Hawaii-specific excess like that. Las Vegas is also the only strongly one-way corridor among the 16 tracked metros: out/in ratio 2.41 in 2019–23 (1,656 vs 689 a year; local IRS data, recomputed). It is #1 from every island on 2019–23 averages. Las Vegas leavers have the second-lowest average AGI of the major corridors ($64.3k), which fits a cost-driven move. Confirmed facts: Boyd 10-K FY2025 (Hawaii patrons were 75% / 37% / 45% of room nights at the Cal, Fremont and Main Street Station; marketing to Hawaii since 1975; Boyd owns a Hawaii travel agency). DBEDT 2025 Annual Visitor Research Table 100: Las Vegas 734,392 seats (+10.6%), Honolulu 468,537 (+23.4%), Phoenix 570,896, Denver 520,202. Data Book Table 1.37: Native Hawaiians in Nevada 26,628 alone or in combination (+63.0%). KTNV, 2021-05-18. Jobs gate the corridor: departures fell 38% (1,379 to 855) when Nevada unemployment averaged 13.2% in 2010 (FRED NVUR).
fact_errors: The parenthetical '(Maui 7.2%, Hawai'i Island 5.7%, Kaua'i 4.7%, O'ahu 5.8% of departing households)' gives each island's share of departures going to Las Vegas, not military shares. Military-county shares for the neighbor islands are 0–1.6%.
Clark County is #1 from Kaua'i on the 2019–23 average but not in 2019–20 (San Diego 49, Clark 44).

The Boyd room-night shares and air seats measure visitors, not movers. The 2025 seat growth falls after the IRS window, which ends in 2022–23. So they show the familiarity channel, not the size of migration.
Native Hawaiian counts cover only part of the Hawaii-linked population in Nevada, which also includes Filipino, Japanese and other residents born in Hawaii.
verdicts.corrected_wording: Las Vegas is the one destination Hawaii residents favor far more than other Americans do. From 2011–14 to 2019–23, Hawaii's moves to Nevada grew 54% while all U.S. moves into Nevada grew 19%, and about 2.4 households leave for Las Vegas for each one that comes back. Its lower costs fit the lower incomes of those who go (about $64k average AGI). The pull is reinforced by a Hawaii community dating to Boyd Gaming's 1970s marketing and by heavy visitor traffic. The flow still depends on Las Vegas jobs: it fell 38% when Nevada's job market collapsed in 2008–10.

verdicts.driver: Military reassignment drives a large share of departures to Texas, Seattle–Tacoma, Colorado Springs, San Diego and the DC area
verdicts.reason: The direction is right, but the 17.7% share is an upper bound. Re-running the researcher's county list shows it mixes counties that are mostly bases with large civilian metros: Pierce/Tacoma, Bexar/San Antonio, El Paso TX, Anne Arundel, Virginia Beach, Chesapeake, Solano, Davis UT, Richland SC, Escambia, Sarpy. Counties strictly dominated by bases (Bell, Coryell, El Paso CO, Kitsap, Cumberland, Onslow, Montgomery TN, Christian KY, Jefferson NY, Liberty GA, Geary/Riley KS, Comanche OK and others) take 9.1% of O'ahu's departures (about 1,970 a year) in 2019–23, up from 7.6% (about 1,390) in 2004–08. The mixed counties add 8.6%. San Diego, excluded from the list, is O'ahu's #2 destination (about 880 a year) and likely heavily Navy and Marine, so the true military share is somewhere around 9% to 20% or more. Persons per return confirm family moves (El Paso CO 2.56, Bell 2.57, El Paso TX 2.69, against a 1.98 average). Colorado Springs is the clearest case. El Paso County, CO stepped up from 198 (2007–08) to 306 (2009–10) and averaged about 365 a year in 2019–23, roughly 47% of all departures to Colorado and about 61% of Colorado's increase since 2004–08. Data Book Table 10.02 confirms 44,604 active-duty personnel at 2024-09-30.
fact_errors: 'Bexar, Bell and El Paso are about a third of departures to Texas' understates it. Statewide they are about 45% (≈790 of ≈1,770 households a year, 2019–23, IRS county outflows recomputed).

The tour-length source is titled as a DoD CIVILIAN OCONUS tour-length notice, not a military one. It could not be retrieved (media.defense.gov is blocked), so the 36-month figure and the 14,000–15,000 rotations a year are unverified. IRS base-county flows (≈2,000–3,800 a year) are far smaller than that, so many military moves either do not show up in IRS county data or go to non-base counties.
El Paso County, CO '170 → 365' depends on dropping cells under 20 returns. Without that threshold it is 190 → 365 (+92%).
verdicts.corrected_wording: Military orders are a separate channel that people do not choose. Counties dominated by bases take about 9% of O'ahu's departing households, rising to about 18% if mixed civilian-military metros such as Tacoma, San Antonio and El Paso are included, and more if San Diego is counted. Military moves make up about half of departures to Colorado (Colorado Springs) and to Texas (San Antonio, Killeen, El Paso), which inflates the apparent growth of those 'exits'. The neighbor islands send almost none.

verdicts.driver: Job markets and real incomes: leavers go where jobs have grown (interior West, Nevada, Texas, Arizona)
verdicts.reason: The FRED payroll figures check out exactly (Aug 2026 vs 2019 average: HI −2.4%, ID +17.2%, UT +15.0%, NV +13.9%, TX +12.9%, AZ +11.4%, CO +6.5%, WA +5.2%, OR +0.5%). So do the Census Vintage 2025 net domestic figures (Hawaii −54,537 over 2021–25) and the unemployment rates (HI 2.3%, NV 5.3% in 2025). Using matched windows (job growth 2011–13 to 2019–22 against growth in Hawaii outflows 2011–14 to 2019–23), the rank correlation across the 8 destination states is about 0.88. That is my calculation from the FRED CSVs and IRS files, n=8. The Las Vegas collapse in 2008–10 also points to jobs. But this is the same pull drawing movers from every state. Measured against all U.S. inflows, Hawaii's flows grew in line with or slower than the national rate in Colorado (+28% vs +29%), Washington (+24% vs +25%), Arizona (+25% vs +32%), Oregon (+14% vs +20%) and Idaho (+39% vs +58%). Job growth is also partly caused by in-migration. Moderate strength.
fact_errors: UHERO is misquoted. The post says 'a 10% higher price level predicts about 0.21 percentage points more net outmigration, and a 10% higher income level predicts about 0.16 percentage points more net in-migration'. There is no '10% lower price-adjusted income → 0.17 pp' result.

UHERO's model explains why people leave Hawaii, not where they go, and the post says the regression 'doesn't tell us whether prices or incomes cause migration.' For Honolulu, it finds prices dominant. The income effect turned negative only in 2022–23, and 'local' factors are the largest component (2023: price −0.26, income −0.01, local −0.94, total −1.09 pp).
Job growth was measured through Aug 2026, but the IRS migration window ends in 2022–23. The 'match' with the fastest-growing exits should use matched periods.
verdicts.corrected_wording: Destinations that added jobs fastest also drew the fastest-growing share of Hawaii's leavers, but that is the national migration pattern, not something special about Hawaii. Outside Nevada, and to a lesser degree Utah, Hawaii's flows grew no faster than everyone else's moves into those states. On the Hawaii side, UHERO finds high prices and persistent local constraints drive departures from Honolulu more than low incomes, although income is now adding to the pressure.

verdicts.driver: Family, community and church networks (Native Hawaiian, Pacific Islander, Latter-day Saint), strongest in Las Vegas and Utah
verdicts.reason: Confirmed: Data Book Table 1.37 figures (Utah 11,753 +80.1%; Colorado 9,873 +74.1%; Idaho 3,840 +99.9%; Texas 23,234 +76.1%); Gardner Institute's 1.6% Pacific Islander share in Utah; LDS membership in Hawaii of 75,827 (as of 2025-12-31). The network story holds for Las Vegas and modestly for Utah. Hawaii-origin moves to Utah rose 53%, against 44% for all U.S. inflows. Utah County's flow nearly doubled after 2015 (about 80 a year in 2011–14 to 158 in 2019–23), and Salt Lake leavers have large households (2.11 per return) and low AGI ($51.4k). It does not hold for the rest of the interior West. Native Hawaiian growth does not track flow growth: the rank correlation across 8 states is about 0.4. Texas Native Hawaiians grew 76%, as fast as Colorado's, yet Hawaii flows to Texas grew only 15%. Nevada's grew a slower 63%, yet Nevada had the fastest flow growth. Causation also runs backward, because Hawaii migrants are part of the Native Hawaiian growth in those states. Growth in the 'alone' count is lower (NV +46%, UT +50%, CO +67%, ID +71%). Colorado and Idaho show no Hawaii-specific excess over national inflows.
fact_errors: 'That matches the ranking of fastest-growing exits' is not borne out. Texas (+76% Native Hawaiian) and Nevada (+63%) invert the ranking.

Utah's Pacific Islanders are 39% Tongan, 30% Samoan and only 7% Native Hawaiian (Gardner Institute, https://gardner.utah.edu/blog/blog-utahs-pacific-islander-community/, 2022-09-23). The Hawaii–Utah link would run through Latter-day Saint and Polynesian (Lā'ie/BYU–Hawaii) ties, which are plausible but untested here.
'Latter-day Saint communities grew fastest' is asserted without data for the destination states.
Direct flights do not fit Boise, which has no nonstop service in DBEDT's 2025 seat table. Seat counts reflect visitor demand.
Salt Lake City is not a growing one-way exit lately. In 2022–23 more households came from Salt Lake (194) than left for it (155), and departures there fell three years running (200 → 181 → 155).
verdicts.corrected_wording: Community ties clearly help explain Las Vegas and probably the Utah County (Provo) corridor, where Hawaii's moves grew faster than the national flow. There is no evidence that networks drive moves to Denver or Boise: Hawaii's flows there grew no faster than everyone else's, and Native Hawaiian population growth by state does not line up with where Hawaii's leavers went.

verdicts.driver: State income taxes: zero/low-tax destinations offer some savings; secondary factor
verdicts.reason: It is weak and secondary, as the researcher says, and the data make it weaker. The Hawaii bracket calculation reproduces from the Tax Foundation table: at $64.3k AGI, $2,073 married filing jointly (3.2%) and $3,357 single (5.2%) under 2025 brackets; with the 2026 $8,000/$16,000 standard deduction, about $1,590–3,080. Growth in Hawaii-origin flows to no-income-tax states (NV +54%, WA +24%, TX +15%, average about 31%) matched growth to income-tax states (UT +53%, ID +39%, CO +28%, AZ +25%, OR +14%, average about 32%), 2011–14 to 2019–23, IRS state inflow files. At typical leaver incomes, Utah (4.55%), Colorado (4.4%), Idaho (5.695%) and Arizona (2.5%) leave almost no gap with Hawaii, and Oregon taxes more. Within the Portland metro, from the 2011–14 base, Clark County WA rose about 50%, Washington County OR about 40% and Multnomah about −7% (IRS county outflows, no threshold), so the evidence on tax sorting is mixed.
fact_errors: The tax gap is about 1/13 to 1/21 of the single-family payment gap, not 1/11 to 1/18. Against the more relevant rent gap (about $15,300 a year vs Las Vegas), it is about 1/5 to 1/7.
The Portland-area county figures (61 → 179, etc.) depend on the 20-return threshold. Without it, Clark County WA was 88 → 179 and Multnomah 177 → 206 (2004–08 → 2019–23).
verdicts.corrected_wording: State income tax is a minor factor. At a typical leaver's income it is worth about $1,600–3,400 a year, against a housing-cost gap of about $15,000 a year in rent (more for owners). Hawaii's flows to no-tax states grew no faster than flows to states with income taxes, and Hawaii's 2026 standard-deduction increase narrows the gap further.

verdicts.driver: Premise: the interior West (Denver, Salt Lake City, Boise) is the fastest-growing exit
verdicts.reason: It holds only against a 2004–08 base, when Las Vegas's own boom inflated the comparison. On the consistent post-2011 IRS series, metro departures grew: Las Vegas 1,033 → 1,657 (+60%), Phoenix 495 → 672 (+36%), Salt Lake City 133 → 179 (+35%), Denver 277 → 359 (+30%), Portland +25%, Seattle–Tacoma +19%, Texas metros +11%, all destinations +10% (local irs20 data, recomputed). At state level, Nevada (+54%) roughly ties Utah (+53%); Idaho (+39%) and Colorado (+28%) are mid-pack. About 61% of Colorado's increase since 2004–08 is Colorado Springs (Army). The flows are small: Ada County (Boise) averaged about 64 households a year. The IRS data end in early 2023. Since then, Census Vintage 2025 shows Colorado's net domestic migration turned negative in 2025 (−12,100) and Utah's fell to about +3,000 a year in 2024–25, so the interior-West pull may already be fading.
fact_errors: Native Hawaiian, Pacific Islander and Latter-day Saint communities, plus direct flights, are offered as reasons for interior-West growth, but Colorado and Idaho flows show no Hawaii-specific growth beyond national trends.
verdicts.corrected_wording: The interior West grew fastest only relative to the mid-2000s. Since 2011, Las Vegas and Phoenix grew faster than Salt Lake City and Denver. Utah, mainly Provo, is the one interior-West corridor that grew faster than the national flow. Colorado's growth is half Army moves to Colorado Springs, Boise's numbers are too small to measure reliably, and Salt Lake City departures have fallen since 2020–21.

missing_drivers: The national migration current. From 2011–14 to 2019–23, Hawaii's flows to Colorado (+28% vs +29% for all U.S. inflows), Washington (+24% vs +25%), Arizona (+25% vs +32%), Oregon (+14% vs +20%), Idaho (+39% vs +58%), Florida (+21% vs +23%) and Tennessee (+21% vs +35%) grew at or below the national rate (IRS stateinflow files, https://www.irs.gov/pub/irs-soi/, retrieved 2026-10-08). Only Nevada (+54% vs +19%), and modestly Utah (+53% vs +44%) and Texas (+15% vs +9%), show Hawaii-specific excess. Most destination 'choices' reflect the same pull acting on all Americans.

UHERO's 'local' factors (isolation, limited housing supply, congestion, industry concentration, limited job availability). In 2023 they are the largest predicted component of Honolulu out-migration: −0.94 of −1.09 pp (UHERO, 2026-03-19).

Renters rather than buyers. Leavers average $64–70k AGI, so most are probably renters. The binding gap is rent (about $1,100–1,600 a month vs the main destinations, Zillow ZORI Aug 2026, reported) and the chance to own anywhere at all, not the O'ahu single-family payment.

Life stage, unmeasured. Retirees (likely Las Vegas and Phoenix) and young adults or students (Oregon, Utah, Las Vegas colleges) may account for a lot. No dataset here gives the age of out-movers. Hawaii's in-movers from the states are 43% under 25 and 22% active duty (local PUMS), a sign of a young, churning population.

Return migration and churn. Inflows from Denver, Seattle–Tacoma, Portland and Phoenix also rose (out/in ratios only 1.27–1.48), and Salt Lake City flipped to a net inflow in 2022–23. Many 'leavers' are mainland-born or military households going home.

Military moves outside base counties. San Diego (about 880 a year from O'ahu), the DC area, and service members who file from home-of-record addresses could put the military share anywhere from about 9% to over 20%.
The Lā'ie/BYU–Hawaii and Tongan/Samoan Latter-day Saint pipeline to Utah County, a plausible reason Provo's flow doubled after 2015. Untested.
Equity cash-out by Hawaii owners who sell and buy outright on the mainland. Plausible for older Las Vegas and Phoenix movers, but IRS data do not identify sellers.
Post-2023 shocks outside the IRS window: the Maui fire aftermath, the mortgage-rate shock, the 2025 expansion of Las Vegas–Honolulu seats, and the 2023–25 stall in Colorado and Utah in-migration.
Tax treatment of retirement income was not checked. If Hawaii already exempts Social Security and employer pensions, the tax motive for retiree movers is smaller still.
challenge.final_answer: Hawaii's departing households leave mainly because housing costs too much, and they land where housing is cheaper and jobs have grown. That mostly follows the same pull that draws movers from every state. Las Vegas is the one place Hawaii residents favor far more than other Americans do. The push is cost. In August 2026 a typical Honolulu asking rent ran about $3,020 a month, roughly $1,300 more than in Las Vegas or Phoenix. For a single-family buyer the payment gap is about $3,700 a month. O'ahu households that moved to another state reported less income than those who stayed ($70k vs $90k average AGI, 2022–23). From 2011–14 to 2019–23, Hawaii's moves to Colorado, Washington, Arizona, Oregon and Idaho grew no faster than all U.S. moves into those states. Over the same period Hawaii's moves to Nevada grew 54%, against 19% nationally. Las Vegas is also the only strongly one-way corridor: about 1,650 households a year leave for it, roughly 2.4 for every one that comes back. That fits a 'ninth island' community built since Boyd Gaming began marketing to Hawaii in the 1970s, and those who go have lower incomes, which fits a cost-driven move. The flow still depends on jobs there: it fell 38% when Nevada's economy collapsed in 2008–10. Military orders are a separate channel. Counties dominated by bases take about 9% of O'ahu's leavers, up to about 18% if Tacoma, San Antonio and El Paso are counted, and these moves explain roughly half of the departures to Colorado (Colorado Springs) and Texas. State income tax matters little, about $1,600–3,400 a year at typical leaver incomes, and flows to no-tax states grew no faster than flows to taxed ones. Calling the interior West the 'fastest-growing exit' holds only against a mid-2000s base. Since 2011, Las Vegas (+60%) and Phoenix (+36%) grew faster than Salt Lake City (+35%) and Denver (+30%). Only Utah, mainly Provo, shows a Hawaii-specific lift. Those corridors are small, about 180–360 households a year, and Salt Lake City departures have fallen since 2020–21. The IRS data stop in early 2023, so later events are not reflected. For brokers, Las Vegas is the corridor worth a standing referral partner, and base-town markets are an orders-driven, seasonal business; lead with the housing-cost gap, not taxes. For families, the cheapest destinations, Las Vegas above all, also have the most volatile job markets. (Verification note: this agent's web-search quota was exhausted. Outside facts were re-checked against saved copies of the primary sources, with fresh downloads of IRS, FRED/FHFA, Census and Zillow data files.)

research.question: Why is Hawaii's market turning toward buyers in 2026 (inventory up 5–25%, price cuts 12–17%, months of supply 6.5–9.6 on three islands) while Oahu houses stay tight (~3 months)? And why did Kauai's recorded sales fall 34% in H1 2026 while Oahu's rose 9%?
research.answer: The 2026 "turn toward buyers" is narrower than the headline numbers suggest, and much of the Kauai-versus-Oahu gap comes from how sales are counted. The market is splitting by property type as much as by island. Oahu houses are scarce: 794 were for sale in August, 27% fewer than in August 2019. That is about 3 months of supply, sellers got a median 100% of their original asking price, and median days on market was 17. Owners with cheap mortgages are not selling, and local, military and two-income buyers keep taking what comes up. Condos are oversupplied: Oahu condo listings are 34% above 2019 and Maui's are 70% above, as HOA dues, master-policy insurance and Maui's Bill 9 phase-out of vacation rentals raise the cost of owning one. Island-wide months-of-supply figures mix the two types. The new buyer's markets are really Kauai and the Big Island. Their pending sales fell 23% and 12% from a year earlier in September while new listings also fell, so listings are piling up because buyers pulled back, not because sellers rushed in. Both islands still have fewer listings than in 2019. Maui has been a buyer's market since mid-2024 and is now clearing: its months of supply is lower than a year ago (9.6 vs 11.1), and condo sales are up 21% at prices about 7% lower. Price-cut shares are about where they were a year ago. Mortgage rates explain what comes next, not the first half. Rates averaged 6.27% in H1 2026 against 6.80% in H1 2025, but the rise to 7.28% on Oct 1 has raised the payment on the same loan by 13.5% since the February low, and it is now showing up in falling pending sales. Recorded deeds include developer closings and transfers that never go through the MLS. Oahu's +9% is almost entirely The Park Ward Village tower, which closed 527 units in Q2 2026 that were pre-sold years earlier. Without it, recorded Oahu sales were about −2%, and MLS resales were flat (+0.1%). Kauai's 2025 base was inflated by a one-time batch of low-priced condo transfers in Lihue: that district fell from 170 recorded sales to 66, and Kauai's dollar volume fell only 4.5% while the count fell 34%. Comparing MLS resales only, the gap is Oahu +0.1% against Kauai −19%. Kauai's decline is real but smaller than −34%. It comes from Kauai's high prices, its heavier dependence on second-home and mainland buyers, and softer tourism. Canadian and Japanese buyers are under 3% of sales, too few to explain much.

drivers.driver: Recorded deeds vs MLS resales: one-time developer and non-MLS closings explain most of the Kauai −34% vs Oahu +9% gap
drivers.quantified_effect: Oahu: The Park Ward Village's 527 Q2 2026 closings are about 11.4 points of Oahu's +9.1%. Without them, recorded H1 sales were about 4,505, −2.3% (assumes no tower of similar size closed in H1 2025; the recorded-minus-MLS condo gap grew by 497, close to 527). Kauai: Lihue accounts for 104 of the 164 lost sales (63%). Outside Lihue, recorded sales fell 18.8%, the same as MLS resales (−18.8%). About 15 of Kauai's 34 points of decline are the one-time Lihue effect. Like-for-like MLS gap: Oahu +0.1% vs Kauai −18.8%.

counter_evidence: Kauai's underlying decline is real, not only a counting artifact: MLS resales fell 18.8% in H1 and 17.0% from January to August, and pending listings were −23% in September. The composition story explains roughly 15 of the 34 points, not all of them.

The nature of the 2025 Lihue condo transfers is not documented: 143 in ZIP 96766 at a median $62,900 against 77 MLS closings. They could be timeshare or fractional intervals, leasehold transfers or bulk deeds. If they were ordinary arm's-length sales, part of Kauai's drop would be genuine demand loss.

The Oahu ex-tower figure (−2.3%) assumes H1 2025 had no new-tower closings of similar size. Ulana closed in Nov–Dec 2025, and smaller projects may have closed in H1 2025. The growth in the recorded-minus-MLS condo gap (+497) is close to the 527 Park Ward Village closings, which supports the assumption without proving it.

The Big Island's +24.9% inventory jump rests on Realtor.com alone. No board inventory series was retrievable, and 15 of its 28 ZIPs carry quality flags. The March Kona low storms, Hurricane Lala and Tropical Storm Moke (August) may also have delayed closings and showings.

Prices are not falling broadly, which argues against a true buyer's market. Oahu house median was up 3–4% YTD (YTD medians: TG $1,173,000 +3.2%, HBR through July $1,185,000 +3%). Big Island house median YTD +0.5%. Kauai house median YTD +10.6%, a mix effect. Only Maui shows clear declines (house −5.8%, condo −8.6% YTD). The 'turn' is mostly lower volume, not price capitulation.

Oahu house 'tightness' is partly a mix effect. Sales above $1.3M nearly doubled in July (HBR), which lifted the median, and Title Guaranty's September Oahu house median was $1,100,000 (−5.2% YoY). Pending house sales were already −7.6% in August, so Oahu houses may be about to loosen.

Maui is not newly turning: its months of supply has fallen year over year (11.1 → 9.6 by the report's method; 12.1 → 11.0 by the board's), and pending sales are up. Its buyer's market dates to mid-2024 (fire aftermath and Bill 9 uncertainty since the 2024 proposal).
Kauai property-tax tiers are not a new 2026 shock: the FY2026–27 notice shows the same rates as the prior year.

The months-of-supply thresholds (under 4 favors sellers, over 6 favors buyers) are convention. Low-turnover island markets have historically sat at higher months of supply without large price declines.
research.for_brokers: Quote MLS resales and recorded sales separately, and remove developer closings before quoting year-over-year changes. Oahu's +9% is a single tower (The Park Ward Village, 527 Q2 closings). Kauai's −34% compares against a one-time batch of Lihue transfers. On a like-for-like basis it is Oahu flat and Kauai about −19%. Expect more distortion: Poipu presales on Kauai and any further Ward Village tower closings will create spikes when they close. Price Oahu houses as a seller's market (17 days on market, 100% of list price), but watch pending sales: they fell 7.6% for houses in August, and the 7.28% rate cut buyers' borrowing power by about 12% since February. Treat Oahu and Maui condos as a buyer's market. Ask for AOAO budgets, reserve studies, master-policy deductibles and lender warrantability before writing an offer, because HOA and insurance costs, not list price, now decide whether a deal works. On Maui, Minatoya-list condo owners facing the 2029/2031 deadlines are a listing source. Disclose the pending lawsuits and the Bill 88 hotel-rezoning path, and don't underwrite vacation-rental income. On Kauai and the Big Island, the problem is fewer buyers (pending sales −23% and −12%), not too many listings, so pricing to the market beats waiting. Mainland buyers fell 31% on Kauai and 16% on the Big Island in H1. Report months of supply by property type and from board data (HBR, RAM). Don't use Realtor.com for Maui listing prices (flagged every month since December 2025) or for Kauai price cuts (that field is near-empty).
research.for_locals: For Oahu families shopping for a house, there is little relief. Few houses are listed (27% fewer than in 2019), and the rate rise to 7.28% means the same monthly payment buys about 12% less house than in February. VA, first-time-buyer and down-payment programs matter more than waiting for price cuts. Condos are where buyers can negotiate on every island, but budget for the full monthly cost: the average small Oahu condo fee was $715 in April 2026, up 48% since 2019. Ask for the association's insurance deductible and any planned special assessments, which can wipe out the price discount. On Maui, condo prices are about 7–9% lower than a year ago and locals are buying more of them. Bill 9 should move more apartment-zoned units into long-term rental or resident ownership by 2029–2031, though lawsuits could delay it. Kauai and Big Island buyers have real leverage now. Sellers there should expect long marketing times (100+ days on Kauai) and price to recent sales rather than 2022 peaks. Rising unemployment (2.7% in August, from 2.2% in January) and the August storm hit to tourism are reasons to keep reserves before stretching to buy.

challenge.question: Why is Hawaii's market turning toward buyers in 2026 (inventory up 5–25%, price cuts 12–17%, months of supply 6.5–9.6 on three islands) while Oahu houses stay tight (~3 months)? And why did Kauai's recorded sales fall 34% in H1 2026 while Oahu's rose 9%?

verdicts.driver: Recorded deeds vs MLS resales: one-time developer and non-MLS closings explain most of the Kauai −34% vs Oahu +9% gap
verdicts.reason: Re-checked against Howard Hughes' Q2 2026 supplemental (8-K Exhibit 99.2, filed 2026-08-05, https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1981792/000162828026053303/hhhsupplemental2q26.htm; local copy read in full). It reports 'Number of Condo Units Closed': 527 in Q2 2026, all at The Park Ward Village, and 0 in Q2 2025. The trailing-twelve-month count to Q2 2025 was 349, which is Victoria Place, and its closings show up in Honolulu's Q4 2024 condo data, so no Ward Village tower closed in H1 2025. In DBEDT QSER/Title Guaranty data, Honolulu recorded condos went from 1,587 in Q2 2025 to 2,079 in Q2 2026. Without the tower that is 1,552 (−2.2%), and H1 total sales ex-tower are 4,505 against 4,613 (−2.3%). The recorded-minus-MLS condo gap grew from 854 to 1,351 (+497), close to 527. Kauai: the TG Kauai Q1 2026 edition (https://www.tghawaii.com/wp-content/uploads/Buyer-Stats-Kauai-Q1-2026.pdf, posted 2026-05-15) shows 51 Lihue sales in Q1 2025, so about 119 of Lihue's 170 H1 2025 sales were in Q2 2025. Those Lihue deals were cheap: Hawaii buyers there averaged about $409K in H1 2025 against $847K in 2024. Kauai recorded sales outside Lihue fell 18.8% (319 → 259). DBEDT MEI board data shows Kauai MLS sales fell 31% in Q1 2026 (126 vs 182) and 6% in Q2 (163 vs 174). The core claim holds. The type of the Lihue transfers (UHERO: 143 condo deals in ZIP 96766 at a median $62,900) is still undocumented.
fact_errors: The cited 10-Q (accession 000162828026053324) could not be verified. The 527 and 0 closing counts are confirmed in the 8-K Exhibit 99.2 supplemental filed 2026-08-05.

The Lihue excess was not spread across H1 2025: Lihue had 51 recorded sales in Q1 2025 and about 119 in Q2 2025, and it stayed above its 2024 pace in H2 2025 (110 against about 75 per half-year in 2024). Call it concentrated in Q2 2025, not strictly one-time.
Kauai's MLS decline depends on the source: −18.8% (DBEDT MEI, H1), −17.0% (MEI, Jan–Aug) or −13.9% (Title Guaranty board stats, Jan–Aug). It is a range, not a single −19%.
Title Guaranty's Oahu district totals sum to 5,026 for H1 2026, against 5,032 in DBEDT QSER (minor).
verdicts.corrected_wording: Recorded deed counts and MLS resale counts measure different things. Oahu's +9.1% recorded gain in H1 2026 includes 527 pre-sold units at The Park Ward Village that closed in Q2 2026. Howard Hughes reported zero Ward Village closings in Q2 2025. Without them, Oahu recorded sales fell about 2%, and MLS resales were flat (+0.1%: houses +3.9%, condos −2.3%). Kauai's −33.5% is measured against Q2 2025, when Lihue recorded about 80 extra low-priced condo transfers of an undocumented type. Adjusted for those, Kauai recorded sales fell about 18–21%, in line with an MLS resale decline of 14–19% depending on the source.

verdicts.driver: Two markets by property type: Oahu houses scarce (rate lock-in, local/military demand) while condos are oversupplied as ownership costs rise (HOA, insurance, Bill 9)
verdicts.reason: The DBEDT MEI board inventory series (local copy of https://files.hawaii.gov/dbedt/economic/data_reports/mei/mei-08p-2026.xlsx, released 2026-10-01) confirms the August figures. Oahu houses: 1,086 (2019) → 794 (2026), −26.9%. Oahu condos: 1,869 → 2,512, +34.4%. Maui houses: 471 → 473. Maui condos: 493 → 839, +70.2%. The HBR August 2026 release (https://www.hicentral.com/mpr/mpr-2026-08.php, 2026-09-06) confirms houses at a median 17 days on market and 100% of original list price, and condos at 37 days and 97.1%. Derived months of supply, 3.18 for houses and 6.91 for condos, recomputes. HMDA VA share in Honolulu (25.1% → 27.1%) and non-owner-occupied shares (Oahu 15.7%, Kauai 39.9%) recompute from local HMDA files. Limits: (1) The lock-in evidence (FHFA WP 24-03, −18.1% sale probability per point) is national, with no Hawaii estimate. (2) The condo-cost evidence (HPR $715 fee, +48% since 2019, 2026-06-12; SB 805 deductible findings; Act 296 signed July 2025) was checked only against search excerpts cached earlier in this session, because the web search budget was used up and hawaiipublicradio.org was blocked. It shows costs rose, not how much of the condo surplus they cause. (3) Year to date, Oahu listing flow is near normal: HBR Jan–Jul new listings were houses −2% and condos −4%, and house new listings were +14.5% in August. Oahu house inventory averaged 8% below 2025 year to date.
fact_errors: The Realtor.com comparison of new listings, September 2019 vs 2026 (Oahu 1,120 → 884), uses a 2019 Realtor.com series with clear Hawaii data problems (Honolulu pending listings averaged about 6 a month in 2019). Use board data (DBEDT/HBR) for comparisons with 2019.
The condo-cost figures (HPR $715 fee, SB 805 deductible findings) are reported or legislative findings. They do not quantify how much of the condo oversupply they cause.
verdicts.corrected_wording: Oahu and Maui have split by property type. Oahu house listings are 27% below August 2019 (794 vs 1,086), houses have about 3.2 months of supply, and they sell in a median 17 days at 100% of asking. Oahu condo listings are 34% above 2019 (about 6.9 months of supply), and Maui condo listings are 70% above, while Maui house listings are flat. Higher HOA dues, master-policy insurance and deductibles, and on Maui the vacation-rental phase-out, plausibly weigh on condos, but the data does not separate their effects. Low house turnover is consistent with rate lock-in (a national FHFA estimate) and steady local and military demand (VA loans were 27% of Honolulu purchase loans in 2025).

verdicts.driver: Demand-led slowdown on Kauai and the Big Island: fewer buyers (mainland and local), while sellers also list less
verdicts.reason: The September Realtor.com figures check out (local copy of https://econdata.s3-us-west-2.amazonaws.com/Reports/Core/RDC_Inventory_Core_Metrics_County_History.csv, data through 2026-09). Pending: Kauai 68 vs 88, Big Island 259 vs 293. Active: Kauai 385 (+8.1%), Big Island 1,365 (+24.9%). The year-to-date picture is weaker and different. Jan–Sep 2026 average active listings were Kauai +1% and Big Island +10%. New listings were Kauai −9.5% and Big Island −9.7%. Average pending were Kauai −15% and Big Island −6%. Kauai's MLS drop was front-loaded and concentrated in condos. Q1 2026 fell 31%, when Freddie Mac rates averaged 6.05–6.18%. Q2 fell 6%. House sales April–August were 161 against 159 (flat), while condos fell 26.6% Jan–Aug (DBEDT MEI). Big Island MLS sales fell only 3% Jan–Aug (houses −2.8%, condos −3.9%). Its turn is a summer listing build-up, measured by Realtor.com only, plus weak September closings (Title Guaranty Residential Sales Report Sep 2026: houses −21.5%, condos −34.7%). Mainland buyer declines check out (DBEDT QSER: Kauai 157 → 109, Big Island 619 → 523). The HMDA drop on Kauai, −40% from 2019 to 2025, recomputes.
fact_errors: 'Listings are piling up because buyers pulled back' fits September, not the year. Kauai's average active listings Jan–Sep 2026 were only 1% above 2025, and new listings fell 9.5%, so supply and demand both shrank.
Big Island MLS sales fell only 3% Jan–Aug 2026. The big drops are in recorded deeds (−8.9% in H1) and in September closings.
'Active listings still 5% and 12% below September 2019' depends on Realtor.com's 2019 Hawaii data, which has known quality problems. Treat it as indicative only.
verdicts.corrected_wording: On Kauai, sales fell because fewer buyers came, but the drop is concentrated in condos (MLS −26% Jan–Aug) and in Q1 2026 (−31%), when mortgage rates were at their lowest of the year. Kauai house sales have been flat since April, and sellers are also listing less (new listings −9.5% Jan–Sep). On the Big Island, MLS sales were nearly flat through August (−3%). The turn is recent: listings rose through the summer (+25% YoY in September per Realtor.com) and closings fell in September. Mainland buyers declined on both islands (Kauai −31%, Big Island −16% in H1 recorded sales).

verdicts.driver: Mortgage rate path: lower in H1 2026 than 2025, then sharply higher to 7.28% on Oct 1; drives late-2026 cooling but not H1 sales
verdicts.reason: The local FRED-derived series, together with the Freddie Mac PMMS weekly file (https://www.freddiemac.com/pmms, through the week of 2026-10-01), confirms the rate figures. H1 average: 6.27% in 2026 vs 6.80% in 2025. February 2026: 6.05%. September 2026 average: 6.86%. Week of Oct 1: 7.28% (7.03% the week before, 6.34% a year earlier). The 10-year Treasury monthly mean was 4.13% in February, 4.99% in September and 5.28% for the partial month of October, so the mortgage spread barely moved (about 1.92 to 2.00 points). The payment math recomputes: P&I on an $880K loan went from $5,303 to $6,021 (+13.5%), and the same payment now carries 11.9% less loan. The same loan's payment was 5.4% lower in H1 2026 than in H1 2025. Further support: Kauai's worst quarter, Q1 2026, came at the rate low. The late-2026 hit is visible. September pending sales fell YoY on Oahu (−10%), Kauai (−23%) and the Big Island (−12%). September closings (Title Guaranty RSR) fell 50% for Kauai houses and 21.5% for Big Island houses. Rates are a statewide shock, though: Maui pending sales rose 12% and Oahu house closings rose 8.8% in September. So rates set the timing, and local factors set the size of the effect.
fact_errors: The October 10-year Treasury figure (5.28%) is a partial-month average through about Oct 7. The 7.28% mortgage rate is a single weekly reading.
Correct as stated otherwise.
verdicts.corrected_wording: Mortgage rates explain the timing of the late-2026 turn, not the first-half sales numbers. Rates averaged 6.27% in H1 2026 against 6.80% in H1 2025, and Kauai's sharpest drop (Q1 2026) came at the year's low. Since February (6.05%) rates have risen to 7.28% (week of Oct 1), raising the payment on the same loan 13.5%. The rise came from Treasury yields, not a wider mortgage spread. Pending sales then fell on Oahu, Kauai and the Big Island, and September closings dropped sharply on Kauai and the Big Island. Maui pending sales and Oahu house closings kept rising, so rates set the timing but local conditions decide how hard each market is hit.

verdicts.driver: Maui Bill 9 explains Maui's condo glut and price reset, but in 2026 Maui is clearing, not newly turning
verdicts.reason: The RAM September 2026 indicators check out (REALTORS Association of Maui Monthly Indicators, current as of 2026-10-01, local copy). Condo months of supply is 12.1 (15.2 a year earlier). Condo closed sales YTD are 620 vs 512 (+21.1%), the condo median is −6.8%, and condo pending YTD is +22.4%. The Bill 9 signing on Dec 15, 2025 and the Jan 1, 2029 and Jan 1, 2031 deadlines are corroborated by several cached search results (Maui Now 2025-12-15, Civil Beat, HPR 2025-12-16), but direct fetches were blocked. 'Explains the glut' overstates Bill 9's role. Maui's August condo listings (DBEDT) went 198 (2023) → 757 (2024) → 870 (2025) → 839 (2026), so the jump came in 2024, after the Lahaina fire and the May 2024 proposal, well before passage. In June 2026 Maui passed Bill 88, now Ordinance 6008, creating H-3/H-4 hotel districts (Maui Now 2026-06-22). Pending resolutions 26-110 and 26-111 could move about 2,056 units (council vote, July 2026; Maui Now 2026-07-28) or 3,823 units (county staff report, Sep 2026, https://www.mauicounty.gov/DocumentCenter/View/164369/092226-Agenda-Item-A1_RESO-26-110_RESO-26-111_Change-Zoning-into-H-3-or-H-4_1Staff-Report) into hotel zoning. Lawsuits are pending (Malter v. Maui County, filed 2025-12-19). That reprieve may help explain Maui's 2026 condo buying rebound. Maui's Realtor.com data is quality-flagged every month since December 2025.
fact_errors: Bill 9 did not start the condo glut: Maui condo listings had already jumped from 198 (Aug 2023) to 757 (Aug 2024), before the bill passed in December 2025.
Omitted: Bill 88/Ordinance 6008 (June 2026) created hotel districts that could keep roughly 2,000–3,800 of the affected units as vacation rentals, softening Bill 9.
The Maui condo median YTD decline is −6.8% (RAM, September) or −8.6% (Title Guaranty board stats, August), depending on source.
verdicts.corrected_wording: Maui's condo glut began in 2024, after the Lahaina fire and when the vacation-rental phase-out was first proposed, and Bill 9 (signed Dec 15, 2025; deadlines 2029/2031) sustains it. In 2026, Maui is clearing rather than newly turning. Condo months of supply is 12.1, down from 15.2. Condo closings are up 21% at a median 6.8% lower, and condo pending sales are up 22% YTD. The June 2026 hotel-zoning law (Bill 88) and pending lawsuits may let thousands of units keep renting to visitors, which makes Bill 9's final effect uncertain.

verdicts.driver: Tourism softness, mainly on Kauai and mostly after H1 (August storms)
verdicts.reason: DBEDT MEI county workbook sums (local series, released 2026-10-01) confirm the Jan–Aug changes. Statewide arrivals +1.7%, international −3.2%. Kauai arrivals +0.9%, Kauai international −13.7%, Kauai spending −2.0%. Oahu spending +6.3%. Big Island spending −0.8%. For H1 alone, Kauai arrivals were +2.8% and spending −0.8%, which rules out tourism as the cause of Kauai's first-half sales drop. August arrivals were −5.6% (DBEDT/HTA release; −5.8% in MEI sums). The storm dates, Hurricane Lala Aug 14–16 and Tropical Storm Moke Aug 22–24, are corroborated by cached excerpts of DBEDT's August 2026 release. New and reported: WestJet is dropping the Vancouver–Lihue nonstop from Dec 7, 2026, citing weak demand (Daily Hive/Beat of Hawaii via cached search, 2026). That is a future headwind, not a 2026 driver. The rating stays 'weak'.
fact_errors: H1 2026 statewide air arrivals were +2.2% (HTA, 4.94M), but DBEDT MEI county sums give +3.2%. Name the source when quoting.
verdicts.corrected_wording: Tourism explains little. In H1 2026, Kauai visitor arrivals were up 2.8% and spending was down 0.8%, so tourism did not cause Kauai's first-half sales drop. Softness came later: August arrivals fell about 5.6% statewide (Hurricane Lala Aug 14–16, Tropical Storm Moke Aug 22–24), Kauai international arrivals were −13.7% Jan–Aug, and WestJet is dropping Kauai's only Canada nonstop from December 2026 (reported). That weighs on the outlook more than on 2026 sales.

verdicts.driver: Canadian and Japanese buyer demand: opposite directions, too small to drive island markets
verdicts.reason: Title Guaranty Buyer Statistics (Q2 2025, Q1 2026 and Q2 2026 editions; https://www.tghawaii.com/wp-content/uploads/Buyer-Stats-Oahu-Q2-2026.pdf, posted 2026-08-31) confirm the counts. Foreign buyers 168 → 220, Japan 91 → 138, Canada 49 → 26, Korea 8 → 37. The conclusion that these buyers are too few to matter survives, but the interpretation needs fixing. Canada's whole decline was on Oahu (31 → 8). Canadian purchases on the other islands held at 18 → 18, so Canada explains none of the neighbor-island weakness. Japan's gain is concentrated in Q2 2026: statewide Japanese purchases were 34 in Q1 and about 104 in Q2. Foreign buyers in the Honolulu district rose from 116 to 181. Both line up with the 527 Park Ward Village closings, which suggests presales signed years earlier rather than new 2026 demand. That is an inference, since Title Guaranty does not identify projects.
fact_errors: Japan's +47 should not be read as rising 2026 Japanese demand: about 70% of Japan's 138 H1 purchases came in Q2 2026, when The Park Ward Village closed, which suggests years-old presales.
Foreign totals differ by source: 168 → 220 (Title Guaranty) vs 175 → 224 (DBEDT QSER).
verdicts.corrected_wording: Foreign buyers are too few to move island markets (about 3% of H1 2026 recorded sales). Canada's drop (49 → 26) was entirely on Oahu. Canadian purchases on the other islands held at 18, so Canada explains none of the neighbor-island slowdown. Japan's rise (91 → 138) came mostly in Q2 2026 in Honolulu, the quarter The Park Ward Village closed, so it likely reflects old presales rather than new demand.

verdicts.driver: Data quirks change the size of the headline numbers (Realtor.com quality flags, months-of-supply definitions, recorded vs MLS universes)
verdicts.reason: Checked in the local Realtor.com county file. quality_flag is 1 for Maui every month from December 2025 to September 2026, and for Hawaii County from November 2025 to January 2026 (also June 2025). Kauai price-reduced listings were 24 of 385 in September (4.8%) against 84 of 414 in August (15.2%). Maui months of supply is 9.6 by the report's method but 11.0 by RAM for all properties including land (houses 7.8, condos 12.1). Realtor.com counted 3,494 Oahu active listings in August against HBR's 3,306 houses and condos (+188). Maui recorded H1 2026 sales were 643 against 759 MLS sales. Title Guaranty's Oahu September 2026 condo count (−55.5% YoY) is distorted by a September 2025 base that included Ulana closings. More quirks: Realtor.com's 2019 Hawaii series is unreliable (Honolulu pending listings averaged about 6 a month in 2019), and Big Island new listings show a one-month spike of 640 in June 2025 against about 300 normally. DBEDT MEI and Title Guaranty board stats also disagree on Kauai's YTD decline (−17.0% vs −13.9%).
fact_errors: Kauai's September price-cut count is 24 of 385 listings at the county level. The '16 of 386' figure is a ZIP-level sum.
Hawaii County was also quality-flagged in June 2025.
verdicts.corrected_wording: Several headline numbers depend on the data source. Maui's Realtor.com data has been quality-flagged every month since December 2025, and Maui's months of supply is 9.6 by the report's method but 11.0 by the Maui board's (houses 7.8, condos 12.1). Kauai's 4.8% September price-cut share is an artifact (24 reduced of 385, against 15.2% in August). Realtor.com's 2019 Hawaii series is unreliable, so use board inventory for comparisons with 2019. Recorded-deed and MLS counts differ: Maui recorded 643 sales in H1 2026 against 759 MLS sales, and new-tower closings inflate or deflate Oahu's recorded year-over-year changes.

missing_drivers: Developer closing calendar as a recurring distortion: Howard Hughes' trailing-twelve-month count to Q2 2026 (1,223 units) minus the 527 Park Ward Village units means about 696 units closed from Q3 2025 to Q1 2026. That matches Ulana, the 696-unit workforce tower. Oahu's H2 2026 recorded sales will therefore look weak against an inflated H2 2025 base. Future Ward Village towers (Kalae and The Launiu 2028; Melia and 'Ilima 2030) will cause new spikes (HHH 8-K Ex. 99.2, 2026-08-05).

Price-tier split: high-end cash and mainland buyers held up while the rate-sensitive middle fell. Kauai recorded dollars fell only 4.5% while the count fell 33.5%. Kauai mainland buyers' average price rose from $1.61M to $2.55M (DBEDT QSER). Kauai's YTD house median is +10.6%, and Oahu house sales above $1.3M nearly doubled in July (HBR). Rising medians partly reflect this mix, not broad strength.

Maui Bill 88 / Ordinance 6008 (June 2026) created hotel districts, and pending resolutions could move about 2,056–3,823 apartment-zoned units into hotel zoning. That partial reprieve from Bill 9 may support Maui's 2026 condo rebound (Maui Now 2026-06-22 and 2026-07-28; Maui County staff report, Sep 2026).

Act 96 'Green Fee': the state transient accommodations tax rose 0.75 points to 11% on Jan 1, 2026, plus up to 3% county surcharge. It is a small added cost on vacation-rental condos statewide (reported, cached search results).

Kauai condo-specific weakness with an unexplained cause: Kauai condo MLS sales fell 26.6% Jan–Aug against −9.6% for houses, and Kauai pending sales were already about 20% below the prior year in December 2025–February 2026, when rates were at their lows.

Labor-market softening: Hawaii unemployment rose from 2.2% (Jan) to 2.7% (Aug 2026) (BLS LAUS, seasonally adjusted). Hawaii weekly initial jobless claims averaged about 2,000 in September 2026 against about 960 a year earlier (DOL series in local data; preliminary, cause not identified, verify before publishing).

Big Island inventory measurement: active listings rose 25% while new listings fell about 10% YTD and MLS sales fell only 3%. That implies fewer withdrawals, longer marketing times or a Realtor.com coverage change. No board inventory series was available to confirm it.
WestJet's cancellation of the Vancouver–Lihue nonstop from Dec 7, 2026 (reported) is a forward-looking headwind for Kauai's Canadian travel and second-home demand.
challenge.final_answer: Hawaii's 2026 'turn toward buyers' is real but narrower and later than the headline numbers suggest, and most of the Kauai-versus-Oahu sales gap comes from how sales are counted. Recorded deeds include developer closings that never go through the MLS. Oahu's +9% recorded gain in the first half came from The Park Ward Village tower, which closed 527 pre-sold units in Q2 2026. Howard Hughes reported zero Ward Village closings a year earlier. Without the tower, Oahu recorded sales fell about 2%, and MLS resales were flat. Kauai's −34% is measured against Q2 2025, when Lihue recorded about 80 unusually cheap condo transfers (median about $63,000) that no source explains. Adjusted for those, Kauai's drop is about 18–21%, close to its MLS resale decline of 14–19% depending on the source. That decline is real, but it is mostly condos (−26%), and it came in the first quarter, when mortgage rates were at their 2026 low. Kauai house sales have been flat since April. The cause of Kauai's condo weakness is not clear from the data. Mortgage rates explain the late-2026 turn instead. They rose from about 6.05% in February to 7.28% on Oct 1, which raises the payment on the same loan 13.5%. Since then, pending sales have fallen on Oahu, Kauai and the Big Island, and September closings dropped sharply on Kauai and the Big Island. Most of the inventory and price-cut figures in the question are September snapshots. Averaged over 2026, listings are flat on Oahu and Kauai and up about 10% on Maui and the Big Island. Oahu houses remain a seller's market, with about 3 months of supply, 17 days on market and 100% of asking. House listings are 27% below 2019, and local and military buyers keep buying. Condos are the oversupplied segment on Oahu (listings 34% above 2019) and Maui (70% above). Rising HOA dues and insurance costs fit that pattern, but they have not been measured directly. Maui has been a buyer's market since 2024, after the fire and the first vacation-rental phase-out proposal, and is now clearing: condo sales are up 21% at about 7% lower prices. Bill 9's long-run effect is uncertain because the June 2026 hotel-zoning law and lawsuits may exempt thousands of units. Tourism softness and Canadian buyers explain little. The jump in Japanese buyers coincides with the Ward Village closings and likely reflects old presales, not new demand. For brokers: quote MLS and recorded numbers separately, strip out developer closings, and use board data rather than Realtor.com for Maui. For local families: Oahu house buyers get little relief from rising rates. Condo and neighbor-island buyers have leverage, but HOA fees, insurance deductibles and special assessments can cancel out a price discount. Confidence: high on the counting explanation, medium on the causes behind it. This check relied on local primary files and search results cached earlier in this session, because new web searches were exhausted and several sites were blocked.

research.question: Why are off-island ownership shares highest in Waikiki (28%), Kahuku/Turtle Bay (26%), Hauula (19%) and the North Shore (17%) on Oahu, and why is Hawaii luxury concentrated on the Kohala Coast, Wailea/Kapalua and Kahala?
research.answer: On Oʻahu, homes owned from off-island are not concentrated where homes cost the most. They are concentrated where zoning and building type let a distant owner rent a unit to visitors, or keep a small managed condo for their own visits. Across 27 Oʻahu ZIPs, the share of residential parcels with an off-island owner rises almost point for point with the share of housing run as vacation rentals (r = 0.91). Median house price has essentially no relationship with it (r = 0.07). Each of the four hotspots is a small pocket of that kind of stock inside an otherwise local ZIP. In Waikīkī, hotel-and-resort-class condo units are 55% off-island owned, against 8% for its houses. In Kahuku, the Kuilima/Turtle Bay plat (94% condo units, in Oʻahu's Kuilima resort area) is 48% off-island, while the Kahuku town plats are 2–5%. In Hauʻula, one Punaluʻu condo plat is 44% off-island, against 13% for houses there; Koʻolauloa also has unusually many Utah owners, which points to Latter-day Saint and BYU–Hawaii ties rather than resort demand. On the North Shore, the high share comes from homes assessed at $3M or more (34%) and from condos (24%), not ordinary houses (12–16%). Neighbor-island luxury clusters for a related reason. The Kona-Kohala coast, Kāʻanapali/Kapalua and Wailea are master-planned resort and club communities built since 1964–75 on dry leeward coastland. They offer golf, beaches, zoning that allows vacation rentals, and new construction. Brokerage maps put 86% of Hawaiʻi Island's 2025 house sales at $3M+ in South Kohala and North Kona, and 82% of Maui's in West and South Maui. The buyers are mostly from the mainland and mostly pay cash. Kahala is the counter-example. It is Honolulu's older luxury neighborhood of large lots and oceanfront estates around Waiʻalae Country Club. Short-term rentals are effectively illegal there and only about 6% of homes are owned off-island; the buyer pool is local up to roughly $10M and becomes global only above that. Measured by asking price per square foot at the ZIP level, Hawaiʻi's resort areas cost about half what Aspen, Newport Coast or Montecito cost. That helps sales to buyers with West Coast home equity. These are associations from tax-roll and sales data. Vacation-rental counts are partly a result of off-island buying, not only a cause.

drivers.driver: Places where short-term rentals are legal or grandfathered (resort zoning, hotel-and-resort tax class, Kuilima/Turtle Bay, condos allowed to keep renting): off-island owners cluster where a unit can earn visitor income

counter_evidence: Cause and effect run both ways. Vacation-rental counts partly measure what off-island owners do, not only what zoning allows. Hauula (13% of housing) and the North Shore (10%) mostly lie outside resort zones, so their rentals are grandfathered, 30-day-plus, or illegal. Resort zoning explains Waikiki and Kuilima, not those two.

A mailing address is not a residence. Timeshare and hotel operators inflate Waikiki: 585 parcels are mailed to LA ZIP 90017 and 269 to Orlando ZIP 32835. In Kahuku, 88 of 363 off-island parcels go to three ZIPs (Portland 97232, Scottsdale 85261, Las Vegas 89109). Excluding those, Kahuku's all-class off-island share falls from about 33% to about 27% and Waikiki's from 34% to about 32%. In the other direction, local managers and trust addresses can hide owners who live off-island.

Some 'mainland' owners are former residents keeping family homes, or military families who moved away. Ko'olauloa's Utah concentration (Laie 44%, Hauula 14% of off-island owners) points to Latter-day Saint and BYU–Hawaii ties rather than resort demand.

Within the hotspots, price is not the driver. Waikiki's off-island share is highest in units assessed under $1M (36%), and Hauula's mainland buyers paid a lower median ($439K) than local buyers ($800K). The North Shore is the exception: $3M+ homes there are 34% off-island against 12% under $1M.

The named luxury places are shorthand for a wider resort-enclave pattern. In 2025 North Kona (Kuki'o, Hualalai, Kohanaiki) had 31 of Hawaii Island's $3M+ house sales against 17 in South Kohala. Ka'anapali (16) outsold Kapalua (11). Kauai's Poipu/Kuki'ula (32) and Princeville/Kilauea fit the same pattern.

Climate is not decisive. Kapalua (about 28 in of rain) is wetter than Ka'anapali (about 23 in), yet it is a luxury hub. Its 2025 water dispute and the canceled Sentry show that amenities depend on water rights. Kahala's appeal does not rest on resort amenities at all.

The per-square-foot comparison mixes asking with sold prices, medians with averages, and ZIPs that blend condos and houses. Hawaii Island's $3M+ houses ($2,267/sq ft average, H1 2026) are priced close to Montecito's asking median, so 'cheaper than the mainland' holds for broad ZIPs, not trophy estates. Insurance, association dues, the new TVU tax tiers and travel costs offset the gap.

Samples are small: 945 residential parcels in Kahuku; 27 Kahuku sales in 2025 in UHERO; Oahu $10M+ buyer origin n=14. Hawaii Life's $10M+ counts are company-reported and internally inconsistent (Hawaii Island 2025: 17 in the text vs 23 in the chart). The Oahu submarket split comes from map bubbles.

Policy is moving. Maui Bill 9 phases out apartment-zoned rentals (2029/2031) while hotel rezoning votes are pending; Honolulu's TVU tax class applies from July 2027; Act 17 (2024) lets counties phase out rentals. Lahaina's post-fire market distorts West Maui. Today's pattern may shift.
Kahala's low off-island share may understate how global its trophy tier is. 62% of Oahu's non-owner-occupied $10M+ homes are entity-held, and an entity's mailing address can be a local agent.
research.for_brokers: Off-island owners sit in particular plats and buildings, not across whole neighborhoods. Prospect using the tax roll: Waikiki hotel-and-resort-class buildings, Kuilima/Turtle Bay plat 5-7-001, Punalu'u condos, $3M+ North Shore oceanfront, and Kawela-area agricultural estates. Kahuku town, Laie houses and Kahala houses are 90–95%+ locally owned, so a mainland-buyer pitch there misreads the market. Check rental legality unit by unit before pricing it into a listing: resort zone or grandfathered status, city registration, whether the federal injunction against the 90-day rule covers the unit, and the building's house rules. Honolulu's new TVU tax class (tiers at $900K and $2M) starts July 2027. On Maui, price hotel- and resort-zoned condos (outside Bill 9) separately from A-1/A-2 condos facing the 2029 (West Maui) and 2031 phase-out, and track the pending H-3/H-4 rezoning votes. These had already weighed on 2026 condo medians: Wailea/Makena -17%, Kapalua -16%. Neighbor-island luxury buyers are mostly mainland and mostly cash (about 74% of Hawaii Island $3M+ sales had no reported purchase mortgage), deals often close off-market, and buyers move on their own travel schedules (86–151 days on market). Market to the Bay Area, LA, Seattle and Portland, which are also the top visitor sources, and frame value against mainland trophy prices per square foot, with the caveats above. In Kahala, sell to local wealth through $10M; treat $10M+ as a global, entity-held tier. Do not prospect in ZIPs 96761, 96767 or 96790 while the emergency ban on unsolicited offers remains in force.
research.for_locals: The off-island ownership numbers for these ZIPs are averages that blend a resort enclave with a local town. Kahuku town, most Laie and Hau'ula houses, and Kahala/'Āina Haina remain 87–98% owned by people living in Hawai'i. Competition from off-island buyers is sharpest for the cheapest homes: older condos in Waikīkī and Punalu'u, where mainland buyers paid a median of about $439K in Hau'ula. These are often a family's first-purchase option, and mainland buyers are pricing them as rental income streams. Off-island owners rarely claim the homeowner exemption (about 6% of mainland-owned residential parcels, against 62% of local-owned), so these units mostly operate as second homes or rentals, not as housing for residents. Where the law stops visitor renting (Honolulu outside resort zones, Maui's apartment districts from 2029/2031, county phase-out powers under Act 17), off-island demand should cool and some units could return to long-term rental or to local buyers. Watch Maui's hotel-rezoning votes: rezoned buildings would keep visitor use permanently. Turtle Bay's 665-acre conservation easement caps new resort building on the North Shore. The neighbor-island luxury enclaves (the Kona-Kohala resorts, Wailea, Kapalua) are largely a separate market of mainland cash buyers. Their main effects on residents come through property-tax revenue, construction and service jobs, and water use, not direct competition for family homes.

challenge.question: Why are off-island ownership shares highest in Waikiki (28%), Kahuku/Turtle Bay (26%), Hauula (19%) and the North Shore (17%) on Oahu, and why is Hawaii luxury concentrated on the Kohala Coast, Wailea/Kapalua and Kahala?

verdicts.driver: Places where short-term rentals are legal or grandfathered (resort zoning, hotel-and-resort tax class, Kuilima/Turtle Bay, condos allowed to keep renting): off-island owners cluster where a unit can earn visitor income
verdicts.reason:
WHAT REPRODUCES (local files): I joined the Honolulu RPAD owner roll (refreshed 2026-10-05) to UHERO Factbook 2026 ZIP rows. Across 27 Oahu ZIPs: Pearson r = 0.902, Spearman 0.80, slope 0.87, and r = 0.82 without 96815 and 96731. Median house price gives r = 0.065 and household income r = -0.40. Statewide across 65 ZIPs: r = 0.79 (R2 0.63) against R2 0.04 for price. All of these reproduce.

WHY IT IS WEAKER THAN IT LOOKS: The STR variable does not measure legality. DBEDT's December 2025 Vacation Rental Performance Report (https://files.hawaii.gov/dbedt/economic/tourism/vacation-rental/hawaii-vacation-rental-performance-2025-12.pdf, fetched 2026-10-08) counts Airbnb, Booking.com, Vrbo and TripAdvisor listings supplied by Lighthouse Intelligence. It says the report 'does not determine or differentiate between units that are permitted or unpermitted.' The ZIP correlation therefore largely measures absentee-owned units marketed to visitors, which partly restates off-island ownership.
- The biggest outlier runs against the mechanism. 96814 Ala Moana/Kaka'ako is 17.4% off-island with a 1.4% STR share, 10 points above the fitted line. That ties the North Shore (17.3%).
- In 96712 only 9% of residential and hotel-class units sit in plats that are at least 30% off-island, and those plats hold 20% of the off-island-owned units. Resort zoning explains little there.

WHERE THE MECHANISM HOLDS: It is best supported at plat and class level, where zoning is fixed. My recompute from RPAD OWNDAT:
- Kuilima plat 5-7-001: 53.0% off-island (n=508, all classes), against 5.1% (n=156) and 2.4% (n=212) in Kahuku town plats 5-6-009 and 5-6-010.
- Ko Olina resort plats: 9-1-056 at 42.1% (n=1,153) and 9-1-057 at 37.7% (n=504).
- Makaha condo plats: 27-39%.
- Oahu hotel-and-resort class: 52.0% non-Hawaii, against 8.5% for the residential class.
- Maui (Parcel Fabric, 2026-10-04): the STR tax class is 84.3% non-Hawaii-mailed, against 34.2% for non-owner-occupied residential and 26.0% for the long-term-rental class.

POLICY RE-CHECKS:
- Maui Now (https://mauinow.com/2025/12/15/maui-council-passes-bill-9-5-3-on-second-and-final-reading/, 2025-12-15) confirms Bill 9 passed 5-3 and was signed. Phase-out is Jan 1, 2029 in West Maui and Jan 1, 2031 elsewhere. It does not affect 6,500 TVR parcels in hotel and resort zoning.
- Avalara (https://www.avalara.com/mylodgetax/en/blog/2024/01/judge-rules-honolulu-short-term-rentals-can-continue-operating.html, Jan 2024) confirms the April 2022 Honolulu ordinance barred 30-89-day rentals outside resort areas, a federal judge enjoined that in Oct 2022, and permits are limited to resort-zoned areas including Waikiki and Ko Olina.

NOT RE-VERIFIED: The web-search budget ran out, so I did not re-check Ordinance 25-44's TVU tax tiers, Hawaii County Bill 108 details, Maui's Sept 2026 5-4 rezoning referral, or Kuilima and Makaha appearing on the resort-zone list.
fact_errors: The vacation-rental share counts listed units whether or not they are legal (DBEDT). It is not a measure of where STRs are legal.

The Maui contrast with the owner-occupied class (3.8%) is nearly automatic, because that class requires the owner to live there. The informative contrast is the STR class at about 84% against the long-term-rental class at 26% and non-owner-occupied residential at 34%.
On current local files, Pearson r is 0.902 (not 0.905), and 0.82 (not 0.83) without Waikiki and Kahuku. The difference does not matter.
Kuilima plat share depends on the universe used: 47.5% (n=436, the researcher's set) against 53.0% (n=508, all classes, my recompute). The conclusion is the same.
The Maui Now final-passage article does not state 'about 7,000 apartment-district units'. It says 'thousands of units' and notes that 6,500 TVR parcels in hotel and resort zones are unaffected.

verdicts.driver: Climate and beaches: every luxury hub sits on a dry, sunny leeward coast; water supply is the limit on amenities

- Kilauea has the state's highest median asking price: $4.35M, $1,779/sf (Realtor.com, Sept 2026).
- On Oahu, Windward Kailua/Lanikai (38) and the North Shore (14) together had about a third of 2025 $3M+ house sales.

The Kawaihae 8.7-inch figure is a long-term average from 1995 DLNR data, not a current NOAA normal.
verdicts.corrected_wording: The Hawai'i Island and Maui resort coasts are among the driest places in the state (Kawaihae about 9 in/yr, Ka'anapali about 23, Kapalua about 28). That made them good sites for resorts and golf. Kaua'i's rainy North Shore (Princeville about 75 in/yr) shows that scenery, beaches and a resort or club community can sustain luxury demand without a dry climate.

verdicts.driver: Ko'olauloa community ties and institutional mailing addresses (an explanation unrelated to resort demand for part of Hauula's and Laie's numbers)
verdicts.reason:

- La'ie: 106 of 717 parcels mail off-island. Utah accounts for 48 (45%), including 15 mailed to ZIP 84150, the Church Office Building ZIP (churchofjesuschrist.org, cited by the researcher; not re-fetched).
- Hau'ula: Utah 37 of 257 off-island (14%).
- Kahuku: Utah 45 of 248 (18%).

No La'ie plat is at least 30% off-island, so ownership there is spread across houses, not concentrated in resort buildings.

HMDA 2025 second-home and investor share of purchase loans: Ko'olauloa 31.9% (n=94) against 15.7% for Oahu, reproduced from local hmda_tract.json.

Part of La'ie's 'off-island' share is church-related institutional ownership rather than households. The BYU-Hawai'i and Hawaii Reserves acreage was not re-verified.
