The Utah pattern also shows in Kahuku (18% of off-island owners), not only Hau'ula and La'ie.
verdicts.corrected_wording: In Ko'olauloa (La'ie, Hau'ula, Kahuku), a notable minority of off-island owners mail to Utah: 45% in La'ie and 14-18% in Hau'ula and Kahuku. Some are church-related institutions and some are likely families tied to BYU-Hawai'i. Part of the area's off-island ownership therefore reflects community ties, not resort demand.

missing_drivers: ZIP size distorts the ranking. Kahuku and Hau'ula rank high because a resort or condo enclave is large relative to a tiny ZIP. Kahuku has 948 residential and hotel units; the Kuilima plat holds about half of them and 80% of the off-island-owned ones. Ko Olina's resort plats (9-1-056 at 42.1%, n=1,153; 9-1-057 at 37.7%, n=504) and Makaha's condo plats (8-4-002 at 27.4%, n=1,350; 8-4-004 at 39.2%; 8-5-017 at 32.7%) are about as off-island-owned as Kuilima. They disappear inside ZIPs 96707 (11%) and 96792 (9.6%). Rank at plat or building level, not ZIP level.

Ala Moana-Kaka'ako (96814) is left out of the question, yet it ties the North Shore: 17.4% against 17.3% of residential parcels, and 18.6% against 15.9% of all parcels. It has almost no vacation rentals (1.4%) and Oahu's second-highest foreign share (4.9-5.1%). Mainland and Asian buyers purchase new high-rise units there as second homes and investments. Caron B (reported) says Japanese corporations bought 27.5% of Oahu luxury condos in Q4 2025 and 21.7% in Q1 2026 (n=23) (https://caronbrealty.com/oahu-luxury-real-estate-report-quarter-4-2025/, 2026-01-12). Japan holds 62% of foreign-owned Oahu parcels. The Ala Moana Hotel condo plat 2-3-038 (hotel-resort class) is 42.5% off-island and 16.8% foreign.

Foreign demand (Japan, Canada, Korea) is concentrated in urban Honolulu condos and is distinct from mainland vacation-rental investors. Among 2023-25 buyers: 96815 was 6.9% foreign with 11.4% of dollars; 96814 was 7.9% foreign with 10.5% of dollars.

Timeshare and other institutional mailing addresses inflate some shares. LA 90017 has 588 parcels mailed to 6 addresses, Orlando 32835 has 270, and NY 10022 has 255. These raise the Waikiki and Kahuku figures. In the other direction, local agents and trusts hide some off-island owners, so the shares are floors.

Land tenure and developer history. Neighbor-island resort enclaves sit where one owner held large coastal tracts of ranch or plantation land (A&B's Wailea, Maui Land & Pineapple's Kapalua, Ka'anapali), which made master planning possible. This was not quantified.

The North Shore pattern is scattered second homes and oceanfront estates, not resort plats. Only 9% of 96712's units are in plats at least 30% off-island. Recent mainland buyers paid a median $2.35M against $1.70M for Hawaii buyers (n=58, small).

Untested factors named in the question or plausible: lot size and privacy, airport proximity (Hualalai and Kuki'o near Kona airport), and insurance and association costs. No data was gathered on them in this pass, so treat them as hypotheses.
challenge.final_answer:
On O'ahu, off-island ownership is concentrated in particular buildings and plats, not whole neighborhoods. The ZIP rankings mostly reflect how big those pockets are relative to their ZIP. The clearest pockets are units run as visitor lodging. Hotel-and-resort-class condos are about 52% owned off-island across Oahu, and the Ala Moana Hotel condo is 43%. The resort-zoned enclaves follow the same pattern: Kuilima/Turtle Bay is about half off-island, against 2–5% in Kahuku town; Ko Olina is 38–42% and Mākaha 27–39%. Kahuku tops the list because Turtle Bay makes up half of a tiny ZIP. Ko Olina is nearly as off-island-owned but is hidden inside the large Kapolei–Makakilo ZIP. Hau'ula's figure comes from Punalu'u condos (44% off-island) plus Utah-linked owners. Lā'ie's comes mostly from Utah-linked owners, including church addresses, and the North Shore's from scattered high-end and condo second homes. Ala Moana–Kaka'ako ties the North Shore at 17% but is missing from the question, and it shows a second route: mainland and Japanese buyers purchase new tower units as second homes, with almost no vacation renting. Across ZIPs, off-island ownership rises with the share of homes listed for vacation rental (r ≈ 0.9) and not with price. That listing count includes illegal units and partly restates absentee ownership, so it shows the two occur together rather than proving that rental rules drive the buying.

Neighbor-island luxury is concentrated where the luxury product was built: master-planned resort and private-club communities, from Ka'anapali (1962) to Hualālai (1996) and the newer North Kona clubs. By a brokerage's map counts, they took about 86% of Hawai'i Island's and 82% of Maui's 2025 $3M+ house sales. Dry leeward weather helped site those resorts but is not required; Kaua'i's rainy North Shore is also a luxury hub. The argument that Hawai'i is cheap next to mainland trophy towns explains why buyers come to Hawai'i, not where they buy. Kahala is the exception: an older residential enclave of large lots near Wai'alae Country Club with no short-stay product, where buyers below roughly $5–10M are mostly local. Across Oahu, homes at $10M and up are mostly not owner-occupied and are often held by entities.

For brokers: prospect by building and plat (Waikiki hotel-condos, Kuilima, Ko Olina, Mākaha, Punalu'u, Kaka'ako towers) and confirm each unit's legal rental status. The ban on unsolicited offers in ZIPs 96761, 96767 and 96790 remains in the Thirty-Second Wildfire Proclamation (signed Aug 24, 2026) through Oct 23, 2026 unless extended.

For local families: most homes in these ZIPs remain 85–98% locally owned, including Kahuku town, Lā'ie and Hau'ula houses, and Kahala. Direct competition is sharpest for older condos in Waikīkī and Punalu'u; in Hau'ula, mainland buyers paid a median of about $439K.

Confidence: medium on the Oahu pattern, where plat-level data is strong but cause and effect is uncertain. Medium-low on why luxury sits where it does, since that rests on company-reported, small counts.

Verification note: the web-search budget ran out partway through. Re-checks used direct downloads of the cited primary sources plus the local data files. A few policy details (Honolulu Ordinance 25-44, Act 17, Maui's September 2026 rezoning vote) were not re-verified.
